title: Session 13 · Final Project Presentations
text:
Your complete project — R script, dataset, written report — was due via Canvas before midnight Sunday. No late submissions, no appeals. Presentations happen in class today.
Thirteen sessions ago the course opened with a statistical model you couldn’t read; today you present one you built. Everything the semester practiced converges here: a real criminal-justice question, data you cleaned yourself, a model fit and interpreted honestly, and — the part that matters most — saying what it all means in plain language. The written project is already in; today is about standing behind it.

title: Session 13 · Final Project Presentations
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this session you can:

deliver an 8-minute, evidence-backed presentation of your project: question, data, methods, results, and what they mean
answer questions about every line of your code — how it works and why you wrote it that way
interpret your findings for a non-statistician, limitations included, without overclaiming

title: Session 13 · Final Project Presentations
text:
Format

8 minutes + 2 minutes of questions, in the order announced at Session 12. At 8 minutes you’ll be stopped so everyone presents — practice once with a timer
Slides or your rendered report on screen — either works, but you must show your one key visualization
You will walk through your code and explain how and why it works. Being unable to confidently explain your own code will affect your grade — this is the point of the AI policy
Questions from the class and from me
The presentation is 8% of your course grade; the full grading criteria are in the presentation spec

title: Session 13 · Final Project Presentations
text:
What makes a good presentation

Lead with the question, not the code
One clear visualization beats three cluttered ones
Interpret in plain language: what would you tell a police chief, a judge, or a journalist?
Own your limitations — every real analysis has them, and naming them is a strength

Thank you for a great semester. 🎓

title: Session 11 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
📽️ Slides: Multiple Linear Regression · 🧪 Lab 11: Multiple Regression — Chicago’s 77 Areas, Then 500 Neighborhoods · 📝 Homework 11 + Project Checkpoint 3 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 10’s correlation said that two variables travel together; regression answers the sharper question — how much the outcome changes per unit of a predictor, and with several predictors, how much each matters after accounting for the others. Least squares gets built from scratch on ten students’ study hours, then scaled up to the interactive 3D plane through Chicago’s 77 community areas, where you watch shared variance get reassigned as a second predictor enters. The humility rules ride along: adjusted associations still aren’t causal effects, and area-level patterns still aren’t people-level claims. Checkpoint 3 fits the first regression on your own project data — and if your outcome is a yes/no, Session 12 hands you the right tool.

title: Session 11 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

fit and interpret lm() with several predictors, reading each coefficient as “holding the others constant”
explain R² — and what happens to a coefficient when a correlated predictor joins the model
run the basic diagnostics: a residuals-vs-fitted plot read honestly, and VIF for multicollinearity
fit the Bayesian version with brm() and report a coefficient with the credible-interval sentence
state what a regression coefficient does — and doesn’t — license you to claim

title: Session 11 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Before class

Read: Stanton Ch. 8 (Linear Multiple Regression)
Install one new package before class: install.packages("car") — we use it for multicollinearity checks (VIF). (brms you already have from ANOVA week; bayesplot rode along with it. The usual reminder applies: the first brm() of a session pauses at “Compiling Stan program…” — that’s normal.)
Bring your laptop and your final-project dataset — Homework 11 contains Checkpoint 3, the first regression model on your own data

title: Session 11 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
In class

From Session 10’s correlation to today’s sharper question: not do two variables move together, but how much does the outcome change per unit of a predictor — holding the others constant
Least squares from scratch: three candidate lines through ten students’ study hours and exam scores, a sum-of-squared-residuals ruler to judge them, and lm() finding the one line no other line beats — then the animated best-fit search, and R² (which, with one predictor, is exactly Session 10’s r, squared)
Two predictors = a plane in 3D — the interactive plotly plane you can grab and spin in the browser, regenerated live from code, plus the recorded guided tour
Why “holding constant” earns its keep: ice cream sales “significantly predict” drownings until temperature enters the model and the association evaporates — and an added-variable plot to see the partialing happen
Real-data thread: violent-crime rates across Chicago’s 77 community areas — unemployment alone (slope ~3.3, R² ≈ .71), then vacancy added (unemployment’s slope drops to ~2.1, R² ≈ .82: shared variance reassigned before your eyes), a third predictor that doesn’t earn its keep, and a units lesson (a −0.0006 coefficient that’s actually ~6 fewer violent crimes per 1,000 residents per $10,000 of income)
Diagnostics: the residuals-vs-fitted plot read honestly (ours fans out at high fitted values — we say so), and VIF for multicollinearity
The Bayesian version: same formula in brm(), posterior distributions for each coefficient visualized with bayesplot, and the credible-interval sentence the confidence interval never allowed — plus model reporting sentences in both traditions
Standing warnings, now attached to coefficients: adjusted associations are not causal effects, and area-level associations are not people-level claims (the ecological fallacy rides along)
Lab 11: the full workflow yourself — Chicago start to finish, then your own model on the Lab 3 neighborhoods (including the residual plot’s tell that a count outcome is starting to strain the linear model)

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces today’s live demos step by step.

title: Session 9 · Midterm Exam

In-class, monitored exam. You write and troubleshoot real R code. Printed notes and homework allowed — no internet, no AI tools.
The first half of the course is complete: describing data, probability, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing in both traditions, ANOVA — plus the whole wrangling thread from ggplot2 through joins. The midterm asks you to show you can use it: an .R script you complete in class, code and interpretation together, drawn only from things we’ve already done. Nothing on it is new; the preparation is re-running your own work until it feels routine.

title: Session 5 · Confidence Intervals on Real Data
text:
📽️ Slides: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals · 🧪 Lab 5: Importing Real Data · 📝 Homework 5 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 4 showed that sample statistics fluctuate in predictable ways; this week cashes that in. If we know how estimates behave, we can attach an honest statement of uncertainty to a single sample’s number — a confidence interval. The hard part isn’t computing the interval (R does that); it’s saying what it means out loud without lying, and reporting size along with direction — detectable ≠ dramatic. That habit is your vaccination for Session 6, where “significant” enters the vocabulary.

explain what a 95% confidence interval does — and does not — mean

What statistical inference is: inductive reasoning under uncertainty (you can’t prove anything from a sample)
John Snow and the Broad Street pump — the founding example of inference from sampled evidence, rebuilt live in R

Confidence intervals: prop.test() and t.test(), the “100 samples, 100 intervals” simulation, and what a 95% CI does and does not mean
Real-data thread: the citywide arrest proportion from one modest sample vs. the truth; do violent crimes happen later in the day than property crimes? (detectable ≠ dramatic)
Lab 5: importing real data — read_csv() from the web, read_excel() on a messy download, col_types, mdy(), problems(), and how to ask for help

title: Session 3 · Reasoning with Probability
text:
📽️ Slides: Reasoning with Probability · 🧪 Lab 3: Data Transformation with dplyr · 📝 Homework 3 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 2 taught you to describe what data are; this week asks what data are likely to be — the first step toward inference. Probability gets taught the course’s way: don’t take a claim on faith, simulate it and watch it happen. Along the way you plant the seed the whole second half of the course grows from — conditional probability, and Bayes’ theorem for reversing it — harvested in Session 6, when the two great traditions of inference meet on the same question. In lab, dplyr hands you the verbs every later analysis will use.

title: Session 1 · Intro & R Setup

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
This Week
Topic: logistic regression — modeling outcomes that are yes or no

Why lm() breaks when the outcome is 0/1
Odds, log-odds, and the odds ratio — the currency of logistic regression
glm(family = binomial), predicted probabilities, and the Bayesian version with brms

Learning goals: fit a logistic regression in both traditions; translate coefficients into odds ratios and predicted probabilities; say the results in plain language without confusing odds with probability.
Also today: the course pays off a promise it made in Session 1.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 10: correlation — how two continuous variables move together
Session 11: multiple regression — a plane through a 3D cloud of points, minimizing squared error, each coefficient’s effect holding the others constant (and lurking variables like the ice-cream/drowning lurker handled by putting them in the model)
Every model so far predicted a number: a crime rate, an incident hour, a chick’s weight
Today: what happens when the outcome only has two values — arrest or no arrest, reoffend or desist, hit again or not?

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: Criminal Justice Runs on Binary Outcomes
text:
Criminal Justice Runs on Binary Outcomes

Was an arrest made?
Does the defendant fail to appear?
Is the parolee re-arrested within three years?
Did the crash involve an intoxicated driver?
Is this neighborhood a high-violence area?


Linear regression predicts continuous outcomes (crime rates, response times). Logistic regression predicts binary outcomes — its currency is probability (0 to 1), expressed along the way as odds and log-odds.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Session 1 Made You a Promise
Remember the opening case study? 40 bank robberies, five zones, one question: where will they hit next?

We built future_hit = 1 if the same zone was hit again within 10 days, 0 otherwise
We fit a model, showed you a coefficient table nobody could read yet, and sent the patrol cars to the West Zone — where the robber was caught
That slide said: “Don’t worry about the machinery today — logistic regression is Session 12.”


Today is Session 12. Let’s reopen the machinery.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Machinery, Reopened
The exact model from Session 1 — one function, one family argument:

robbery_model <- glm(
  future_hit ~ 0 + scale(day_of_year) + prior_robberies_in_zone + zone,
  data = robberies, family = binomial
)


glm() = generalized linear model — regression’s family business
family = binomial is the switch that makes it logistic: predict a 0/1 outcome
Everything else looks exactly like the lm() formulas from Session 11



Two formula details you can safely skim: 0 + drops the global intercept so each zone gets its own baseline, and scale() puts day-of-year on a standard scale. Read the table, not the formula — today is about the family switch.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Reading It With Today’s Eyes

The estimate column is in log-odds — that’s why it looked like gibberish in August; by the end of today it won’t
exp(estimate) turns each one into an odds ratio — West’s is by far the largest, which is why West had the highest predicted probability of a repeat hit. That’s why the cars went west.
Those −17.5s with standard errors in the thousands? North and South never saw a repeat hit within 10 days — with zero events, the model can’t estimate their log-odds. 39 robberies is small data, and the output says so honestly.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: Logistic vs. Linear: The Road and the Hill
text:
Logistic vs. Linear: The Road and the Hill
Linear regression is a straight road — it keeps going forever in both directions. Logistic regression is a curved hill that flattens at 0 and 1, because probabilities can’t go below 0 or above 1.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Watch Linear Regression Fail
Predicting graduated the academy (yes/no) from study hours:

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
What Went Wrong

The linear model happily predicts values like 1.2 and −0.3 — probabilities that cannot exist
Inside the middle of the data the two lines nearly agree; the damage is at the edges — exactly where predictions get used (“what about a recruit who studies a lot?”)
The fix is the logit transformation: instead of modeling the probability directly, model something built from it that a straight line can live on
(The full derivation is Ph.D.-stats material — what you need is the ladder on the next slides)

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Model You Already Know
\[Y = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2 + \varepsilon\]

\(Y\): outcome (dependent variable)
\(b_0\): intercept (value of \(Y\) when all X’s are zero)
\(b_1, b_2\): slope coefficients (effect of each X, holding the others constant)
\(\varepsilon\): error term (what’s left unexplained)


The right-hand side is an unbounded straight line. Probability is trapped in [0, 1]. Something has to give.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Step 1 — Probability to Odds
Suppose 3 out of 4 parolees complete supervision: \(p = 0.75\).
\[\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3 \quad \text{("three to one")}\]



Probability

Log-odds

Step 2 — odds to log-odds: odds run 0 to ∞; log-odds run −∞ to +∞. That’s a scale a straight line can live on.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Logistic Model
Just treat logit(\(p\)) — the log-odds — as your Y. Then…
\[\text{logit}(p) = \ln\!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2\]

Same intercept, same slopes, same “holding the others constant”
The line now predicts log-odds, which convert back to a probability that politely stays between 0 and 1 — the curved hill








But the coefficients are log-odds!!! Nobody thinks in log-odds. So what do we do with them?

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: What Do We Do With Log-Odds?
text:
What Do We Do With Log-Odds?


EXPONENTIATE!


exp(coefficient) = the odds ratio: multiply the odds of the outcome by this much for each one-unit increase in X, holding the other predictors constant.

Positive log-odds → ratio above 1 → odds grow.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Two Traditions, Same Curve








Approach
What it estimates
Interpretation




Frequentist
Point estimates and confidence intervals
“If we repeated this 100 times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true β.”


Bayesian
Posterior distributions for each β
“Given our data and priors, there’s a 95% probability β lies in this range.”



Exactly the split you know from Sessions 6 and 8 — nothing new, just a new model underneath it.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Frequentist Version
Toy data first — 32 cars from a 1974 Motor Trend issue, predicting manual transmission (1) vs. automatic (0) from horsepower and weight. Small enough to check every number; real CJ data in a few minutes.

data(mtcars)
cars_df <- mtcars |>
  rownames_to_column("car") |>
  mutate(am = as.factor(am))   # 0 = automatic, 1 = manual

model_freq <- glm(am ~ hp + wt, data = cars_df, family = binomial)
summary(model_freq)

The Frequentist Version


Call:
glm(formula = am ~ hp + wt, family = binomial, data = cars_df)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) 18.86630    7.44356   2.535  0.01126 * 
hp           0.03626    0.01773   2.044  0.04091 * 
wt          -8.08348    3.06868  -2.634  0.00843 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

Residual deviance: 10.059  on 29  degrees of freedom

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Reading the Output: Exponentiate

exp(coef(model_freq))

         (Intercept)                   hp                   wt 
156145483.5063244998         1.0369208455         0.0003085967 



hp: log-odds 0.036 → odds ratio 1.037 — each additional horsepower multiplies the odds of a manual transmission by about 1.04 (+3.7%), holding weight constant
wt: log-odds −8.08 → odds ratio 0.0003 — each additional 1,000 lbs cuts the odds by ~99.97%, holding horsepower constant
Wildly different sizes partly because the units differ: one horsepower is a nudge; a thousand pounds is a different car

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
From Effects to Cases: predict()
Odds ratios describe effects. For an actual case, ask for the probability directly:

two_cars <- cars_df |>
  filter(car %in% c("Honda Civic", "Cadillac Fleetwood")) |>
  select(car, hp, wt)

two_cars |>
  mutate(p_manual = predict(model_freq, newdata = two_cars, type = "response"))

                 car  hp    wt         p_manual
1 Cadillac Fleetwood 205 5.250 0.00000009787752
2        Honda Civic  52 1.615 0.99954591741880



type = "response" returns probabilities: the light Civic is a near-certain manual (99.95%); the 5,250-lb Fleetwood, near-certain automatic. Report both: odds ratios for effects, predicted probabilities for cases.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Session 11’s Plane, Bent

Last session: two predictors + linear regression = a flat plane floating through the 3D cloud
Same two predictors + logistic regression = a curved sheet: a plateau near probability 1, a floor near 0, and an S-shaped cliff between them
The surface is the model: its height at any (hp, wt) combination is the predicted probability of a manual transmission there
Let’s build it from nothing but predict()

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Building the Surface
Ask the model for a prediction at every combination of horsepower and weight — a 40 × 40 grid, 1,600 predictions:

hp_seq <- seq(min(cars_df$hp), max(cars_df$hp), length.out = 40)
wt_seq <- seq(min(cars_df$wt), max(cars_df$wt), length.out = 40)
grid   <- expand.grid(hp = hp_seq, wt = wt_seq)

grid$prob <- predict(model_freq, newdata = grid, type = "response")

# Reshape the 1,600 predictions into a grid; t() puts rows on the
# wt (y) axis and columns on the hp (x) axis, which is what plotly expects
z_matrix <- t(matrix(grid$prob, nrow = length(hp_seq), ncol = length(wt_seq)))

The observed cars sit at height 0 (automatic) or 1 (manual); the surface passes between them.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The 3D Logistic Surface

data_points <- cars_df |>
  mutate(prob = as.numeric(as.character(am)))   # 0 = auto, 1 = manual

plot_ly(width = 950, height = 520) |>
  add_markers(data = data_points,
              x = ~hp, y = ~wt, z = ~prob,
              color = ~am, colors = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),
              symbol = I("circle"), size = I(50),
              name = "Observed Data") |>
  add_surface(x = hp_seq, y = wt_seq, z = z_matrix,
              colorscale = list(c(0, 'lightblue'), c(1, 'firebrick')),
              opacity = 0.6,
              name = "Predicted Probability Surface") |>
  layout(
    title = "Logistic Regression: Curved Probability Surface",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "Horsepower (hp)"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Weight (1000 lbs)"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Probability (Manual Transmission)")
    )
  )

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Same Formula, Bayesian Machinery

model_bayes <- brm(am ~ hp + wt, data = cars_df,
                   family = bernoulli(),
                   chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


family = bernoulli() is brms’s name for a 0/1 outcome — the switch that family = binomial flips in glm()
Everything else is the Session 8 pattern: chains = 2, iter = 2000, the compile pause, refresh = 0 to silence the log
The prior: none stated → brms defaults again. Your project’s model will use these too — say so in your methods: “brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705”
Instead of one estimate per coefficient, we get a full posterior distribution for each log-odds coefficient

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Posterior Odds Ratios
Exponentiate the posterior summaries — dropping the intercept row, whose posterior is astronomically wide with only 32 cars:

exp(fixef(model_bayes)[-1, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])

        Estimate               Q2.5       Q97.5
hp 1.05233926370 1.0168277428244001 1.120707968
wt 0.00001855298 0.0000000008757284 0.006666486



Same story as glm(): horsepower nudges the odds of a manual up; weight crushes them
The payoff is the sentence you’re allowed to say: “Given the data and priors, there’s a 95% probability the true odds ratio lies in this interval” — and with 32 cars, those honest intervals are huge. Watch them tighten on real data next.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Question
What separates Chicago’s high-violence community areas from the rest?

areas |> count(high_violence)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  high_violence     n
  <lgl>         <int>
1 FALSE            39
2 TRUE             38



high_violence ships in the file (it’s in the codebook): is the area’s violent-crime rate above the citywide median? 38 above, 39 at or below.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Making a Binary Outcome
The line that built it:
areas |> mutate(high_violence = violent_rate > median(violent_rate))

R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, so a logical column drops straight into glm()
If your project outcome isn’t binary yet, it may be one mutate() away too
One caution: cutting a continuous variable in half throws away information — defensible when the yes/no version is the question you actually care about

Look First (Always)
One predictor at a time before the model — unemployment against the outcome, with the fitted logistic curve:

Unemployment: OR 1.45 [1.19, 1.85] — each additional point of unemployment multiplies an area’s odds of high-violence status by ~1.45 (+45%), holding vacancy constant

The Bayesian Version, Real Data

exp(fixef(v_bayes)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])

Intercept         0.001792006 0.00007756542 0.02117534
unemployment_rate 1.492292997 1.21912215721 1.92093080
pct_vacant        1.366238869 1.03527533301 1.87703700



Both traditions land in the same place: posterior odds ratios near the glm() estimates, credible intervals excluding 1. With 77 areas instead of 32 cars, the intervals are usably tight.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
How to Report It: Frequentist

“Each one-point increase in the unemployment rate was associated with 45% higher odds of being a high-violence area (OR = 1.45, 95% CI [1.19, 1.85]), holding vacancy constant. Predicted probabilities ranged from about 3% for the least-disadvantaged areas to over 99% for the most.”


The effect (as an odds ratio), the uncertainty, and a probability a reader can feel — all three, every time.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
How to Report It: Bayesian

“Given the data and priors, each one-point increase in unemployment multiplied the odds of high-violence status by about 1.5 (posterior mean OR 1.49, 95% credible interval [1.22, 1.92]).”


Same three ingredients — and this one gets to make a direct probability statement about the odds ratio itself.

section: Your Turn (3 minutes, with a neighbor)
text:
Your Turn (3 minutes, with a neighbor)

A reentry study models re-arrest within 12 months and reports two log-odds coefficients: risk score (per point): 0.7 · completed programming: −0.5

Convert both to odds ratios (Rosetta Stone, or exp() in R)
Say each in a sentence a police chief would understand
Audit your neighbor: did they say odds — or slip into probability?

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
This Week
Topic: measuring how two numeric variables move together

Association vs. causation (and the lurking third variable)
Covariance → Pearson’s r: one number for direction and strength
What r cannot see — and why you always plot first
Inference on r: frequentist cor.test() and Bayesian, via the correlation package
Real data: which structural features of Chicago’s 77 areas track violence — and what that does not say about individuals

Learning goals: interpret r’s sign and size; test it in both traditions; explain the ecological fallacy in one sentence.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 6: two group means — is this mean different from that one?
Session 8: three or more group means — ANOVA
Both had the same shape: a categorical IV (the groups) and a numeric DV
Session 9: the midterm. You survived. Welcome to the second half.
Today: both variables are numeric — no groups at all. The question changes from “do groups differ?” to “do two measures move together?”
This is the doorway to regression (Sessions 11–12), where your final projects live

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
What Does Correlation Tell Us?
When two variables move together, how can we describe that relationship?

One goes up when the other goes up → positive correlation
One goes up when the other goes down → negative correlation
Changes in one don’t track changes in the other → no correlation


Direction is only half the story. The strength of the relationship tells how tightly the changes are linked — that’s the number we build today.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Which Is Which?
Positive, negative, or nothing? Make your call for each panel:

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Which Is Which? — Revealed


The lines make it obvious — and the r values put a number on what your eye already knew.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Real-World Examples

Positive: hours studied ↑, exam scores ↑
Negative: officers on shift ↑, response times ↓
Near zero: shoe size vs. GPA


Your turn: give me a CJ example of each — and one pair you suspect people believe is correlated but isn’t.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Correlation Does NOT Mean Causation

Correlation shows association, not cause and effect
Ice cream sales and violent crime rise together every year. Does ice cream cause violence???
Two variables can move together because of a third variable — summer heat drives both — or by pure coincidence
When you see a correlation, ask: does X cause Y? Y cause X? Does Z drive both? Or is it luck?
Correlation is a pattern, not proof of cause. Beware the evil lurking third variable!

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
section: Covariance: Moving Together, in Raw Units
text:
Covariance: Moving Together, in Raw Units
Observation by observation: do x and y sit on the same side of their means?
\[\text{cov}(x, y) \;=\; \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n - 1}\]

Both above average (or both below) → positive products → positive covariance; opposite sides → negative covariance
The sign is trustworthy: covariance tells you whether two variables move together
The size is not — watch what happens on real data

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
The Units Problem
Two covariances with violent crime, from our 77 Chicago community areas:

cov(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)

[1] 107.7543

cov(areas$median_income,     areas$violent_rate)

[1] -482660.1



Is −482,660 a “stronger” relationship than 108? No idea — the first number lives in dollars × crimes per 1,000, the second in percentage points × crimes per 1,000. Covariance is glued to its units. You can’t compare across pairs.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Correlation Rescales It
Divide the covariance by both standard deviations and the units cancel:
\[r \;=\; \frac{\text{cov}(x, y)}{s_x \, s_y}\]

cov(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate) /
  (sd(areas$unemployment_rate) * sd(areas$violent_rate))

[1] 0.8398579

cor(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)   # same thing, one function

[1] 0.8398579



Always between −1 and +1, unit-free, comparable: income runs r = −0.71 with violence — so unemployment (0.84) tracks violence more tightly than income does, direction aside.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Reading r: The Conventional Bands









Range of r
Strength
Direction
Example interpretation




+0.8 to +1.0
Very strong
Positive
More prior arrests → much higher recidivism score


+0.4 to +0.7
Moderate
Positive
More training hours → higher confidence


0 to +0.3
Weak
Positive
Slight upward trend


−0.3 to 0
Weak
Negative
Slight inverse trend


−0.7 to −0.4
Moderate
Negative
More absences → lower grades


−1.0 to −0.8
Very strong
Negative
More speed → less accuracy




These bands are conventions, not laws — in messy social-science data, a “moderate” r can be a major finding.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Calibrate Your Eye

By ±0.5 the trend is visible; below ±0.2 your eye mostly sees noise — and it’s right.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Anscombe’s Quartet: Four Identical Summaries

anscombe_long <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c(".value", "set"), names_pattern = "(.)(.)")

anscombe_long |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x), mean_y = mean(y), r = cor(x, y), .by = set)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  set   mean_x mean_y     r
  <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 1          9   7.50 0.816
2 2          9   7.50 0.816
3 3          9   7.5  0.816
4 4          9   7.50 0.817



Four little datasets that ship with R (Anscombe, 1973). Same means, same r = 0.82 to two decimals — statistically interchangeable. Right?

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Anscombe’s Quartet, Seen

Only Set 1 is what you picture when someone says “r = 0.82.” Always plot before you correlate.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
section: Limitation 1: r Only Sees Straight Lines
text:
Limitation 1: r Only Sees Straight Lines

Think stress vs. performance: an inverted U. r ≈ 0 means no linear relationship — not no relationship.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
section: Limitation 2: One Point Can Manufacture a Correlation
text: Limitation 2: One Point Can Manufacture a Correlation

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
What Just Happened

Twenty points of pure noise happened to give r = −0.28 — small samples produce correlations out of nothing; that’s why we’ll test, not just compute
Adding one extreme pair swung r from −0.28 to +0.42 — a single point flipped the sign and manufactured a “moderate positive” correlation
Neither number describes a real relationship
Outliers can also work the other way, hiding a real correlation
Defenses: plot first (you’d catch this instantly) — and a correlation that doesn’t care about wild values —

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
A Rank-Based Backup: Spearman’s rho
Replace each value with its rank (1st, 2nd, 3rd…), then correlate the ranks. Spearman asks only: is the relationship consistently up or consistently down?

c(pearson  = cor(outlier_data$x, outlier_data$y),
  spearman = cor(outlier_data$x, outlier_data$y, method = "spearman"))

   pearson   spearman 
 0.4235804 -0.1142857 



To Spearman, the wild point is just “rank 21”: it drifts from -0.29 to -0.11 — sign intact, still weak — while Pearson swung 0.70 and flipped sign. When data are skewed or outlier-prone, check Spearman alongside Pearson.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
From Incidents to Areas
The anchor data’s second level (codebook): all 237,472 of 2025’s incidents, aggregated to the 77 community areas and joined with Census measures:

areas |>
  select(community, violent_rate, unemployment_rate, median_income, pct_vacant) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  community   violent_rate unemployment_rate median_income pct_vacant
  <chr>              <dbl>             <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Rogers Park         21.7               7.1         60916        9.5
2 West Ridge          12.2               7.3         70823        7.7
3 Uptown              22.8               4.7         70067        9.1



A classic criminology-of-place question: which structural features of a neighborhood track its violence? Correlation is exactly the right first tool.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Look First: Unemployment and Violence

One dot = one community area. This is about as strong as area-level associations get in criminology.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
section: The Full Menu, in One Dataset
text:
The Full Menu, in One Dataset

Strong positive, moderate positive, strong negative — and one genuine nothing (median age). Real data span the whole menu.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
These Are Areas, Not People
Our r = 0.84 says: community areas with higher unemployment rates record more violent crime per 1,000 residents.






The ecological fallacy: using an aggregate-level association to make claims about individuals. Our data contain no individuals — every resident of an area gets the same 77 values. Nothing here says unemployed people commit violence.




The classic demonstration (Robinson, 1950): across U.S. states, more foreign-born residents went with higher literacy; across individuals, foreign-born residents had lower literacy. Same data, opposite signs — immigrants had settled in high-literacy states. Aggregation can weaken, exaggerate, or even flip an individual-level relationship.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Saying It Out Loud (Area-Data Edition)
✅ Defensible:

“Community areas with higher unemployment rates recorded higher violent-crime rates (r = 0.84).”

❌ Not defensible:

“Unemployed residents commit more violent crime.” (An individual-level claim — these data can’t see individuals.)


“Unemployment drives up violence.” (A causal claim — concentrated disadvantage, disinvestment, and policing patterns all lurk behind both variables.)

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
section: Income: When Pearson and Spearman Disagree
text:
Income: When Pearson and Spearman Disagree

The decline is real but bent — steep across the lower-income areas, nearly flat past ~$90k — and income is right-skewed. The rank-based Spearman (−0.82) runs stronger than Pearson (−0.71) because it only asks “downhill?”, not “straight line?”.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
From Description to Inference
We can see r = 0.84. Two honest questions remain — one per tradition:

Frequentist: if nothing truly connected these variables, how often would 77 paired observations line up this tightly by luck?
Bayesian: given the data, what range of correlation values is credible?
One wrinkle: these 77 areas are all of Chicago, not a sample from a bag of Chicagos. Read the null as a claim about the process generating neighborhood outcomes, not about a larger population of areas we sampled from.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
The Frequentist Test on r

Null hypothesis: ρ = 0 — no linear association in the process that generated the data
Test statistic: a t with n − 2 degrees of freedom — the same machinery as Sessions 6–8
Same logic as every test we’ve run: if ρ were zero, how surprising is an r like ours?


In R, one function does the whole thing — and hands you a confidence interval too.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
cor.test()

cor.test(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  areas$unemployment_rate and areas$violent_rate
t = 13.4, df = 75, p-value < 0.00000000000000022
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7585749 0.8954023
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.8398579

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Reading It Honestly

r = 0.84, t(75) = 13.4, p < .001 — a null world essentially never makes 77 paired observations line up this tightly
95% CI [0.76, 0.90] — Session 5’s reading still applies: the procedure captures the true value in 95% of replications; this particular interval either does or doesn’t
Perspective: with n = 77, any |r| above about 0.22 clears p < .05. Significance is a low bar — the strength is the story
And nothing in this output upgrades association to causation, or areas to individuals

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
The Whole Matrix at Once
Real analyses rarely stop at one pair. cor() takes every numeric column you feed it:

areas |>
  select(violent_rate, unemployment_rate, median_income, pct_vacant) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)

                  violent_rate unemployment_rate median_income pct_vacant
violent_rate              1.00              0.84         -0.71       0.81
unemployment_rate         0.84              1.00         -0.81       0.67
median_income            -0.71             -0.81          1.00      -0.55
pct_vacant                0.81              0.67         -0.55       1.00



Symmetric, 1s on the diagonal — a compact map of the association structure. But: no tests, no intervals.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Same Matrix, With Uncertainty: correlation()

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1        |        Parameter2 |     r |         95% CI |  t(75) |         p
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
violent_rate      | unemployment_rate |  0.84 | [ 0.76,  0.90] |  13.40 | < .001***
violent_rate      |     median_income | -0.71 | [-0.80, -0.57] |  -8.66 | < .001***
violent_rate      |        pct_vacant |  0.81 | [ 0.72,  0.88] |  12.00 | < .001***
unemployment_rate |     median_income | -0.81 | [-0.88, -0.72] | -12.05 | < .001***
unemployment_rate |        pct_vacant |  0.67 | [ 0.52,  0.78] |   7.78 | < .001***
median_income     |        pct_vacant | -0.55 | [-0.69, -0.37] |  -5.67 | < .001***

p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979)
Observations: 77

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Bayesian Correlation: The Idea

Instead of a single r and a p-value, you get a posterior distribution of plausible correlation values (ρ)
You can ask direct questions: given my data, what’s the probability ρ > 0?
The prior encodes mild skepticism — real-world correlations are rarely extreme — gently pulling estimates toward 0
Same package, one new argument: bayesian = TRUE
And unlike brms in Session 8, no compilation wait — this samples in a blink

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
correlation(..., bayesian = TRUE)

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: posterior sampling, keeps printed values stable
bayes_pair <- areas |>
  select(violent_rate, unemployment_rate) |>
  correlation(bayesian = TRUE)
bayes_pair

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1   |        Parameter2 |  rho |       95% CI |      pd | % in ROPE
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
violent_rate | unemployment_rate | 0.82 | [0.73, 0.87] | 100%*** |        0%

Parameter1   |         Prior |          BF
------------------------------------------
violent_rate | Beta (3 +- 3) | 6.64e+17***

Observations: 77

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Reading the Bayesian Output

rho = 0.82 — the posterior median, a touch below the frequentist 0.84: that’s the prior’s gentle pull toward zero
95% CI [0.73, 0.87] — a credible interval: given data and prior, 95% probability ρ lies in this range. The direct statement Session 5 taught you the confidence interval can’t make.
pd = 100% — the posterior probability the correlation is positive — and 0% in ROPE: none of the posterior sits in a “practically zero” band
BF ≈ 10¹⁷ — the data are astronomically more likely under “correlated” than “not.” On Session 6’s scale, anything past 100 is extreme evidence; this is 10¹⁷.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
The Posterior, Seen

The entire heap of credible values sits far from 0 (dashed line). That picture is what pd = 100% and the huge BF are summarizing.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
The Bayesian Matrix

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: posterior sampling
areas |>
  select(violent_rate, unemployment_rate, median_income, pct_vacant) |>
  correlation(bayesian = TRUE) |>
  summary()

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter         | pct_vacant | median_income | unemployment_rate
------------------------------------------------------------------
violent_rate      |    0.79*** |      -0.68*** |           0.82***
unemployment_rate |    0.64*** |      -0.79*** |                  
median_income     |   -0.52*** |               |                  



Same map as the frequentist matrix, but every entry is now a posterior median with full uncertainty machinery behind it.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
But the Priors…
The default prior is "medium" skepticism. Loosen it and see what moves:

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: posterior sampling
areas |>
  select(violent_rate, unemployment_rate) |>
  correlation(bayesian = TRUE, bayesian_prior = "wide")

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1   |        Parameter2 |  rho |       95% CI |      pd | % in ROPE
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
violent_rate | unemployment_rate | 0.83 | [0.75, 0.89] | 100%*** |        0%

Parameter1   |               Prior |          BF
------------------------------------------------
violent_rate | Beta (1.73 +- 1.73) | 2.05e+18***

Observations: 77

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
What Changed? Almost Nothing — Here

The wide prior is less skeptical of big correlations, so it shrinks rho toward 0 slightly less — the estimate creeps closer to the raw r = 0.84
With 77 areas of strongly correlated data, the data dominate: the prior choice moves the second decimal
With 15 areas and a modest correlation, the same choice could visibly move the estimate — priors matter most when data are thin
Practical rule for this course: defaults are fine — but say which prior you used. If your conclusion survives medium and wide, say that too; it’s a free robustness check.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Frequentist vs. Bayesian Correlation








Feature
Frequentist (Pearson’s r)
Bayesian (ρ)




Output
Single value, r
Posterior distribution of ρ


Uncertainty
95% confidence interval
95% credible interval


Evidence measure
p-value
Posterior probability, Bayes factor


Prior information
None
Included (by prior width)


Interpretation
“If no true correlation…”
“Given data, how probable is each value of ρ?”

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
How to Report It

Frequentist: “Across Chicago’s 77 community areas, unemployment was strongly associated with the violent-crime rate, r = .84, t(75) = 13.4, p < .001, 95% CI [.76, .90]. This is an area-level association; it does not speak to individuals.”


Bayesian: “The posterior median correlation was ρ ≈ .82, 95% credible interval [.73, .87], BF₁₀ ≈ 10¹⁷ — overwhelming evidence for a strong positive area-level association.”

Direction, strength, uncertainty, and the level of analysis — every time.

title: Associations Between Variables: Correlation
text:
Your Turn (5 Minutes)
pct_no_hs_diploma — the share of an area’s adults without a high-school diploma. Before you compute anything: write down your predicted sign and rough size of its correlation with violent_rate.
areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv")

ggplot(areas, aes(pct_no_hs_diploma, violent_rate)) + geom_point()
cor.test(areas$pct_no_hs_diploma, areas$violent_rate)

Most people predict a strong positive. The data: r = 0.17, p = .14 — indistinguishable from nothing. Yet pct_bachelors runs a solid −0.45. Plausible-sounding covariates can fail, and correlated predictors tangle — untangling them is exactly Session 11’s job.

Real Analysis Is 80% Preparation

Finding data that can actually answer your question
Importing it without silently mangling anything
Discovering what’s wrong with it (something always is)

…and then the t-test is one line of code


Every dataset in this course so far arrived clean because I cleaned it. That subsidy ends today.

text:
The Pipeline You Already Own








Step · learned in
The job
Tools




Import · Session 5
get data into R intact
read_csv(), read_excel(), col_types, mdy()

one row = one observation
pivot_longer(), pivot_wider()

You learned the first four steps in reverse order. Today you run the whole thing left to right for the first time.

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Step 1 · Import
Back to the Alaska crash data — but this time the date is handled at the door:

crashes <- read_csv(
  "https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv",
  col_types = cols(date = col_date(format = "%m/%d/%Y"))
)
# (equivalent Lab 5 habit: import, then mutate(date = mdy(date)))

sum(is.na(crashes$date))   # zero NAs = every date parsed

[1] 0


20,000 crashes, 2022–2026. Two roads to a real date column — col_types up front, or mdy() after. Either way: verify the parse.

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Step 2 · Clean & Derive
The file has no “night” or “weekend” column. Files never do — you build the variables your question needs:

crashes <- crashes |>
  mutate(
    hour    = hour(time),
    weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,   # Mon = 1 … Sat = 6, Sun = 7
    night   = hour >= 22 | hour < 4              # 10 p.m. – 3:59 a.m.
  )
crashes |> count(night)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  night     n
  <lgl> <int>
1 FALSE 14972
2 TRUE   5028


Night hours hold 25% of all crashes — but 39% of intoxication-involved ones. One mutate() made that pattern visible.

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Step 3 · Describe
The Homework 5 question, back for a verdict: do crashes involving an intoxicated driver injure more people?

crashes |>
  summarize(
    crashes  = n(),
    mean_inj = mean(injuries),
    sd_inj   = sd(injuries),
    .by = intox_any
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  intox_any crashes mean_inj sd_inj
      <dbl>   <int>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1         0   18455    0.743  0.997
2         1    1545    1.13   1.18 


0.74 vs. 1.13 injured people per crash. Point estimates — you know by now that’s not the final word.

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Step 4 · Visualize

inj_summary <- crashes |>
  mutate(intox_group = factor(intox_any, labels = c("No intox", "Intox involved"))) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_inj = mean(injuries), sd_inj = sd(injuries),
            .by = intox_group) |>
  mutate(se = sd_inj / sqrt(n),
         ci_lo = mean_inj - 1.96 * se,
         ci_hi = mean_inj + 1.96 * se)   # Session 5, by hand

ggplot(inj_summary, aes(intox_group, mean_inj)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi),
                  color = crju_colors["garnet"], linewidth = 1.2, size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Mean injuries per crash, with 95% confidence intervals",
       subtitle = "Alaska crash data, n = 20,000",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean injuries per crash")

title: Applied Data Workshop
text: Step 4 · Visualize

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Step 5a · Test It — Frequentist

t.test(injuries ~ intox_any, data = crashes)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  injuries by intox_any
t = -12.489, df = 1732.6, p-value < 0.00000000000000022
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 0 and group 1 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.4474533 -0.3259893
sample estimates:
mean in group 0 mean in group 1 
      0.7433758       1.1300971 


Same gotcha as Homework 5: R computes group 0 − group 1, so the negative signs mean the intoxication group is higher.

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Step 5b · Test It — Bayesian
BayesFactor insists the grouping variable be a factor — so we hand it one:

crashes <- crashes |>
  mutate(intox_group = factor(intox_any, labels = c("No intox", "Intox involved")))

ttestBF(formula = injuries ~ intox_group, data = crashes)

Bayes factor analysis
--------------
[1] Alt., r=0.707 : 2.133904e+43 ±0%

Against denominator:
  Null, mu1-mu2 = 0 
---
Bayes factor type: BFindepSample, JZS


BF10 ≈ 2 × 1043: the data are astronomically better predicted by “the groups differ” than by “no difference.”


Depending on your R settings, this may print as 2.06e+43 or as a 44-digit integer — same number, different formatting. Don’t panic either way.

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Two Grammars, One Verdict

Frequentist: if the true difference were zero, data like ours would essentially never occur — t(1733) = −12.5, p < .001
Bayesian: the difference model beats the no-difference model by a factor of ~1043
The estimate, in English: intoxication-involved crashes average 0.33 to 0.45 more injured people per crash (95% CI)

title: Applied Data Workshop
text:
Two Grammars, One Verdict, continued

The two frameworks agree here because the evidence is overwhelming; with small samples and borderline evidence, they can part ways — that’s when running both matters
What neither test says: why. Intoxication crashes also differ in hour, speed, and road conditions — an observational gap no test statistic closes

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
This Week
Topic: The logic of inference, using confidence intervals

What statistical inference actually is (and isn’t)
Point estimates and why they’re not enough
Confidence intervals: building them, reading them, and — hardest of all — saying what they mean out loud without lying

Learning goals: explain in your own words what a 95% confidence interval does and does not mean; compute CIs for a proportion and a difference in means from real data.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Two Threads, One Course


Statistics thread — lecture + homework
Stanton Ch. 4 → confidence intervals: building them, and saying them out loud honestly

Wrangling thread — lab
R4DS Ch. 7–8 → read_csv(), read_excel(), and the import traps real files set

The two threads meet at the Session 7 workshop — where you import a messy file and put an honest interval on what you find in it.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 3: probability — the rules randomness follows
Session 4: sampling distributions — take many samples, and the sample statistics themselves form a distribution with predictable behavior
Today: we cash that in. If we know how sample statistics behave, we can attach an honest statement of uncertainty to a single sample’s estimate.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Does “Inference” Mean?
Inference: a reasoning process that begins with some information and leads to some conclusion.
Inductive inference: reasons from specific cases to the more general — a cat jumps from a tree and lands on its feet; you infer something about cats generally.
Statistical inference: dealing systematically with situations where we have uncertain or incomplete information. Conclusions drawn inductively from samples are never fixed or firm.







You cannot PROVE anything from samples or by using statistical inference.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: If We Can’t Prove Anything, What Are We Doing?
text:
If We Can’t Prove Anything, What Are We Doing?
We collect data and analyze it with inferential statistics to build up a weight of evidence that influences our certainty about one conclusion or another.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Let’s Look at the Classic Example
text:
Let’s Look at the Classic Example

1854 — cholera breaks out in Soho, London
The debate: bad air (“miasma”) or contaminated water?
John Snow couldn’t test every household in London — that’s the whole population
So he mapped the sample of evidence he could get: deaths, and where people got their water

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sampled Evidence: Deaths and Pumps

# A tibble: 12 × 2
     pid deaths_nearest
   <int>          <int>
 1     7            359
 2    10             64
 3     6             61
 4     9             27
 5     4             24
 6     8             16
 7     3             12
 8     5              6
 9    13              4
10    11              2
11    12              2
12     2              1

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text: Sampled Evidence: The Map

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Sampled Evidence: Broad Street Accumulates Deaths Fastest
text: Sampled Evidence: Broad Street Accumulates Deaths Fastest

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Why This Is Statistical Inference

Why wasn’t Snow just describing the map?
What bigger claim was he making about the whole city — and about cholera itself?

That jump — from the data you have to the world you don’t — is what we mean by inference.

Review from previous weeks — why do we sample?
We almost never have access to the totality of the population data. At its best, a sample is representative of a population.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: A Rare Luxury: We Know the Truth
text:
A Rare Luxury: We Know the Truth
Our Chicago file holds ~30,000 incidents from 2025. Today, pretend the file is the whole population — then we can check our inferences against the truth.

crimes |> summarize(pop_arrest_rate = mean(arrest), n = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  pop_arrest_rate     n
            <dbl> <int>
1           0.161 30000


The “true” citywide arrest proportion is 16.1%. Lock that in — in real research you never get to see this number.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Now Act Like a Researcher: Draw One Sample
text:
Now Act Like a Researcher: Draw One Sample
A researcher can rarely afford all 30,000 case files. Suppose we pull a random sample of 250 incidents:

sample_250 <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250)

sample_250 |> summarize(sample_arrest_rate = mean(arrest))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  sample_arrest_rate
               <dbl>
1              0.148



This is a point estimate — the sample’s best single guess at the population value.
14.8% vs the true 16.1%. Close-ish. But how good is this estimate? How certain are we?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Caution! Samples Fluctuate
Draw a fresh sample of 250 and the estimate moves. Do it 1,000 times:

many_estimates <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) {
  crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250) |> summarize(p = mean(arrest)) |> pull(p)
})

ggplot(tibble(p = many_estimates), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crimes$arrest),
             color = crju_colors["garnet"], linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample estimates of the arrest rate (n = 250 each)",
       subtitle = "Garnet line = the true population value",
       x = "Sample arrest proportion", y = "Number of samples")

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text: Caution! Samples Fluctuate

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
What the Fluctuation Tells Us

quantile(many_estimates, c(0.025, 0.975))   # what is this telling us?

 2.5% 97.5% 
0.120 0.208 



95% of sample estimates landed between about 12% and 21% — that’s the sampling distribution from Session 4, live
Any single sample’s estimate could easily be a couple points off the truth
So reporting “14.8%” alone is overconfident — we owe our reader a range that reflects the fluctuation
Problem: this required 1,000 samples and a known population. A real researcher has one sample. Now what?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Our First Inferential Tool
The confidence interval turns one sample into an honest range, using what Session 4 taught us about how sample statistics behave:
\[\text{estimate} \; \pm \; \underbrace{1.96 \times SE}_{\text{margin of error}}\]

SE (standard error) = the standard deviation of the sampling distribution, estimated from the one sample you have
1.96 comes from the normal distribution: ±1.96 SDs covers the middle 95%

Bigger samples → smaller SE → narrower interval.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: R Does This For Us: prop.test()
text:
R Does This For Us: prop.test()

prop.test(sum(sample_250$arrest), n = 250)


    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  sum(sample_250$arrest) out of 250, null probability 0.5
X-squared = 122.5, df = 1, p-value < 0.00000000000000022
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1075899 0.1995409
sample estimates:
    p 
0.148 



Our one sample of 250 says: point estimate 14.8%, 95% CI 10.8% to 20.0%. The true value (16.1%) is inside — this time. But “95% confident” of what, exactly?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text: The Classic Picture, Seen

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Just Happened

Each of the 100 samples produced a different interval — the interval is a random quantity, the population value is fixed
97 of our 100 intervals captured the true arrest rate; 3 missed (the garnet ones)
In the long run, the 95% procedure captures the truth in ~95% of replications — that long-run capture rate is the entire meaning of “95% confident”
The researchers who drew the garnet samples did nothing wrong — and their data give no warning that theirs are the unlucky intervals

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
In Practice
If we reran our whole study many times — drawing a new sample each time and constructing a new confidence interval each time — in 95% of those replications the interval would contain the true population value.






IMPORTANT:

Our 95% CI does not necessarily contain the true population value
Our 95% CI is not a statement about the probability that this particular interval is correct
It is a long-run prediction based on numerous replications





WTF?!? — yes, everyone reacts this way. Point at the 100-intervals plot until it clicks.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Saying It Out Loud
✅ Defensible:

“We estimate the citywide arrest rate at 14.8% (95% CI: 10.8% to 20.0%). Values in this range are consistent with our data.”


“The method we used captures the true value 95% of the time.”

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Saying It Out Loud: What Not to Say
text:
Saying It Out Loud: What Not to Say
❌ Not defensible:

“There is a 95% probability the true arrest rate is between 10.8% and 20.0%.” (The truth is fixed — it’s either in there or it isn’t.)


“95% of arrest rates fall in this interval.” (The CI is about the population parameter, not individual observations.)

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: The Sentence You Wanted to Say
text:
The Sentence You Wanted to Say

“There’s a 95% probability the truth is in this interval” is forbidden only under frequentist rules: probability attaches to the procedure, never to the parameter
Attaching probability to a claim itself is exactly what Session 3’s Bayes’ theorem does — and the license costs a stated prior
Next week we compute an interval you can say that sentence about: the credible interval
If the forbidden sentence felt like the natural reading all along — your intuitions were Bayesian. You’re in good company

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Buys Precision
Same procedure, three sample sizes, one draw each:

map(c(100, 250, 1000, 4000), \(n) {
  s  <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = n)
  ci <- prop.test(sum(s$arrest), n = n)$conf.int
  tibble(n = n, estimate = mean(s$arrest),
         lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2], width = ci[2] - ci[1])
}) |>
  list_rbind()



# A tibble: 4 × 5
      n estimate    lo    hi  width
  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   100    0.22  0.146 0.316 0.170 
2   250    0.192 0.146 0.247 0.101 
3  1000    0.154 0.132 0.178 0.0457
4  4000    0.163 0.152 0.175 0.0231



Quadrupling n roughly halves the width — precision grows with \(\sqrt{n}\), so it gets expensive fast.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: A Real Question: Do Violent Crimes Happen Later in the Day?
text:
A Real Question: Do Violent Crimes Happen Later in the Day?
Street lore says violence is a nighttime phenomenon. Property crime, the daytime hustle. Our data:

vp <- crimes |> filter(crime_category %in% c("Violent", "Property"))

vp |> summarize(mean_hour = mean(hour), sd_hour = sd(hour),
                n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  crime_category mean_hour sd_hour     n
  <chr>              <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1 Violent             12.8    6.87  9148
2 Property            12.5    6.63 10371



Two point estimates: violent crimes average hour 12.8, property 12.5. Is that ~15-minute gap real, or sample fluctuation?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Let’s Look at It Visually

ggplot(vp, aes(crime_category, hour, fill = crime_category)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(crju_colors[c("blue", "garnet")])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Hour of day (0–23)")


The boxes nearly coincide — the eye can’t settle this one. We need inference.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Resample the Difference
Same trick as before — resample each group, compute the difference in means, repeat:

violent_hours  <- vp$hour[vp$crime_category == "Violent"]
property_hours <- vp$hour[vp$crime_category == "Property"]

mean_diffs <- replicate(1000, {
  mean(sample(violent_hours,  length(violent_hours),  replace = TRUE)) -
  mean(sample(property_hours, length(property_hours), replace = TRUE))
})

quantile(mean_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975))   # what is this telling us?

      2.5%      97.5% 
0.05568685 0.43652029

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text: Resample the Difference, Seen

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: The Two-Sample t-Test Gives the CI Directly
text:
The Two-Sample t-Test Gives the CI Directly

t.test(hour ~ crime_category, data = vp)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by crime_category
t = -2.6061, df = 19021, p-value = 0.009164
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Property and group Violent is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.44272107 -0.06263688
sample estimates:
mean in group Property  mean in group Violent 
              12.54334               12.79602 


Watch the direction: R orders groups alphabetically, so this tests Property − Violent — the mirror image of our resampled Violent − Property differences. Same finding, flipped sign.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Reading That Output Honestly

t.test(hour ~ crime_category, data = vp)$conf.int

[1] -0.44272107 -0.06263688
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95



The 95% CI for the difference (Property − Violent) runs from −0.44 to −0.06 hours — it excludes zero, so the data are consistent with violent crimes genuinely averaging later
But look at the magnitude: the difference is somewhere between about 4 and 27 minutes. Detectable ≠ dramatic.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Reading That Output Honestly, Continued

With ~19,500 incidents, we can detect tiny differences. The CI hands you both facts at once: direction (probably real) and size (small). Never report the first without the second.
This is your vaccination against next week’s topic — a “significant” result can be substantively trivial

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Probability = Long-Run Proportion
Claim: a fair coin lands heads with probability 0.5. Don’t trust me — flip some coins:

flips <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE)
flips

 [1] "heads" "heads" "heads" "tails" "tails" "tails" "heads" "tails" "heads"
[10] "heads"

mean(flips == "heads")

[1] 0.6




# six more batches of ten flips each:
replicate(6, mean(sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE) == "heads"))

[1] 0.6 0.1 0.5 0.6 0.6 0.7


Ten flips is not the long run — batches of 10 bounce around, and none is entitled to land exactly on 0.5.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Our Simulation Verbs, In Words
You just met the two verbs that power every simulation this semester:

sample() — run one random event (flip the coins, drop the toast)
replicate(k, expr) — repeat the whole recipe k times and collect the answers
One run = a trial; many runs = the long run
Later today, rbinom() compresses “flip six coins and count the heads” into a single call



A plain-language reference for all the course’s simulation verbs lives on the Resources page.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
The Long Run, Seen

lln <- tibble(flip = sample(c(1, 0), size = 100000, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(n_flips = row_number(),
         running_prop = cummean(flip))

ggplot(lln, aes(n_flips, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of flips (log scale)", y = "Running proportion of heads")


Wobbly early, pinned to 0.5 eventually. A probability is the value the long-run proportion settles on. Every probability “fact” today gets this treatment.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Real Stakes: P(Arrest) in Chicago
Our anchor data: 30,000 real Chicago incidents from 2025. Each incident either ended in an arrest or didn’t — 30,000 recorded trials.

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608


Pick a 2025 incident at random and the probability it ended in arrest is about 0.16 — arrest is the exception, not the rule.
(arrest is TRUE/FALSE; mean() of a logical is the proportion of TRUEs. You’ll use this trick constantly.)

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: The Long Run Works on Real Data Too
text:
The Long Run Works on Real Data Too
Read case files one at a time, tracking the running arrest proportion:

running <- tibble(arrest = sample(crimes$arrest, size = 5000)) |>
  mutate(n_cases = row_number(),
         running_prop = cummean(arrest))

ggplot(running, aes(n_cases, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Case files read (log scale)", y = "Running proportion arrested")


The first few dozen cases can wander far from 0.16. Thousands pin it down. Small samples lie; long runs don’t.

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: A Reality Show About Dropped Toast
text:
A Reality Show About Dropped Toast
Imagine a restaurant where the waiters always drop the food. Each order = six pieces of toast; each piece lands topping-down or topping-up.

One piece of toast falling = one event
One dropped order of six = one trial

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
The Toast Data: 100 Dropped Orders
Here’s data from 100 trials:

toast <- tibble(
  jelly_down = 0:6,
  trials     = c(4, 9, 20, 34, 21, 11, 1)
)
toast

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  jelly_down trials
       <int>  <dbl>
1          0      4
2          1      9
3          2     20
4          3     34
5          4     21
6          5     11
7          6      1

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Proportions ≈ Probabilities

toast |> mutate(prob = trials / sum(trials))

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  jelly_down trials  prob
       <int>  <dbl> <dbl>
1          0      4  0.04
2          1      9  0.09
3          2     20  0.2 
4          3     34  0.34
5          4     21  0.21
6          5     11  0.11
7          6      1  0.01



Rule #1: probabilities across all outcomes sum to 1:

toast |> summarize(total_prob = sum(trials / sum(trials)))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  total_prob
       <dbl>
1          1

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Simulate Your Own Toast Drops

drops <- rbinom(n = 100, size = 6, prob = 0.5)
# rbinom() generates random trials of the "binomial distribution"
# n = 100 gives the number of trials
# size = 6 asks for six pieces of toast in each trial
# prob = 0.5 says there's an even (50:50) chance of jelly-down or jelly-up

tibble(jelly_down = drops) |> count(jelly_down)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  jelly_down     n
       <int> <int>
1          0     1
2          1     8
3          2    23
4          3    32
5          4    22
6          5    13
7          6     1


Compare to the reality-show table — same shape, without filming a single waiter.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Run It Again — It Changes

two_runs <- tibble(
  run = rep(c("Run 1", "Run 2"), each = 100),
  jelly_down = c(rbinom(100, size = 6, prob = 0.5),
                 rbinom(100, size = 6, prob = 0.5))
)
ggplot(two_runs, aes(jelly_down)) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  facet_wrap(~run) +
  labs(x = "Jelly-down count (out of 6)", y = "Trials")


Same process, different picture — sampling variability. 100 trials is still a shortish run. Try running it yourself!

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Cumulative Probabilities
“What’s the probability of 3 or fewer jelly-down?” Add up the outcomes as you go:

cum_toast <- tibble(jelly_down = rbinom(n = 100000, size = 6, prob = 0.5)) |>
  count(jelly_down) |>
  mutate(prob = n / sum(n),
         cum_prob = cumsum(prob))
ggplot(cum_toast, aes(jelly_down, cum_prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  labs(x = "Jelly-down count", y = "P(this count or fewer)")


Each bar = probability of that count or fewer. The last bar is always 1 — rule #1 again.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Linked Outcomes
Now each falling piece of toast has two classifications: how it lands (down/up) and its topping (jelly/butter). Ten dropped pieces:

toast10 <- tribble(
  ~topping, ~landed, ~n,
  "Jelly",  "Down",  2,
  "Jelly",  "Up",    1,
  "Butter", "Down",  3,
  "Butter", "Up",    4
)
toast10 |> pivot_wider(names_from = landed, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  topping  Down    Up
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Jelly       2     1
2 Butter      3     4


A contingency table: rows = one classification, columns = the other, cells = counts of events with both.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Marginal Totals Answer Questions

Total toast-drop events? How many landed down? Up?
More likely to land down or up?
Which topping is more common, butter or jelly?


toast10 |> summarize(n = sum(n), .by = landed)    # column margins


The row/column sums live in the margins of the table — hence marginal probabilities.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Marginal Totals Answer Questions

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  landed     n
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 Down       5
2 Up         5

toast10 |> summarize(n = sum(n), .by = topping)   # row margins

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  topping     n
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 Jelly       3
2 Butter      7

sum(toast10$n)                                    # grand total

[1] 10

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: Super Challenge: Does the Topping Matter?
text:
Super Challenge: Does the Topping Matter?
Jelly landed down 2/3 of the time (0.67); butter 3/7 (0.43). Is jelly really doomed — or is 10 pieces of toast just a short run? Simulate a world where topping makes no difference:

sim_gap <- function() {
  p_jelly  <- rbinom(1, size = 3, prob = 0.5) / 3   # 3 jelly pieces, fair
  p_butter <- rbinom(1, size = 7, prob = 0.5) / 7   # 7 butter pieces, fair
  abs(p_jelly - p_butter)
}
gaps <- replicate(10000, sim_gap())
mean(gaps >= 2/3 - 3/7)   # how often does pure chance produce our gap?

[1] 0.611

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Super Challenge: The Verdict
Even with no real difference, chance alone produces a gap at least this big well over half the time. Ten drops can’t answer the question.
(This simulate-a-boring-world move is the seed of hypothesis testing — coming in Session 6.)

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
A Real Contingency Table
Same structure, real stakes — crime category × arrest, 30,000 Chicago incidents:

crimes |>
  count(crime_category, arrest) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arrest, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category `FALSE` `TRUE`
  <chr>            <int>  <int>
1 Other             7867   2614
2 Property          9615    756
3 Violent           7694   1454


count() gets the cell counts; pivot_wider() lays them out as the table. This is today’s lab skill set doing probability work.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Joint Probabilities, For Real
Joint — divide every cell by the grand total:

crimes |>
  count(crime_category, arrest) |>
  mutate(p = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  crime_category arrest     n      p
  <chr>          <lgl>  <int>  <dbl>
1 Other          FALSE   7867 0.262 
2 Other          TRUE    2614 0.0871
3 Property       FALSE   9615 0.320 
4 Property       TRUE     756 0.0252
5 Violent        FALSE   7694 0.256 
6 Violent        TRUE    1454 0.0485


P(Property and arrest) ≈ 0.025 — a joint probability.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Marginal Probabilities, For Real
Marginal — collapse one classification:

crimes |> count(crime_category) |> mutate(p = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category     n     p
  <chr>          <int> <dbl>
1 Other          10481 0.349
2 Property       10371 0.346
3 Violent         9148 0.305


P(Property) ≈ 0.35 — a marginal probability, next to the joint P(Property and arrest) ≈ 0.025 from the last slide.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
The Restaurant Work Schedule
Back at the toast restaurant — hours worked by four servers:

hours <- tribble(
  ~day,        ~Anne, ~Bill, ~Calvin, ~Devon,
  "Monday",        6,     0,       5,      8,
  "Tuesday",       0,     6,       6,      0,
  "Wednesday",     8,     5,       0,      8,
  "Thursday",      4,     6,       5,      8,
  "Friday",        8,     8,       5,      8,
  "Saturday",      8,    10,       8,      8,
  "Sunday",        0,     3,       6,      0
)
hours_long <- hours |> pivot_longer(-day, names_to = "server", values_to = "hours")

Two interesting questions:

You sit down and Bill is your server. What day is it most likely to be?
You know it’s Monday. Who is most likely to be your server?

text:
Converting to Proportions
Every cell divided by the grand total (147 hours) — the joint probabilities:

hours_long |>
  mutate(p = hours / sum(hours)) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = day, names_from = server, values_from = p)

# A tibble: 7 × 5

1 Monday    0.0408 0      0.0340 0.0544
2 Tuesday   0      0.0408 0.0408 0

5 Friday    0.0544 0.0544 0.0340 0.0544
