title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Question 2: It’s Monday — Who’s Serving?
Same move, conditioning the other way:

hours_long |>
  filter(day == "Monday") |>
  mutate(p_server_given_monday = hours / sum(hours))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  day    server hours p_server_given_monday
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl>                 <dbl>
1 Monday Anne       6                 0.316
2 Monday Bill       0                 0    
3 Monday Calvin     5                 0.263
4 Monday Devon      8                 0.421


Devon (0.42). Note the asymmetry: P(Saturday | Bill) and P(Bill | Saturday) are different questions with different answers. The direction of conditioning matters — a lot. Bayes’ theorem, in a few minutes, is the formula for flipping it.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Conditioning = filter(), Then Proportion
In real data, conditional probability is just subset, then take the mean:

crimes |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category p_arrest     n
  <chr>             <dbl> <int>
1 Violent          0.159   9148
2 Other            0.249  10481
3 Property         0.0729 10371


P(arrest | Property) ≈ 0.07; P(arrest | Other) ≈ 0.25. Knowing the crime category changes the arrest probability — the two variables are dependent.

title: Reasoning with Probability
Reasoning with Probability
text:
When Conditioning Changes Nothing: Independence

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608

crimes |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = domestic)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  domestic p_arrest     n
  <lgl>       <dbl> <int>
1 FALSE       0.161 24194
2 TRUE        0.160  5806


P(arrest | domestic) and P(arrest | not domestic) are essentially identical to the overall P(arrest) — in this sample, knowing an incident was domestic tells you almost nothing about arrest.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Independence, Defined
Definition: A and B are independent when P(A | B) = P(A). Conditioning that moves the number = dependence; conditioning that doesn’t = independence.

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: The Question We Keep Almost Asking
text:
The Question We Keep Almost Asking

The restaurant taught us direction matters: P(Saturday | Bill) ≠ P(Bill | Saturday)
The narcotics trap was the same lesson with teeth: P(arrest | narcotics) ≈ .97 is not P(narcotics | arrest)
Real life keeps handing you one conditional — test accuracy, match rates, hit rates — and asking you for the other one
There is a formula for flipping the direction — legally

title: Reasoning with Probability
Reasoning with Probability
text:
Bayesian Updating, Watched Live
Start moderately confident a coin is fair — a prior belief centered on “fair” — then flip it 100 times and update after every flip:

This morning we watched a coin’s long-run proportion converge. Same coin, new question: what do we believe about it, updated flip by flip? Beliefs are provisional, quantified, and revised by evidence — that is the entire philosophy in one gif.

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: The Dreaded Adamsitis Strain of Ianfluenza
text:
The Dreaded Adamsitis Strain of Ianfluenza
A screening problem (any resemblance to a frequent co-author is coincidental):

Prevalence 1% — 10 cases per 1,000 people
Sensitivity .90 — catches 90% of true cases
Specificity .95 — clears 95% of the healthy

Two questions that sound identical — and are not:

\(P(\text{test says} + \mid \text{actually sick})\) — what the brochure advertises
\(P(\text{actually sick} \mid \text{test says} +)\) — what you want in the exam room

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Count It Out: 1,000 People




Test says +
Test says −
Total




Sick (1%)
9 caught
1 missed
10


Healthy
~50 false alarms
~941 cleared
990


Total
~59
~942
1,000



Look closely — this is a contingency table, and P(sick | +) is the same move as P(day | Bill): shrink to the “test says +” column, re-proportion.

\[
P(\text{sick} \mid +) \;=\; \frac{9}{9 + 50} \;\approx\; 15\%
\]
The test is “90% accurate” — and a positive result still means you are probably fine.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Priors Matter

Read the test result the intuitive way — “the test is 90% accurate, so I’m 90% sick” — and you have silently treated \(P(\text{data} \mid H)\) as \(P(H \mid \text{data})\)
The base rate (the prior: 1%) is what separates 90% from 15%. Ignoring it makes the test look far more powerful than it really is
Criminal justice runs on rare events: false confessions, officer-involved shootings, risk-assessment flags, gunshot-residue matches. Base-rate neglect is not a party trick here — it convicts people

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Hold This Thought Until Session 6

Today planted two seeds: the Super Challenge (simulate the boring world, see if chance explains your gap) and Bayes’ theorem (update beliefs by evidence)
Those are the two great traditions of statistical inference — frequentist and Bayesian
Session 6 runs both, side by side, on one real Chicago question
Until then: every conditional probability you meet, ask which direction is this?

The Situation
Over three months, 40 bank robberies strike across a city’s five zones: North, South, East, West, and Downtown.

No clear pattern. No suspects. No leads.
The robber hits banks, disappears, and resurfaces days later in a different part of the city.
Detectives are stumped. The media is escalating. Public concern is growing.
Then someone makes a call to the PD’s new crime analyst team:



“Can you help us predict where they’ll hit next?”

title: Statistics is Awesome!
section: You Already Think Like a Bayesian
text:
You Already Think Like a Bayesian
Look at what you just did with the robbery case:

You started with a vague hunch spread across five zones — statisticians call that a prior
Each new robbery was evidence that reshaped the hunch
The model’s “predicted risk by zone” is an updated belief, given the data
Sending officers to the West Zone = deciding under quantified uncertainty
The formal name is Bayesian updating. The formula arrives in Session 3; the full machinery in Session 6 — side by side with the other great tradition, the frequentist one

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Types of Data
Qualitative (categorical)

Describe groups or labels (zone, sex, race)
Text / interviews

Quantitative (numerical)

Measurable amounts (age, prior robberies)
Discrete = whole counts (number of robberies)
Continuous = can take any value (income, age)

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Levels of Measurement








Level
Definition
Examples




Nominal
Categories without order
Race, sex, zone


Ordinal
Ordered categories, unequal gaps
Likert scales


Interval
Meaningful differences, no true zero
Temperature (°C)


Ratio
Meaningful differences and true zero
Robbery counts, age

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Why Does the Level Matter?

Your variable’s scale determines the math you’re allowed to do
It also determines the plot you should make
Using the wrong scale leads to wrong conclusions

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Scale Determines the Math: Nominal

# WRONG: the "mean zone" is meaningless
rob$zone |> as.numeric() |> mean()

[1] 3.17




# RIGHT: counts and percentages
rob |>
  count(zone) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  zone         n   pct
  <fct>    <int> <dbl>
1 Downtown    32  16  
2 East        28  14  
3 North       59  29.5
4 South       36  18  
5 West        45  22.5

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Scale Determines the Math: Ordinal

# Summarize a Likert item (ordinal): median & IQR
rob |>
  summarize(med = median(risk_likert), iqr = IQR(risk_likert))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    med   iqr
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     4     3

# Association with a numeric variable: Spearman (rank-based)
cor(rob$risk_likert, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.001707403

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Interval vs. Ratio

mean(rob$temp_c)             # ~20 °C

[1] 20.07643

mean(rob$temp_c * 1.8 + 32)  # same temperatures in °F

[1] 68.13757


Temperature has no true zero — 0 °C is just where water freezes.

“30 °C is 10 °C warmer than 20 °C” ✔ (differences are fine)
“20 °C is twice as hot as 10 °C” ✘ (ratios are meaningless)



mean(rob$age)

[1] 40.605


Age has a true zero — a 40-year-old is twice as old as a 20-year-old. Differences and ratios both work.

Treating Ordinal as Numeric Can Mislead

educ <- rep(1:5, each = 50)                 # ordinal codes 1..5

title: Resources
section: The simulation verbs, in plain language
text:
The simulation verbs, in plain language
Every simulation in this course is built from a tiny vocabulary. When code looks dense, translate it with this table:








Verb
Reads as
First appears




sample(x, size, replace)
“run one random event” — draw size values from x
Session 3


replicate(k, expr)
“repeat the whole recipe k times and collect the answers”
Session 3


rbinom(n, size, prob)
“flip size coins and count the successes — done n times”
Session 3


\(x) ...
an anonymous function: “a mini-recipe with slot x”
Sessions 3–4


map_dbl(v, \(x) ...)
“for each element of v, run the recipe; return one number each” — replicate(), tidyverse-flavored
Session 4


map(v, \(x) ...)
same, but each result can be a whole object — results arrive as a list column
Session 4


list_rbind(l)
“stack a list of small tibbles into one tibble”
Session 5


expand_grid(a = ..., b = ...)
“every combination of these values, as rows”
Session 4


set.seed(705)
“start the random-number generator at a fixed spot, so results reproduce”
everywhere



Two idioms worth naming once:

The thousand-times pattern: tibble(draw = 1:1000) |> mutate(stat = map_dbl(draw, \(d) ...)) — “do it 1,000 times, keep every answer in a column.” This powers most figures in Sessions 4–6.
List columns: s = map(draw, \(d) sample(...)) makes a column where each cell holds an entire sample. You never need to write one from scratch in this course — you only need to read past it and watch what’s computed from it.

text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different data and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 11 (and Checkpoint 3’s first regression on your own data) will feel routine.
Problems that use data need only this setup — the same 100 cities as the Session 10 practice bank, where poverty and the violent-crime rate ran r = .61. Correlation said the two travel together; regression asks how much, and what a second predictor changes. One row = one city — every sentence you write stays at that level.
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)   # Problem 5 only — expect the usual compile pause
library(car)    # for vif()

cities <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/cities-wide.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 11
section: Problem 1 · One predictor: make the slope speak units
text:
Problem 1 · One predictor: make the slope speak units
Regress vcr_2025 (violent crimes per 100,000 residents) on poverty_rate (percentage points). Interpret the slope with units, say what the intercept means here (and whether any real city lives there), and connect R² to Session 10’s r = .61.






Tip





Solution

city_m1 <- lm(vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate, data = cities)
summary(city_m1)


Call:
lm(formula = vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate, data = cities)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-477.63  -91.04   13.49   94.26  390.25 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   110.298     37.778   2.920  0.00435 ** 
poverty_rate   14.461      1.906   7.586 1.92e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 150.8 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:   0.37, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3635 
F-statistic: 57.54 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 1.92e-11

cor(cities$poverty_rate, cities$vcr_2025)^2

[1] 0.3699531




Slope ≈ 14.5: each additional percentage point of city poverty is associated with about 14.5 more violent crimes per 100,000 residents, in this sample. Units on both ends or the number means nothing.

Intercept ≈ 110: the predicted rate for a city with 0% poverty — no city in the data comes close (the minimum is 4.4%), so it anchors the line rather than describing anywhere real.

R² = .37, which is exactly .61² — with one predictor, R² is last session’s correlation squared: poverty accounts for about 37% of the city-to-city variance in violent-crime rates, leaving 63% to everything else.

A slope is a rate with units (outcome units per predictor unit); R² is the share of outcome variance the model captures — two different questions about the same line.

title: Practice Problems · Session 11
section: Problem 2 · A second predictor: does it earn its keep?
text:
Problem 2 · A second predictor: does it earn its keep?
Cities differ in police staffing too. Add police_per_10k (sworn officers per 10,000 residents) to the model. Compare the poverty slope across the two models, interpret the staffing coefficient with its 95% CI, and check what happens to adjusted R². Then write the honest one-sentence conclusion about staffing.






Tip





Solution

city_m2 <- lm(vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate + police_per_10k, data = cities)
summary(city_m2)


Call:
lm(formula = vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate + police_per_10k, data = cities)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-448.76  -91.34    5.14   85.70  379.28 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     179.978     59.917   3.004  0.00339 ** 
poverty_rate     14.592      1.897   7.694 1.19e-11 ***
police_per_10k   -3.232      2.166  -1.492  0.13889    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 149.9 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3841,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3714 
F-statistic: 30.25 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: 6.188e-11

confint(city_m2)

                   2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept)    61.060105 298.896503
poverty_rate   10.828022  18.356175
police_per_10k -7.530335   1.066661

c(adj_m1 = summary(city_m1)$adj.r.squared,
  adj_m2 = summary(city_m2)$adj.r.squared)

   adj_m1    adj_m2 
0.3635241 0.3713927 


The poverty slope barely moves (14.46 → 14.59) — poverty and staffing are nearly uncorrelated here (r ≈ .05), so there was almost no shared variance to reapportion. The staffing coefficient is −3.2 violent crimes per 100k per additional officer per 10k residents, 95% CI [−7.5, 1.1], p = .14: the interval spans zero, and adjusted R² ticks up only trivially (.364 → .371). The honest sentence: “Holding poverty constant, police staffing showed no reliable association with the violent-crime rate in these cities.” A new predictor has to earn its coefficient — a CI straddling zero and a flat adjusted R² is the data declining the offer, and saying so is a legitimate finding.

title: Practice Problems · Session 11
section: Problem 3 · The lurking third variable, caught in the act
text:
Problem 3 · The lurking third variable, caught in the act
Across 90 towns, an analyst finds that towns with more licensed pawn shops report far more burglaries, and drafts a memo proposing pawn-shop license caps. Simulate the analyst’s data — note what actually generates both variables:

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: keeps this particular draw stable
towns <- tibble(
  population = runif(90, 10, 120),                        # thousands of residents
  pawn_shops = 1 + 0.09 * population + rnorm(90, 0, 1.4),
  burglaries = 30 + 5.5 * population + rnorm(90, 0, 55)   # per year
)


Fit burglaries ~ pawn_shops. How does the coefficient look — and does anything in the output warn you it’s misleading?
Now add population. What happens to the pawn-shop coefficient, and what does that tell the memo’s author?







Tip





Solution

lm(burglaries ~ pawn_shops, data = towns) |> summary() |> coef() |> round(3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   63.323     25.188   2.514    0.014
pawn_shops    48.350      3.217  15.031    0.000

lm(burglaries ~ pawn_shops + population, data = towns) |> summary() |> coef() |> round(3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   37.007     12.830   2.884    0.005
pawn_shops     1.365      3.347   0.408    0.684
population     5.290      0.329  16.056    0.000



About 48 more burglaries per additional pawn shop, p < .001 by a mile — and nothing in the output warns you. The model can only see the variables you gave it.
Holding population constant, the pawn-shop coefficient collapses to ≈ 1.4 with p ≈ .68 — nothing — while population comes in at ≈ 5.3 burglaries per additional thousand residents. Bigger towns simply have more of both. That collapse is “holding constant” doing real work: comparing towns of the same size, pawn-shop counts tell you nothing about burglary. And the sobering corollary: regression can only hold constant the lurkers you measured and included — the ones you didn’t are still at large.

title: Practice Problems · Session 11
section: Problem 4 · Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
text:
Problem 4 · Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
Back to the real model, city_m2 from Problem 2. Make the residuals-vs-fitted plot and run vif(). For each: what is it checking, and what does it show here?






Tip





Solution

tibble(fitted = fitted(city_m2), residual = resid(city_m2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Fitted violent-crime rate", y = "Residual")






vif(city_m2)

  poverty_rate police_per_10k 
      1.002158       1.002158 


The residual plot checks whether the model’s misses are patternless: no curve (the straight-line shape isn’t visibly wrong) and roughly even spread across the fitted range. This one is what healthy looks like — a shapeless band centered on zero, no bend, no widening, with the biggest misses (reaching roughly ±400) scattered across the range rather than piling up at one end. Compare Lab 11’s Chicago plot, where the spread visibly widened at high fitted values; that’s the kind of pattern this plot exists to catch.
VIF checks a different disease — predictor redundancy. Both values sit at ≈ 1.00 (poverty and staffing share almost nothing, r ≈ .05), so each coefficient is estimated on its own information. The residual plot audits the misses; VIF audits the predictors — one model, two separate health checks.

title: Practice Problems · Session 11
section: Problem 5 · Both traditions, one sentence each
text:
Problem 5 · Both traditions, one sentence each
Fit the Bayesian twin of city_m2 with brm() (expect the Compiling Stan program… pause — normal, not frozen), look at the posterior summaries, and then write the pair of reporting sentences: one frequentist (estimate, CI, p) and one Bayesian (the credible-interval sentence you’re allowed to say) about the poverty coefficient.






Tip





Solution

city_bayes <- brm(vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate + police_per_10k, data = cities,
                  chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


fixef(city_bayes) |> round(2)

               Estimate Est.Error  Q2.5  Q97.5
Intercept        178.32     60.45 62.08 294.22
poverty_rate      14.65      1.97 10.71  18.35
police_per_10k    -3.18      2.20 -7.46   1.01


The posterior lands almost exactly on lm()’s estimates — expected with brms default priors (say so when you report: “brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705”) and 100 cities of data.

Frequentist: “Holding police staffing constant, each additional percentage point of poverty was associated with about 14.6 more violent crimes per 100,000 residents (b = 14.59, 95% CI [10.8, 18.4], p < .001).”


Bayesian: “Given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the poverty coefficient lies between roughly 10.9 and 18.3 — zero is not a credible value.”

Same formula, nearly identical numbers — what changes is the sentence each tradition licenses, and the Bayesian one makes the direct probability statement the confidence interval never could.

title: Practice Problems · Session 11
text:
Problem 6 · The sentence audit
Four sentences drafted from the Problem 2 model. Two are defensible; two are not. Sort them, and fix the broken ones.


“Holding police staffing constant, each additional percentage point of poverty was associated with about 14.6 more violent crimes per 100,000 residents (95% CI [10.8, 18.4]).”
“Poverty drives up violent crime in American cities.”
“R² = .38, so the model correctly predicts 38% of cities.”
“Police staffing showed no reliable association with the violent-crime rate in these cities (b = −3.2, 95% CI [−7.5, 1.1]).”








Tip





Solution

confint(city_m2) |> round(1)

               2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept)     61.1  298.9
poverty_rate    10.8   18.4
police_per_10k  -7.5    1.1

summary(city_m2)$r.squared

[1] 0.3840918


Defensible: (a) and (d). Both state an adjusted association, with magnitude, units, uncertainty, and the holding-constant clause — and (d) shows that “no reliable association” is a reportable result, not a failure.
(b) fails twice: “drives up” is a causal verb no cross-sectional model earns (lurkers we never measured are still at large — Problem 3’s lesson), and “American cities” generalizes a 100-city sample to a population the data can’t speak for. Fix: “In these 100 cities, higher poverty was associated with higher violent-crime rates, holding staffing constant.”
(c) misreads R²: .38 is the share of variance in the outcome the model accounts for — not an accuracy rate, and not a count of cities predicted “correctly.” Fix: “The two predictors together account for about 38% of the city-to-city variance in violent-crime rates.” The audit habit: check every regression sentence for causal verbs, level of analysis, units, and what R² actually is.

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different data and numbers than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 8 (and the midterm’s ANOVA questions) will feel routine.
Every problem here runs on typed-in or built-in data, so the only setup you need is:
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)      # Problem 5 only — expect the usual compile pause
library(emmeans)

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
section: Problem 1 · The pile of t-tests, quantified
text:
Problem 1 · The pile of t-tests, quantified
Your department compares mean response times across five patrol sectors. A colleague proposes “keeping it simple”: a separate t-test on every pair of sectors, each at the usual 5% false-alarm risk.

How many pairwise tests is that? (choose() counts them.)
If all five sectors truly have the same mean, what is the probability that at least one test comes up “significant” anyway?







Tip





Solution

choose(5, 2)          # pairwise tests among 5 groups

[1] 10

1 - 0.95^choose(5, 2) # P(at least one false alarm across all of them)

[1] 0.4012631


Ten tests, and roughly a 40% chance of at least one bogus “significant” difference when nothing differs at all. That’s why ANOVA asks one omnibus question — are all five means plausibly equal? — at a single 5% risk, and saves the pairwise digging for an adjusted follow-up (Problem 4).

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
text:
Problem 2 · Two variances, by hand
Dispatch pulls five response times (minutes) from each of three sectors — small on purpose, so you can see every number:

sectors <- tibble(
  minutes = c(7, 9, 8, 10, 8,       # Adams
              12, 14, 13, 15, 13,   # Baker
              8, 10, 9, 7, 9),      # Charlie
  sector  = factor(rep(c("Adams", "Baker", "Charlie"), each = 5))
)

Compute each sector’s mean and variance, then the within-group variance (average of the three variances), the between-group variance (variance of the three means), and their ratio. What is the ratio telling you, in signal-and-noise terms?






Tip





Solution

sector_stats <- sectors |>
  summarize(sector_mean = mean(minutes), sector_var = var(minutes), .by = sector)
sector_stats

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  sector  sector_mean sector_var
  <fct>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Adams           8.4        1.3
2 Baker          13.4        1.3
3 Charlie         8.6        1.3

within_var  <- mean(sector_stats$sector_var)   # noise: spread inside sectors
between_var <- var(sector_stats$sector_mean)   # signal: spread OF the means

within_var

[1] 1.3

between_var

[1] 8.013333

between_var / within_var

[1] 6.164103


The sector means (8.4, 13.4, 8.6) are about 6 times more spread out than the chance bouncing inside sectors would produce — between dwarfs within, which is the signature of a real group difference. Between-group variance is the signal, within-group variance is the noise, and the ratio is your first, unscaled look at F.

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
section: Problem 3 · aov() and reading the F table
text:
Problem 3 · aov() and reading the F table
Run aov(minutes ~ sector, ...) on the same data and look at summary(). Then connect it to Problem 2: which table entry is your within-group variance? Why is Mean Sq for sector not 8.01? And what do F and p say?






Tip





Solution

sector_model <- aov(minutes ~ sector, data = sectors)
summary(sector_model)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
sector       2  80.13   40.07   30.82 1.87e-05 ***
Residuals   12  15.60    1.30                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Mean Sq Residuals = 1.30 — the within-group variance from Problem 2, exactly.

Mean Sq sector = 40.07 = 5 × 8.01 — the between-group variance scaled by the group size. A 5-minute gap between means built on 5 calls each is stronger evidence than the same gap built on 2, so aov() bakes the sample size into the signal.

F(2, 12) = 30.8 — which is 5 × our hand ratio of 6.16 — with p ≈ 0.00002: an F this large essentially never happens when the three sectors truly share a mean.

The F table is Problem 2’s two variances dressed up: same logic, with the group size folded into the signal.

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
section: Problem 4 · Real(ish) data: warpbreaks and Tukey
text:
Problem 4 · Real(ish) data: warpbreaks and Tukey
R ships warpbreaks: 54 industrial loom runs, recording how many times the yarn broke during each run under low, medium, or high tension (L/M/H, 18 runs each). Quality-control question: does mean breakage differ by tension setting?
Compute the group means, run the ANOVA, then TukeyHSD(). Which pairs differ? One pair shows no reliable difference — name it and report the interval that told you so.






Tip





Solution

data("warpbreaks")

warpbreaks |>
  summarize(mean_breaks = mean(breaks), sd_breaks = sd(breaks), n = n(),
            .by = tension)

  tension mean_breaks sd_breaks  n
1       L    36.38889 16.446487 18
2       M    26.38889  9.121009 18
3       H    21.66667  8.352527 18

warp_model <- aov(breaks ~ tension, data = warpbreaks)
summary(warp_model)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
tension      2   2034  1017.1   7.206 0.00175 **
Residuals   51   7199   141.1                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

TukeyHSD(warp_model)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = breaks ~ tension, data = warpbreaks)

$tension
          diff       lwr        upr     p adj
M-L -10.000000 -19.55982 -0.4401756 0.0384598
H-L -14.722222 -24.28205 -5.1623978 0.0014315
H-M  -4.722222 -14.28205  4.8376022 0.4630831


F(2, 51) = 7.2, p ≈ .002 — the omnibus F says something differs. Tukey says what: M − L (−10.0, interval [−19.6, −0.4], p ≈ .04) and H − L (−14.7, interval [−24.3, −5.2], p ≈ .001) both exclude 0 — low tension breaks more yarn than either alternative. But H − M spans 0 ([−14.3, 4.8], p ≈ .46): no evidence medium and high differ. A significant omnibus F never means every pair differs — Tukey names the pairs while holding the family-wise false-alarm rate at 5%.

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
section: Problem 5 · The Bayesian version: brm() + emmeans() + pairs()
text:
Problem 5 · The Bayesian version: brm() + emmeans() + pairs()

Fit the Bayesian twin of Problem 4’s model (expect the Compiling Stan program… pause — that’s normal, not a crash), then get the posterior pairwise differences. Which 95% HPD intervals cross zero, and does the Bayesian verdict match Tukey’s?






Tip





Solution

warp_bayes <- brm(breaks ~ tension, data = warpbreaks,
                  chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


warp_post <- emmeans(warp_bayes, ~ tension)
warp_post

 tension emmean lower.HPD upper.HPD
 L         36.6      30.2      41.8
 M         26.4      20.1      31.8
 H         21.6      16.3      27.2

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 

pairs(warp_post)

 contrast estimate lower.HPD upper.HPD
 L - M       10.05      1.56      18.0
 L - H       14.79      5.91      22.5
 M - H        4.65     -2.66      12.9

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 



plot(pairs(warp_post)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "firebrick")







L − M (≈ +10, HPD roughly [2, 18]) and L − H (≈ +14.7, roughly [7, 23]) exclude 0 — credible differences. M − H (≈ +4.7, roughly [−3, 13]) crosses 0 — zero remains a credible value, so no credible difference. Same verdict as Tukey, pair for pair. One nuance worth noticing: these Bayesian intervals are per-comparison, while Tukey deliberately widens its intervals to hold the family-wise rate — with only 3 contrasts the two land in the same place, but on borderline pairs they can disagree — worth watching for whenever you run both. When an HPD interval crosses zero, “no difference” is still on the table; when it doesn’t, the difference is credible.

title: Practice Problems · Session 8
text:
Problem 6 · Audit the memo
A crime-analyst memo about the warpbreaks-style analysis contains these four sentences. Two are wrong. Find them, say why, and fix them.


“The omnibus test was significant, F(2, 51) = 7.2, p = .002, so all three tension settings differ from one another.”
“To be thorough, we also ran all three pairwise t-tests without adjustment and report those p-values instead of Tukey’s.”
“Tukey’s HSD keeps the family-wise false-alarm rate at 5% across all three comparisons.”
“Low tension averaged about 15 more breaks per run than high tension, 95% CI [5.2, 24.3].”








Tip





Solution

# Unadjusted pairwise p-values vs. Tukey's family-wise-adjusted ones:
pairwise.t.test(warpbreaks$breaks, warpbreaks$tension, p.adjust.method = "none")


    Pairwise comparisons using t tests with pooled SD 

data:  warpbreaks$breaks and warpbreaks$tension 

  L      M     
M 0.0147 -     
H 0.0005 0.2386

P value adjustment method: none 

TukeyHSD(aov(breaks ~ tension, data = warpbreaks))$tension[, "p adj"]

        M-L         H-L         H-M 
0.038459768 0.001431503 0.463083097 


(a) is wrong. A significant omnibus F licenses only “at least one mean differs” — and Tukey showed H vs. M does not differ. Fix: “…so not all three tension means are equal; pairwise comparisons follow.”
(b) is wrong. Reporting unadjusted pairwise p-values quietly triples the false-alarm exposure — Problem 1’s pile-of-t-tests problem in miniature. Compare the two outputs above: every unadjusted p is smaller than its Tukey counterpart (e.g., M vs. L: .015 unadjusted vs. .038 adjusted) precisely because the unadjusted version ignores the other tests being run. Fix: report the Tukey-adjusted results.
(c) and (d) are fine — (d) is just Tukey’s H − L row with the sign flipped, magnitude and interval intact. The concept to keep: per-comparison p-values and family-wise p-values answer different questions, and after a significant F, the family-wise one is the honest one.

title: Practice Problems · Session 5
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different numbers and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 5 (and the midterm’s inference questions) will feel routine.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
prisoners <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/prisoners.csv")
crimes    <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 5
section: Problem 1 · The margin of error, by hand
text:
Problem 1 · The margin of error, by hand
Using prisoners (300 records), build a 95% CI for the mean of months_served with nothing but Session 4 parts: the sample mean, the standard error (sd / sqrt(n)), and ±1.96. Then check yourself against t.test(prisoners$months_served)$conf.int.






Tip





Solution

m  <- mean(prisoners$months_served)
se <- sd(prisoners$months_served) / sqrt(nrow(prisoners))

m

[1] 36.45667

se

[1] 1.456781

c(lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se)

      lo       hi 
33.60138 39.31196 

t.test(prisoners$months_served)$conf.int

[1] 33.58982 39.32351
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


By hand: 33.6 to 39.3 months. t.test() agrees to a decimal (it uses the t-distribution’s 1.97 instead of the normal’s 1.96 — with n = 300 that’s a rounding error). The whole machine is just estimate ± 1.96 × SE: last week’s standard error, cashed in.

title: Practice Problems · Session 5
text:
Problem 2 · A proportion with prop.test()

What share of these 300 prison records are drug offenses? Get the point estimate and a 95% CI with prop.test(). One warning: the output prints a p-value testing whether the proportion equals 0.5 — that’s not a question anyone asked. Read past it to the interval.






Tip





Solution

prisoners |> summarize(prop_drug = mean(offense_type == "Drug"))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  prop_drug
      <dbl>
1     0.297

prop.test(sum(prisoners$offense_type == "Drug"), n = nrow(prisoners))


    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  sum(prisoners$offense_type == "Drug") out of nrow(prisoners), null probability 0.5
X-squared = 48.803, df = 1, p-value = 2.83e-12
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2462485 0.3523909
sample estimates:
        p 
0.2966667 


Point estimate 29.7%, 95% CI 24.6% to 35.2%. With only 300 records, the confidence interval spans about ±5 points — honest uncertainty that the lone number “29.7%” hides.

title: Practice Problems · Session 5
text:
Problem 3 · Which sentence survives?
Four draft sentences about Problem 2’s interval. Exactly one is defensible — which, and what’s wrong with each of the others?


“There is a 95% probability that the true proportion of drug offenses is between 24.6% and 35.2%.”
“We estimate that 29.7% of admissions are drug offenses (95% CI: 24.6% to 35.2%); the procedure that built this interval captures the true share 95% of the time.”
“If we drew many new samples of 300, 95% of their sample proportions would land between 24.6% and 35.2%.”
“We are 95% sure our sample’s proportion is correct.”








Tip





Solution

round(prop.test(sum(prisoners$offense_type == "Drug"),
                n = nrow(prisoners))$conf.int, 3)

[1] 0.246 0.352
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


(b) survives. (a) attaches a probability to this particular interval — under frequentist rules the truth is fixed, so it’s either in there or it isn’t; the 95% belongs to the procedure. (c) confuses the interval with the sampling distribution: future samples produce new intervals around their own estimates, not values inside this one. (d) is doubly wrong — the sample proportion is known exactly (29.7%); the uncertainty is entirely about the population. Confidence-interval interpretation in one line: the 95% describes the long-run capture rate of the method, never the odds on one interval.

title: Practice Problems · Session 5
text:
Problem 4 · Buy precision with n
Using crimes, estimate the proportion of incidents classified as Violent (crime_category == "Violent") from a random sample of 300, then from a sample of 1,200 — slice_sample(), then prop.test() for each. Before you run it: quadrupling n should do what to the CI’s width? Verify.






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
map(c(300, 1200), \(n) {
  s  <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = n)
  ci <- prop.test(sum(s$crime_category == "Violent"), n = n)$conf.int
  tibble(n = n, estimate = mean(s$crime_category == "Violent"),
         lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2], width = ci[2] - ci[1])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

# A tibble: 2 × 5
      n estimate    lo    hi  width
  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   300    0.3   0.249 0.356 0.106 
2  1200    0.299 0.274 0.326 0.0526


This run: width ≈ 0.106 at n = 300 vs ≈ 0.053 at n = 1,200 — quadrupling the sample cut the width almost exactly in half, because CI width shrinks with √n. Precision is bought on a square-root discount: four times the data for twice the precision.

title: Practice Problems · Session 5
section: Problem 5 · Two groups, one honest sentence
text:
Problem 5 · Two groups, one honest sentence
Do drug and property offenders differ in time served? Filter prisoners to those two offense types, compare the group means of months_served, then run t.test(months_served ~ offense_type, ...). Careful on two fronts: which direction is R subtracting, and does the CI include zero? Finish with a one-sentence report a warden could read.






Tip





Solution

dp <- prisoners |> filter(offense_type %in% c("Drug", "Property"))

dp |> summarize(mean_months = mean(months_served), sd_months = sd(months_served),
                n = n(), .by = offense_type)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  offense_type mean_months sd_months     n
  <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl> <int>
1 Property            37.1      26.6    74
2 Drug                33.1      24.5    89

t.test(months_served ~ offense_type, data = dp)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  months_served by offense_type
t = -0.98293, df = 150.35, p-value = 0.3272
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Drug and group Property is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -11.953437   4.011439
sample estimates:
    mean in group Drug mean in group Property 
              33.12360               37.09459 


R orders groups alphabetically, so this is Drug − Property: the point estimate says drug offenders served about 4 fewer months, but the 95% CI runs from −12.0 to +4.0 months — zero sits comfortably inside. The honest sentence: “Drug offenders in our sample averaged about four fewer months served than property offenders, but with 163 records the data are consistent with anything from 12 fewer months to 4 more — including no difference at all.” A two-group CI that crosses zero doesn’t prove the groups are equal; it says this sample can’t settle the direction. (Compare the homework’s crash data, where the interval excluded zero — learn to say both outcomes out loud.)

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different numbers and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, the homework (and the midterm’s probability section) will feel routine.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
section: Problem 1 · Contraband in the long run
text:
Problem 1 · Contraband in the long run
Suppose 8% of traffic stops turn up contraband. Simulate 10,000 nights of 10 stops each with rbinom(). In what proportion of nights does the squad find contraband 2 or more times?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
nights <- rbinom(n = 10000, size = 10, prob = 0.08)
mean(nights >= 2)

[1] 0.1918


About 19% of nights. Note the move: simulate the process, then take a mean() of a logical condition — the same shape as every probability we computed in class.

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
section: Problem 2 · Build the table, read the margins
text:
Problem 2 · Build the table, read the margins
Using crimes, make a contingency table of primary_type × arrest for just THEFT and BATTERY incidents (filter(primary_type %in% c("THEFT", "BATTERY"))). Then compute: (a) the joint probability that a randomly chosen incident from this subset is a BATTERY and ended in arrest; (b) the marginal probability of BATTERY.






Tip





Solution

tb <- crimes |> filter(primary_type %in% c("THEFT", "BATTERY"))

tb |>
  count(primary_type, arrest) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arrest, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  primary_type `FALSE` `TRUE`
  <chr>          <int>  <int>
1 BATTERY         4418   1010
2 THEFT           6320    631

# (a) joint — divide the cell by the subset's grand total:
mean(tb$primary_type == "BATTERY" & tb$arrest)

[1] 0.08158979

# (b) marginal:
mean(tb$primary_type == "BATTERY")

[1] 0.4384845


The joint divides by everything in the subset (both crime types, both arrest outcomes). If you divided the BATTERY-and-arrest count by the number of BATTERY rows, you computed a conditional — that’s Problem 3.

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
section: Problem 3 · Both directions of the conditional
text:
Problem 3 · Both directions of the conditional
Still in the THEFT/BATTERY subset: compute P(arrest | BATTERY) and P(BATTERY | arrest). Then, in one sentence, explain why the two numbers differ so much when they come from the same cells.






Tip





Solution

tb <- crimes |> filter(primary_type %in% c("THEFT", "BATTERY"))

# P(arrest | BATTERY): shrink to BATTERY rows, take the mean
tb |> filter(primary_type == "BATTERY") |> summarize(p = mean(arrest))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      p
  <dbl>
1 0.186

# P(BATTERY | arrest): shrink to arrest rows, ask how many are BATTERY
tb |> filter(arrest) |> summarize(p = mean(primary_type == "BATTERY"))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      p
  <dbl>
1 0.615


Same cells, different denominators: the first re-proportions within battery incidents, the second within arrests. Direction matters — P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A) except by coincidence.

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
section: Problem 4 · Is time of day independent of arrest?
text:
Problem 4 · Is time of day independent of arrest?
Create a logical variable night = hour >= 20 | hour < 4 on the full crimes data. Compare P(arrest | night), P(arrest | not night), and the overall P(arrest). Closer to independent or dependent?






Tip





Solution

crimes |>
  mutate(night = hour >= 20 | hour < 4) |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = night)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  night p_arrest     n
  <lgl>    <dbl> <int>
1 TRUE     0.167  9917
2 FALSE    0.158 20083

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608


The conditional probabilities sit close to the marginal — knowing an incident happened at night moves the arrest probability only slightly. In these data, night is nearly independent of arrest (remember the definition: independence means P(A | B) = P(A)). Hedge accordingly: “essentially independent in this sample.”

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
text:
Problem 5 · The burglar alarm (Bayes’ theorem)
A home-security company advertises that its alarm detects 99% of break-ins. The alarm also goes off on 2% of days with no break-in (cats, wind, deliveries). Suppose the daily probability of a break-in attempt on a given house is 0.5% (5 in 1,000).
The alarm is ringing. Build the counting table for 10,000 days and compute P(break-in | alarm).






Tip





Solution

break_ins    <- 10000 * 0.005          # 50 break-in days
caught       <- break_ins * 0.99       # 49.5 -> alarm rings
quiet_days   <- 10000 - break_ins      # 9,950 days without a break-in
false_alarms <- quiet_days * 0.02      # 199 false rings

caught / (caught + false_alarms)       # P(break-in | alarm)

[1] 0.1991952


About 20%. Four out of five rings are cats and wind, because quiet days outnumber break-in days 199:1. The “99% accurate” figure is P(alarm | break-in) — the transposed conditional. Ignoring the 0.5% base rate is exactly the mistake the Ianfluenza example warned about.

title: Practice Problems · Session 3
text:
Problem 6 · Verify it by simulation
Session 3’s rule: don’t take a probability claim on faith. Simulate 100,000 days of Problem 5’s alarm and check your answer.






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
days <- tibble(
  break_in = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 100000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.005, 0.995))
) |>
  mutate(alarm = if_else(
    break_in,
    sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 100000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.99, 0.01)),
    sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 100000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.02, 0.98))
  ))

days |> filter(alarm) |> summarize(p_break_in = mean(break_in), rings = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  p_break_in rings
       <dbl> <int>
1      0.207  2519


The long run lands where the counting table said it would — right around 20%.

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
The midterm is in class and monitored. You write and troubleshoot real R code. You may use your printed notes and homework — no internet, no AI tools. (This is the assessment the AI policy warns you about: if AI has been writing your homework, this is where it shows.)
How it works mechanically: you get an .R script with the questions plus the data files it needs, all distributed together — you answer in the script and submit it. Two things to know in advance:
Best preparation: the practice banks for Sessions 2–8 — ungraded problems with hidden solutions, in exactly the exam’s style.

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
1. Data & measurement

Explain the four levels of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio)
Give examples of each, especially from criminal justice research

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
2. Descriptive statistics

Calculate mean, median, and mode in R
Compute variance and standard deviation in R
Explain what the standard deviation means in plain language
Make and interpret a histogram
Explain why an outlier affects the mean more than the median or mode

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
3. Probability & sampling

Simulate random events (e.g., sample(), rbinom())
Count outcomes with count() or table()
The difference between small and large samples (law of large numbers)
Build and interpret a contingency table
Calculate and interpret a conditional probability from a table
Reverse a conditional with Bayes’ theorem using a counting table: base rate + sensitivity/false-positive rate → P(condition | positive test)

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
4. Inference & confidence intervals

Compute group means
Make and interpret a boxplot
Run a two-sample t-test with t.test()
Interpret a 95% confidence interval (what it means when the CI includes 0 vs. not)

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
5. Frequentist vs. Bayesian thinking

What a p-value means (and doesn’t mean)
How Bayesian probability statements differ — P(hypothesis | data)
Why priors matter and how ignoring them can mislead
The recidivism example: same data, different interpretations
Run and interpret a Bayesian t-test with ttestBF()

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
6. Comparing groups / ANOVA

Make a boxplot of groups
Run a one-way ANOVA with aov() and interpret the output (at least one group mean differs)
Interpret a Bayesian ANOVA using the workflow we practiced (brms + emmeans) — on the exam the model arrives pre-fit (readRDS()); you run emmeans(), plot(), and pairs() on it
Interpret pairwise comparisons (posterior interval crossing 0 = no credible difference)

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
General advice

Practice running the R code from your homework, labs, and in-class exercises — the midterm only asks you to do things we’ve already done.
Make sure you can both run the code and explain in words what the output means.
Focus on big ideas: variability, sampling, inference, and comparing groups.
Don’t overthink the Bayesian part — it will be at the same level as what you’ve already done in class and on homework.

title: Midterm Study Guide
text:
R you should know cold
mean(x); median(x)
library(modeest); mfv(x)                  # mode
var(x); sd(x)

# plots (ggplot as practiced in lab; base equivalents also fine)
ggplot(df, aes(x)) + geom_histogram()
ggplot(df, aes(group, y)) + geom_boxplot()

# counting & contingency tables
df |> count(x, y)
table(df$x, df$y)

# inference
t.test(y ~ group, data = df)              # two-sample t-test + CI
library(BayesFactor); ttestBF(...)        # Bayesian t-test

# ANOVA

# Bayesian ANOVA workflow (exam version: the model is pre-fit)

plot(bayes_anova)

title: Midterm Study Guide
section: Concepts you should be able to explain
text:
Concepts you should be able to explain

Levels of measurement — nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio (with examples)
Mean/median/mode — what each tells you; effect of outliers
Variance & SD — measure of spread; SD ≈ typical distance from the mean
Law of large numbers — small samples fluctuate; large samples stabilize
Contingency tables — marginal totals, conditional probability
Confidence intervals — CI includes 0 → difference not supported; excludes 0 → supported
p-value — probability of data this extreme (or more) if the null is true
Bayesian probability — probability of the hypothesis given the data; priors matter — a low base rate can turn a “90% accurate” test into a mostly-wrong one
ANOVA — compares variance between groups vs. within groups
Bayesian ANOVA — pairwise posterior intervals; crossing 0 = no credible difference

title: Lab 11 · Multiple Regression: Chicago’s 77 Areas, Then 500 Neighborhoods
text:
Goal: run the complete multiple-regression workflow from today’s lecture — fit with lm(), interpret coefficients in holding-constant language, diagnose with a residual plot and VIF, then fit the Bayesian twin with brms and read the posteriors — first on the Chicago community-area data from lecture, then on your own model with the Lab 3 neighborhoods.
There’s no new data-skills content today: this lab is pure statistics practice. (Homework 11 brings the wrangling back — you’ll clean a file before regressing on it.)
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. The Exit Ticket gets submitted to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 11 · Multiple Regression: Chicago’s 77 Areas, Then 500 Neighborhoods
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)
library(bayesplot)
library(brms)
library(car)

areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv")







One new package today: install.packages("car") — we use it for VIF. (bayesplot came along free when you installed brms for ANOVA week, so library(bayesplot) should just work.) And the usual brms reminder: the first brm() of a session pauses at Compiling Stan program... for a minute. Not frozen. Compiling.



Our walkthrough data are the 77 Chicago community areas — every 2025 incident aggregated to the area level and joined with census measures (codebook on the Data page). One row per area, not per person or per crime. Keep that word — area — in every sentence you write today.
The question: how do unemployment and vacant housing relate to an area’s violent-crime rate — each adjusted for the other?

title: Lab 11 · Multiple Regression: Chicago’s 77 Areas, Then 500 Neighborhoods
text:
Walkthrough
Look first
Always. Before any model:

ggplot(areas, aes(unemployment_rate, violent_rate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "77 community areas, 2025",
       x = "Unemployment rate (%)",
       y = "Violent crimes per 1,000 residents")







A strong, roughly linear, upward relationship — with the high-violence areas scattering farther from the line. Remember that scatter; it comes back in diagnostics.
One predictor

chi_m1 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)
summary(chi_m1)


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-32.137  -6.340  -2.670   5.843  43.339 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -2.7444     2.8629  -0.959    0.341    
unemployment_rate   3.3007     0.2463  13.400   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.27 on 75 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7054,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7014 
F-statistic: 179.5 on 1 and 75 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Three numbers to pull out of that wall of output, in order of importance:


The slope (~3.3): each additional percentage point of unemployment is associated with about 3.3 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents.

Multiple R-squared (~0.71): unemployment alone accounts for about 71% of the variance in violent-crime rates across areas.

The slope’s p-value: far below .05 — a slope this steep essentially never shows up when the true slope is zero.
Two predictors
Areas with high unemployment also tend to have more vacant housing. Does each carry its own association, or is one riding the other’s coattails?

chi_m2 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)
summary(chi_m2)


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-27.6759  -5.8167  -0.9943   4.5144  26.7266 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -9.2679     2.4616  -3.765 0.000332 ***
unemployment_rate   2.1156     0.2620   8.075 9.35e-12 ***
pct_vacant          1.9352     0.2859   6.769 2.65e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.708 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.818, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8131 
F-statistic: 166.3 on 2 and 74 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Compare the unemployment slope across the two models: ~3.3 alone → ~2.1 with vacancy in the model. That drop is the whole point of multiple regression: part of what the simple model credited to unemployment was really variance it shares with vacancy. Each coefficient is now an adjusted association — unemployment’s relationship with violence among areas with similar vacancy, and vice versa. Both stay strongly significant, and R² rises to ~0.82.
Interpretation sentences worth copying:

“Holding vacancy constant, each additional percentage point of unemployment is associated with about 2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents.”
“Holding unemployment constant, each additional percentage point of vacant housing is associated with about 1.9 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents.”
What we may not say: anything with “causes,” “drives,” or “increases” as an action verb — and nothing about individual people. These are adjusted associations between areas (Session 10’s ecological fallacy never left).
Diagnose: the residual plot
The model assumes its misses are patternless. Look:

chi_diag <- tibble(fitted = fitted(chi_m2), residual = resid(chi_m2))

ggplot(chi_diag, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Fitted violent-crime rate", y = "Residual")







What to check, in order: (1) no curve — the cloud shouldn’t bend (a bend means the straight-plane shape is wrong); (2) even spread — here the spread visibly widens at higher fitted values, so the model misses by more in high-violence areas. That fanning doesn’t bias the slopes, but it means the error bars are least trustworthy exactly where the stakes are highest — say so when you report.
Diagnose: VIF
If predictors are near-duplicates of each other, the model can’t apportion credit between them and the coefficients wobble. VIF puts a number on the redundancy:

vif(chi_m2)

unemployment_rate        pct_vacant 
         1.807177          1.807177 


Rules of thumb: above 5, pay attention; above 10, you have a problem. Ours sit around 1.8 — unemployment and vacancy are correlated (r ≈ 0.67) but each still brings its own information. If you ever do see a huge VIF: drop one of the offenders, or combine them into an index. More data won’t fix redundancy.
The Bayesian version
Same formula, same brm() pattern as ANOVA week:

chi_bayes <- brm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
                 data = areas,
                 chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


summary(chi_bayes)

 Family: gaussian 
  Links: mu = identity 
Formula: violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant 
   Data: areas (Number of observations: 77) 
  Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 2000

Regression Coefficients:
                  Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
Intercept            -9.25      2.42   -13.93    -4.68 1.00     2613     1686
unemployment_rate     2.12      0.27     1.58     2.64 1.00     1531     1419
pct_vacant            1.92      0.29     1.36     2.48 1.00     1472     1317

Further Distributional Parameters:
      Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
sigma     9.82      0.79     8.50    11.55 1.00     1935     1529

Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).


Reading the Regression Coefficients block: Estimate is the posterior mean (it lands almost exactly on lm()’s estimate — expected with default priors and 77 areas), and l-95% CI / u-95% CI bound the credible interval. Both intervals sit clearly away from zero. Quick health checks: Rhat at 1.00 and ESS in the hundreds-plus mean the chains behaved.

mcmc_areas(chi_bayes, pars = c("b_unemployment_rate", "b_pct_vacant"),
           prob = 0.95) +
  labs(title = "Posteriors for the two predictors",
       subtitle = "Shaded = central 95% credible interval")







The interpretation rule, carried over from ANOVA week: if a coefficient’s 95% credible interval includes 0, zero remains a credible value — no credible association. If it excludes 0, the association is credible, and you may say: “given the data and priors, there’s a 95% probability the coefficient lies in this range.” (The sentence the confidence interval never let you say.)

title: Lab 11 · Multiple Regression: Chicago’s 77 Areas, Then 500 Neighborhoods
text:
Your Turn
Back to the 500 simulated neighborhoods from Lab 3 — poverty, unemployment, disorder, and last year’s assault counts:

nbhd <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/neighborhoods.csv")

Work in your own script. Comment each answer.
1. Make the units speak. poverty_rate and unemployment_rate are stored as proportions (0–1), so a raw slope would describe an absurd 0%-to-100% jump. Rescale before fitting — lecture’s “watch the units” lesson, applied:

nbhd <- nbhd |>
  mutate(poverty_pct      = poverty_rate * 100,
         unemployment_pct = unemployment_rate * 100)
# Then look first: scatterplot assaults ~ poverty_pct with an lm smooth.

2. Fit and interpret. Regress assaults on poverty_pct and unemployment_pct. In comments: one holding-constant sentence per coefficient (units: assaults per percentage point), and what R² says. Expect a much humbler R² than Chicago’s — real-feeling individual-ish noise, and that’s fine; say what the model does explain, not more.

# nbhd_m <- lm(assaults ~ poverty_pct + unemployment_pct, data = nbhd)
# summary(nbhd_m)

3. The diagnostics moment. Residual plot + VIF, exactly as in the Walkthrough. Two things to note in comments: (a) the residuals form diagonal stripes — that’s because assaults only takes small whole values (0, 1, 2, …), not a bug, but it is a hint that a count outcome bends the linear model’s assumptions (counts and yes/no outcomes get their own tools — that story starts next session); (b) the VIF values — poverty and unemployment are correlated here (r ≈ 0.48), so is it redundancy trouble or not?

# residual plot on nbhd_m, then vif(nbhd_m)

4. The Bayesian twin. Fit the brm() version (same options as the Walkthrough; ~500 rows samples fast), look at summary(), and make the mcmc_areas() plot for b_poverty_pct and b_unemployment_pct. In comments: one frequentist sentence and one Bayesian sentence about the poverty coefficient — each including the size of the association (assaults per percentage point, or per 10 points if that reads better), not just “significant”/“credible.”

# nbhd_bayes <- brm(assaults ~ poverty_pct + unemployment_pct, data = nbhd,
#                   chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)

5. (Stretch) Does disorder earn its keep? Add disorder_level to the frequentist model (make it a factor with levels Low → Moderate → High → Very High first). Check the coefficients and the adjusted R². Does observed disorder tell you anything about assaults that poverty and unemployment didn’t already? Connect your answer to lecture’s third-predictor slide.
(Reading a factor in lm(): R drops the first level — Low — as the reference, so each disorder_level coefficient is that level’s difference from Low, holding the other predictors constant. Same idea as ANOVA’s group comparisons, wearing regression clothes.)

title: Lab 8 · ANOVA: Three Classrooms, Then Real Crashes
text:
Goal: run the complete ANOVA workflow from today’s lecture — the two variances by hand, aov() + Tukey’s HSD, and the Bayesian version with brms + emmeans — first on a small classroom example where you can check every number, then on real Alaska crash data.
The R4DS wrangling thread wrapped up before the break, so there’s no new data-skills content today: this lab is pure statistics practice.
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. The Exit Ticket gets submitted to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 8 · ANOVA: Three Classrooms, Then Real Crashes
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(emmeans)

crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv")







First time using brms? Install both new packages before anything else: install.packages(c("emmeans", "brms")). And when you run your first brm() model of a session, R will sit at Compiling Stan program... for a minute before sampling starts. That’s normal — Stan is compiling your model into C++. It is not frozen. If instead you get an error mentioning a compiler or toolchain, flag me down.



Our walkthrough data are the three classrooms from lecture — typed in by hand, because 15 numbers you can see beat 15,000 you can’t when you’re learning what a method does:

classrooms <- tibble(
  score     = c(75, 80, 78, 74, 77,    # Class 1
                88, 90, 92, 85, 87,    # Class 2
                70, 65, 68, 72, 66),   # Class 3
  classroom = factor(rep(c("Class 1", "Class 2", "Class 3"), each = 5))
)

The question: did these three classrooms perform differently, or are the differences just the usual student-to-student bounce?

title: Lab 8 · ANOVA: Three Classrooms, Then Real Crashes
text:
Walkthrough
Look first
Always. Before any test:

class_means <- classrooms |>
  summarize(mean_score = mean(score), .by = classroom)

ggplot(classrooms, aes(classroom, score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.2, width = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = class_means, aes(y = mean_score),
             shape = 23, size = 5, fill = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Test scores by classroom",
       subtitle = "Dots = individual students · Diamonds = class means",
       x = NULL, y = "Test score")







Class 2 sits high, Class 3 sits low, and the spread inside each class is modest. That’s the whole ANOVA story in one picture — the rest of the lab is putting numbers on it.
The two variances, by hand
Within-group variance = the average spread inside a class. Between-group variance = the spread of the class means themselves.

class_stats <- classrooms |>
  summarize(class_mean = mean(score), class_var = var(score), .by = classroom)
class_stats

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  classroom class_mean class_var
  <fct>          <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Class 1         76.8       5.7
2 Class 2         88.4       7.3
3 Class 3         68.2       8.2

within_var  <- mean(class_stats$class_var)    # average spread inside a class
between_var <- var(class_stats$class_mean)    # spread of the class means

within_var

[1] 7.066667

between_var

[1] 102.76

between_var / within_var                      # signal-to-noise ratio

[1] 14.54151


The class means are about 14.5 times more spread out than chance bouncing within classes would produce. Strong signal.






NoteWhy won’t this ratio match aov()’s F?





Because aov() scales the between-group signal by the group size before comparing it to the noise: a gap between means built on 5 students each is stronger evidence than the same gap built on 2. With equal groups, F = group size × our hand ratio — here, 5 × 14.5 ≈ 72.7. Watch for exactly that number below. Same logic, different units.



The frequentist ANOVA

class_model <- aov(score ~ classroom, data = classrooms)
summary(class_model)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
classroom    2 1027.6   513.8   72.71 1.96e-07 ***
Residuals   12   84.8     7.1                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Reading the table against our hand math:


Mean Sq Residuals = 7.1 — our within-group variance, exactly

Mean Sq classroom = 513.8 — our between-group variance × 5 (the group size): 5 × 102.76

F(2, 12) = 72.7, p ≈ 0.0000002 — far beyond anything a null world produces. Something differs.
Which classes differ? Tukey’s HSD
The omnibus F never says which pairs. Tukey’s HSD tests every pair while keeping the family-wise false-alarm rate at 5% (remember the pile-of-t-tests problem from lecture):

TukeyHSD(class_model)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = score ~ classroom, data = classrooms)

$classroom
                 diff        lwr        upr     p adj
Class 2-Class 1  11.6   7.114603  16.085397 0.0000456
Class 3-Class 1  -8.6 -13.085397  -4.114603 0.0006899
Class 3-Class 2 -20.2 -24.685397 -15.714603 0.0000001


All three intervals exclude 0 with tiny adjusted p-values: every class differs from every other class.
The Bayesian version
Same formula, Bayesian machinery. Fit once, then let emmeans do the summarizing:

class_bayes <- brm(score ~ classroom, data = classrooms,
                   chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


class_post <- emmeans(class_bayes, ~ classroom)
class_post

 classroom emmean lower.HPD upper.HPD
 Class 1     76.8      74.2      79.7
 Class 2     88.4      85.8      91.4
 Class 3     68.2      65.6      71.0

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 


One row per class: posterior median and 95% HPD interval for that class’s mean.

pairs(class_post)

 contrast          estimate lower.HPD upper.HPD
 Class 1 - Class 2    -11.6    -15.45     -7.71
 Class 1 - Class 3      8.6      4.56     12.67
 Class 2 - Class 3     20.2     16.46     24.01

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 



plot(pairs(class_post)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2)







The interpretation rule for pairwise differences: if an interval crosses 0, zero (“no difference”) remains a credible value — no credible difference. If it excludes 0, the difference is credible. Here none of the three intervals crosses 0, so the Bayesian analysis agrees with Tukey: all three classes differ.

title: Lab 8 · ANOVA: Three Classrooms, Then Real Crashes
text:
Your Turn
Work in your own script. Comment each answer.
1. Flatten the classrooms. Erase the group differences but keep the within-class spread:

classrooms_flat <- classrooms |>
  mutate(score = case_when(

  filter(primary_cause %in% c("speeding", "distracted", "wildlife"))

3. Both traditions on crash3. Run aov() + summary(), then TukeyHSD(). In comments: which pairs differ? One pair should not — name it, and report the interval that told you so. Then fit the Bayesian version (this one samples on ~8,800 rows — give it a minute or two) and check pairs():

# aov() + summary() + TukeyHSD() on crash3
# then:
# crash_bayes <- brm(injuries ~ primary_cause, data = crash3,
#                    chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)
# crash_post  <- emmeans(crash_bayes, ~ primary_cause)
# pairs(crash_post)

Do the two traditions agree about which pair shows no real difference? And practically: how many more people are injured in the average speeding crash than the average wildlife crash?
4. (Stretch) All nine causes. Rerun aov() and TukeyHSD() on the full crashes data — 9 groups means 36 pairwise comparisons. How many come out significant? Why would running 36 unadjusted t-tests instead be a terrible idea? (Lecture’s false-alarm table has the number.)

title: Lab 8 · ANOVA: Three Classrooms, Then Real Crashes
text:
Exit Ticket
Submit a short R script to Canvas before you leave, containing:

title: Lab 6 · Joining Data
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)

glimpse(crimes)

areas |> select(community_area, community, median_income, unemployment_rate) |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  community_area community   median_income unemployment_rate

title: Lab 6 · Joining Data
text:
Walkthrough
A question neither file can answer alone
Do incidents in lower-income community areas end in arrest at a different rate than incidents in higher-income areas?
Look at what that question needs: arrest lives in crimes (one row per incident), and median_income lives in areas (one row per community area). No single file has both. This is the everyday reality of CJ data — incidents in one system, census context in another, personnel records in a third. Joins are how you put them together.
Keys first, join second
A join matches rows using a key. Before joining anything, identify:

the primary key — the column(s) that uniquely identify each row of one table
the foreign key — the matching column in the other table

community_area should be the primary key of areas: one row per area. Never assume — check:

areas |> count(community_area) |> filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: community_area <dbl>, n <int>


Zero rows means no duplicates — community_area really does uniquely identify each of the 77 areas. In crimes, community_area is a foreign key: thousands of incidents point to each area. That’s a many-to-one join — many incidents, one area each.

left_join() — and a trap on the very first try

joined_naive <- crimes |> left_join(areas, by = "community_area")

joined_naive |> select(id, community.x, community.y) |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
        id community.x    community.y   
     <dbl> <chr>          <chr>         
1    28545 Roseland       Roseland      
2    28546 South Lawndale South Lawndale
3 13707861 Belmont Cragin Belmont Cragin


Where did community.x and community.y come from? Both tables have a column named community, and it wasn’t part of the key — so R kept both copies and slapped suffixes on them. Harmless here (they agree), but confusing, and with messier data the two versions might not agree.
The cleaner habit: select just the columns you need from the right-hand table before joining.

joined <- crimes |>
  left_join(
    areas |> select(community_area, median_income, unemployment_rate),
    by = "community_area"
  )

joined |> select(id, community, arrest, median_income) |> head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
        id community      arrest median_income
     <dbl> <chr>          <lgl>          <dbl>
1    28545 Roseland       FALSE          48745
2    28546 South Lawndale TRUE           54569
3 13707861 Belmont Cragin FALSE          68284


Row-count discipline
A many-to-one join should return exactly the rows of the left table, just wider. Verify it every time:

nrow(crimes)

[1] 30000

nrow(joined)

[1] 30000


If the joined table had grown, that would mean the “one” side secretly had duplicate keys — every duplicate multiplies your rows and silently corrupts every count and mean downstream. nrow() before and after is a two-second insurance policy.
Now answer the question
Split areas at the median of median_income and compare arrest rates:

joined |>
  mutate(income_group = if_else(median_income < median(areas$median_income),
                                "Lower-income area", "Higher-income area")) |>
  summarize(arrest_rate = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = income_group)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  income_group       arrest_rate     n
  <chr>                    <dbl> <int>
1 Lower-income area        0.183 16326
2 Higher-income area       0.134 13674


Incidents in lower-income areas end in arrest about 18% of the time, versus about 13% in higher-income areas — a gap we could not have computed from either file alone.






Interpret with care. This is an area-level pattern attached to incidents. It does not tell us why — the mix of offense types differs across areas, police deployment differs, reporting differs. And median_income describes the area, not the people involved in any incident. Joins expand what you can ask; they don’t excuse you from thinking about what the answer means.



When keys don’t match: a small disaster on purpose
Our Chicago files join perfectly, which is lovely and completely unrepresentative of real life. Here’s a tiny example with the kind of flaws you’ll actually meet — a table of incidents and a lookup table of district commanders:

incidents_toy <- tribble(
  ~incident_id, ~district,
  101, "Central",
  102, "Central",
  103, "Harrison",
  104, "Shakespeare"
)

district_info <- tribble(
  ~district,    ~commander,
  "Central",    "Diaz",
  "Harrison",   "Okafor",
  "Town Hall",  "Reyes"
)

Incident 104 is in a district the lookup table doesn’t know; Town Hall has a commander but no incidents. Watch what each join does with the mismatches:

incidents_toy |> left_join(district_info, by = "district")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  incident_id district    commander
        <dbl> <chr>       <chr>    
1         101 Central     Diaz     
2         102 Central     Diaz     
3         103 Harrison    Okafor   
4         104 Shakespeare <NA>     


left_join() keeps every left-hand row and fills the holes with NA — incident 104 survives, commander unknown.

incidents_toy |> inner_join(district_info, by = "district")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  incident_id district commander
        <dbl> <chr>    <chr>    
1         101 Central  Diaz     
2         102 Central  Diaz     
3         103 Harrison Okafor   


inner_join() keeps only rows that match — incident 104 is silently gone. Four incidents in, three out, no warning. If you didn’t check row counts, you’d never know you dropped data.

anti_join() — find the orphans before you commit
anti_join() returns the left-hand rows that have no match — it’s the diagnostic you run before choosing a join:

incidents_toy |> anti_join(district_info, by = "district")   # incidents with no district info

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  incident_id district   
        <dbl> <chr>      
1         104 Shakespeare

district_info |> anti_join(incidents_toy, by = "district")   # districts with no incidents

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  district  commander
  <chr>     <chr>    
1 Town Hall Reyes    


Run it both directions on our real files:

crimes |> anti_join(areas, by = "community_area") |> nrow()

[1] 0

areas  |> anti_join(crimes, by = "community_area") |> nrow()

[1] 0


Zero and zero: every incident matches an area, every area has incidents. Our keys are clean — and the only reason we know that is that we checked.
The missing-values moment (the Ch. 18 skim, cashed in)
That NA commander left_join() created is a genuine missing value, and NAs are contagious by design:

toy_joined <- incidents_toy |> left_join(district_info, by = "district")

toy_joined |> filter(is.na(commander))   # locate the missing

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  incident_id district    commander
        <dbl> <chr>       <chr>    
1         104 Shakespeare <NA>     


The same discipline applies to missingness that arrives with the data. Our crime file has incidents with no coordinates (blocked addresses, data-entry gaps):

sum(is.na(crimes$latitude))

[1] 190

mean(crimes$latitude)

[1] NA

mean(crimes$latitude, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 41.84574


One missing value poisons the whole mean until you decide — explicitly — what to do about it. na.rm = TRUE is a decision (“compute on the cases we have”), not a reflex. The worst option is not noticing the NAs exist; that’s what sum(is.na(...)) is for.

title: Lab 4 · Tidy Data: Pivoting Longer and Wider
text:
Goal: learn to reshape data between wide and long form with pivot_longer() and pivot_wider(), and pick up the workflow habits that keep your analyses reproducible. This lab assumes you’ve read R4DS Ch. 5 (Data tidying) and Ch. 6 (Workflow: scripts and projects).
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. The Exit Ticket gets submitted to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 4 · Tidy Data: Pivoting Longer and Wider
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)

cities  <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/cities-wide.csv")
reentry <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/reentry-wide.csv")

cities holds 100 cities (simulated, but realistic): a few city characteristics plus violent crime rates for 2015–2025. reentry holds 150 reentry-program participants with a monthly employment indicator (1 = employed that month) for their first 12 months after release. Look first — always look at your data first:

glimpse(cities)
