title: Lab 4 · Tidy Data: Pivoting Longer and Wider
text:
Walkthrough
What’s wrong with this data?
Nothing — for a spreadsheet. cities is wide: each year’s violent crime rate lives in its own column (vcr_2015 … vcr_2025). That’s fine for eyeballing, but notice what it breaks in R:

You can’t put year on the x-axis of a ggplot — there is no year variable. Year is data, but it’s trapped in the column names.
You can’t summarize() an average rate per year, or filter to years after 2020, for the same reason.

R4DS’s tidy-data rules: every variable is a column, every observation is a row. Here one observation is really “a city in a year” — so tidy form needs 100 × 11 = 1,100 rows, not 100.

pivot_longer() — column names become data

cities_long <- cities |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("vcr_"),   # which columns to gather
    names_to = "year",            # where their NAMES go
    values_to = "violent_rate"    # where their VALUES go
  )

cities_long

# A tibble: 1,100 × 9
   city_id  city   region population_2020 poverty_rate unemployment_rate
   <chr>    <chr>  <chr>            <dbl>        <dbl>             <dbl>
 1 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 2 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 3 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 4 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 5 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 6 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 7 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 8 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
 9 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
10 CITY_001 City 1 South           478692         20.4              13.3
# ℹ 1,090 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: police_per_10k <dbl>, year <chr>, violent_rate <dbl>


1,100 rows — one per city-year. But look at year: it’s the text "vcr_2015", not a number. parse_number() strips the text and keeps the digits:

cities_long <- cities_long |>
  mutate(year = parse_number(year))

cities_long |> select(city, year, violent_rate)

# A tibble: 1,100 × 3
   city    year violent_rate
   <chr>  <dbl>        <dbl>
 1 City 1  2015          549
 2 City 1  2016          561
 3 City 1  2017          510
 4 City 1  2018          512
 5 City 1  2019          516
 6 City 1  2020          604
 7 City 1  2021          641
 8 City 1  2022          525
 9 City 1  2023          539
10 City 1  2024          519
# ℹ 1,090 more rows


Now the analysis is one-liners
Average violent crime rate per year, across all 100 cities:

cities_long |>
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(violent_rate), .by = year)

# A tibble: 11 × 2
    year mean_rate
   <dbl>     <dbl>
 1  2015      431.
 2  2016      419.
 3  2017      415.
 4  2018      415.
 5  2019      404.
 6  2020      460.
 7  2021      459.
 8  2022      392.
 9  2023      378.
10  2024      372.
11  2025      373.


Notice the story hiding in there — rates climb into 2020–2021, then fall. And a line plot over time, impossible ten minutes ago, is now routine:

cities_long |>
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(violent_rate), .by = c(region, year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_rate, color = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Violent crime rate by region, 2015-2025",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean violent crimes per 100k", color = "Region")








pivot_wider() — and back again
Sometimes you want wide (for a table in a report, or to compute 2025 minus 2015):

cities_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = violent_rate,
    names_prefix = "vcr_"
  ) |>
  select(city, region, vcr_2015, vcr_2025) |>
  mutate(change = vcr_2025 - vcr_2015)

# A tibble: 100 × 5
   city    region    vcr_2015 vcr_2025 change
   <chr>   <chr>        <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>
 1 City 1  South          549      525    -24
 2 City 2  Midwest        660      456   -204
 3 City 3  South          401      277   -124
 4 City 4  South          326      203   -123
 5 City 5  Midwest        424      383    -41
 6 City 6  Midwest        535      371   -164
 7 City 7  Northeast      246      192    -54
 8 City 8  South          364      265    -99
 9 City 9  West           278      177   -101
10 City 10 South          404      277   -127
# ℹ 90 more rows


pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() are inverses — data flows freely between shapes once you can name which columns hold names and which hold values.
Workflow hygiene: scripts and projects
Three habits from R4DS Ch. 6 that I will hold you to all semester:


Everything in a script, nothing only in the console. The console is for experimenting; the script is the record. If it matters, it’s in the script.

Use an RStudio Project for this course. File > New Project… once, then always open the course via the .Rproj file. Your working directory is then always the project folder, paths stay relative, and your code runs on any machine — including mine when I grade it.

Never rely on the Environment pane. Objects in memory are disposable; your script + your data are the source of truth. Prove it to yourself right now: Session > Restart R, then re-run your script top to bottom. If it doesn’t reproduce everything, fix the script — you just saved a future you from a very bad day. (I also recommend Tools > Global Options > un-check “Restore .RData into workspace at startup.”)

title: Lab 2 · First Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)

prisoners <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/prisoners.csv")

prisoners holds records for 300 incarcerated persons (simulated, but realistic): demographics, offense type, sentence, and well-being measures. Look at it first — always look at your data first:

title: Lab 2 · First Plots with ggplot2
text:
Walkthrough
A histogram — the shape of a numeric variable
Today’s lecture was about summarizing numeric variables. A histogram is the picture version:

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of incarcerated persons",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Count")







Anatomy of every ggplot: data (prisoners), aesthetics (aes(x = age) — which variables map to which visual channels), and geometry (geom_histogram() — how to draw them).
How does the picture relate to the numbers?

prisoners |>
  summarize(mean_age = mean(age), median_age = median(age), sd_age = sd(age))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_age median_age sd_age
     <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
1     34.5         34   10.2








NoteWhat’s the |> symbol?





That’s the pipe — it feeds whatever is on its left into the function on its right, so you can read code top-to-bottom as “take the data, then do this, then do that.” R4DS uses it everywhere. In older code (and in the Stanton book) you’ll see %>% instead — for our purposes they’re interchangeable.



A bar chart — counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = offense_type)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Offense types", x = NULL, y = "Count")







A boxplot — a distribution split by groups

The five-number-summary as a picture, one box per offense type:

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = offense_type, y = sentence_years)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  labs(title = "Sentence length by offense type",
       x = NULL, y = "Sentence (years)")







The box is the middle 50% (median = the line inside); the dots are outliers — the same “one 30-year sentence” problem from lecture, visible instantly.

title: Homework 12 · Your Final Model + Project Checkpoint 4
text:
Instructions: complete the following in a single .R script file and submit it via Canvas for credit. This week the entire homework is about your final project — there is no practice dataset. Every part below uses the dataset you selected in Session 7 and have been building through Checkpoints 1–3.
(Session 12 closes with a code clinic — no new material, just you, your code, and me. Bring whatever state this homework is in: the clinic exists to unstick Parts 1–3 while you still have a week to finish them.)

title: Homework 12 · Your Final Model + Project Checkpoint 4
text:
Part 1: Your Cleaned Variables
Run summary() and str() on the cleaned and transformed variables you plan to use in your final model — the outcome and every predictor. Paste the output into your script as comments directly below each call, so I can see exactly what you saw.
# For example, if your model variables live in a cleaned data frame:
model_vars <- my_data |>
  select(outcome_variable, predictor_1, predictor_2, predictor_3)

summary(model_vars)
# (paste the output here as comments)
str(model_vars)
# (paste the output here as comments)
What I’m checking: every variable is the type your model needs (numeric predictors numeric, a binary outcome coded 0/1, logical, or a two-level factor), the values are plausible (no impossible numbers, no accidental character columns), and any missing values are ones you know about.

title: Homework 12 · Your Final Model + Project Checkpoint 4
text:
Part 2: Your Model Equation
Write out, in a comment, the equation you plan to use to answer your research question. For example, if you were running a multiple linear regression model on violent crime, it might look like this:
# ViolentCrime = Intercept + Poverty + HighSchool + SingleParent + Error
Be sure to specify whether you’re running a linear or logistic regression model — and add one sentence on why: what type of variable is your outcome?
It can be that simple. I just want to see that you understand your dependent variable and all of the independent variables you plan to include in the model. Make sure your equation matches the cleaned variables in your Part 1 output — every term in the equation should appear in your summary()/str() results, and nothing extra.

title: Homework 12 · Your Final Model + Project Checkpoint 4
text:
Part 3: Project Checkpoint 4 (final)






This is the last of the four project checkpoints. Checkpoint 1 described your variables, Checkpoint 2 measured their associations, Checkpoint 3 fit a first model — Checkpoint 4 is the real thing: the model you intend to defend at presentations. It is graded on completion and quality of reasoning, not on whether your results are exciting. Null findings, honestly interpreted, are full-credit findings. The Session 12 code clinic comes before this checkpoint on purpose: bring the shaky parts to class, then finish the checkpoint with those problems solved.



In a clearly marked section at the end of your .R script (e.g., # ---- PROJECT CHECKPOINT 4 ----):

Fit your final model — in both traditions. The frequentist fit (lm() for a continuous outcome, glm(family = binomial) for a binary one) and the Bayesian fit (brm() with the same formula — default priors are fine, standard settings: chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0; expect the compile pause). Both fits must match your Part 2 equation. (This is the final-project requirement — see Step 3 — so Checkpoint 4 is where you get it running with a week of slack.)
Interpret the key coefficients in comments, on the right scale:

Linear: the change in your outcome per one-unit change in each predictor, holding the others constant — with units.
Logistic: exponentiate. Odds ratios per one-unit change, holding the others constant — and at least one predicted probability for a concrete, meaningful case, as we did in class.
Include the uncertainty from both fits — the 95% CI and the 95% credible interval — plus one sentence comparing them: do the two traditions agree here, and what does the posterior let you say that the p-value doesn’t?

Produce ONE table or figure you plan to show at presentations. A tidy coefficient table, a plot of predicted values or probabilities, a well-labeled scatterplot with your fitted line — your choice, but it must be presentation-ready: real variable names, labeled axes or columns, a title. Not raw console output.
Write the three sentences you’d say about it to a non-statistician. As a comment block. Imagine a police chief, a judge, or a city council member: no “log-odds,” no “p < .05,” no Greek letters. What did you find, how sure are you, and why should they care? These three sentences are the spine of your Session 13 presentation — write them now and presentation prep gets much easier.

If anything above breaks — the model won’t run, a coefficient makes no sense, the output contradicts Checkpoint 3 — say so in your comments — and if it surfaced by clinic day, bring it to class. Finding that out now, with a week before the full project is due, is precisely what this checkpoint is for.

title: Homework 12 · Your Final Model + Project Checkpoint 4
text:
If You Get Stuck
If you run into problems cleaning or transforming your data, email me the code you’re using (copy and paste into the email is fine — no need to attach a script), along with a short explanation of what you’re trying to do and what the issue is. I’m happy to help with the data-cleaning process. There’s usually a simple fix that’s easy to miss when you’re still learning R.
Looking ahead: this checkpoint is due the Sunday after Session 12; the full project (script, dataset, and written report) follows one week later, due via Canvas before midnight the Sunday before Session 13. Presentations are at Session 13. Details on the Final Project page.

title: Homework 10 · Correlation with the Chicago Areas + Project Checkpoint 2
text:
Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answers to any interpretive questions. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
Parts 1–3 use the community-area level of the Chicago anchor dataset (codebook) — 77 community areas with 2025 crime rates and Census-based structural measures. One row = one area, not one person; several questions turn on remembering that.

title: Homework 10 · Correlation with the Chicago Areas + Project Checkpoint 2
text:
Setup
library(tidyverse)
library(correlation)

areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv")
glimpse(areas)

title: Homework 10 · Correlation with the Chicago Areas + Project Checkpoint 2
section: Part 1: Plot It, Then Summarize It
text:
Part 1: Plot It, Then Summarize It

Make a scatterplot of violent_rate (y-axis) against pct_vacant (x-axis), the share of an area’s housing units sitting vacant. Add a fitted line with geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE). In a comment: describe the shape — direction, roughly linear or not, any outliers that could be driving things (today’s Anscombe lesson).
Compute Pearson’s r for that pair with cor(). In a comment: interpret it in one sentence using the direction-and-strength language from lecture (e.g., “a [strength] [direction] association between …”).
Now the same two steps — scatterplot, then cor() — for violent_rate against median_age. In a comment: interpret this r the same way.
In a comment (2–3 sentences): your r in Q3 should be very close to zero. State one thing a near-zero r does tell you and one thing it does not rule out — and say what, in your Q3 plot, lets you go beyond the number alone. (Hint: what shape of relationship did the lecture show hiding behind r ≈ 0?)

title: Homework 10 · Correlation with the Chicago Areas + Project Checkpoint 2
text:
Part 2: Frequentist Inference on r

Run cor.test(areas$pct_vacant, areas$violent_rate). In a comment: report the result in one lecture-style sentence — r, degrees of freedom, p-value, and the 95% CI — and state what the null hypothesis was.
Run the matrix version with the correlation package:
areas |>
  select(violent_rate, pct_vacant, pct_renter, pct_bachelors) |>
  correlation()
In a comment: which variable has the strongest association with violent_rate, and which the weakest? Why are these p-values Holm-adjusted — what Session 8 problem is that protecting you from?
In a comment (2–3 sentences): your Q6 output shows pct_renter correlates positively with violent_rate. A classmate concludes: “renters are more dangerous than homeowners.” Name the mistake, explain why these data cannot support that sentence, and write a corrected sentence that stays at the level the data actually measure.

title: Homework 10 · Correlation with the Chicago Areas + Project Checkpoint 2
text:
Part 3: Bayesian Correlation

Run the Bayesian version on violent_rate and pct_bachelors, leaving the prior at its default:
set.seed(705)   # the Bayesian version samples from the posterior
areas |>
  select(violent_rate, pct_bachelors) |>
  correlation(bayesian = TRUE)
In a comment: report rho, the 95% credible interval, pd, and the Bayes factor — then one sentence saying what the evidence shows, including direction and strength.
Rerun Q8 with bayesian_prior = "wide". In a comment: what changed, how much, and why so little? (What about this dataset lets the data overpower the prior choice?)
In a comment (2–3 sentences): state one thing the 95% credible interval from Q8 lets you say that a 95% confidence interval never could. (Session 5 taught you the careful long-run reading; contrast it directly.)

title: Homework 10 · Correlation with the Chicago Areas + Project Checkpoint 2
text:
Part 4: Project Checkpoint 2






This section uses YOUR final-project dataset — the one you explored in Checkpoint 1 (Homework 8). This is the second of four checkpoints, and it does for your project exactly what Parts 1–3 did for Chicago: put numbers on the relationships you think are there. What you find here feeds directly into Checkpoint 3, where you’ll run the regression these associations point toward. As before, Checkpoint 2 is graded on completion and quality of reasoning — not polish, and not whether your correlations turn out strong.



In a clearly marked section at the end of your .R script (e.g., # ---- PROJECT CHECKPOINT 2 ----):

Compute and visualize the association between your outcome variable and each of your 2–3 candidate predictors from Checkpoint 1. (Swapping a predictor since Checkpoint 1 is fine — one comment line saying why.)

For each numeric predictor: a scatterplot against your outcome plus Pearson’s r — or Spearman’s rho if the plot shows serious skew or outliers, with a comment saying why you switched.
For a categorical predictor: r doesn’t apply — make a grouped boxplot or a table of group means instead, and say that’s why.

Run one full correlation test — frequentist cor.test() or Bayesian correlation(bayesian = TRUE), your choice — on the predictor that looks most promising, and report it in one lecture-style sentence.
Write a paragraph (as a comment block, roughly 5–8 sentences) covering:

what each association looks like — direction, strength, and whether the shape in the plot makes the coefficient a fair summary (the Anscombe check);
any surprises — a predictor you expected to matter that shows almost nothing, a sign pointing the “wrong” way, an association that one outlier appears to own;
which predictors now look worth carrying into your Checkpoint 3 regression, and whether any look weak enough to reconsider.


If something here looks broken — every correlation is essentially zero, your outcome barely varies, a predictor turns out to be categorical when you thought it was numeric — say so in your paragraph and come talk to me. Finding that now, two checkpoints before the final write-up, is this assignment working exactly as designed.

title: Homework 7 · Workshop Write-Up & Final-Project Dataset Selection
text:
Instructions: complete the following in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answering the interpretive prompts. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
This homework finishes what Lab 7 started: the pipeline, run on the dataset you’re proposing for your final project — and it doubles as your formal dataset selection, which is due now so your project can start moving at the Session 8 checkpoint. Requirements and milestones for the project live on the final project page.
If Lab 7 went well, most of Part 1 is already sitting in your lab script — clean it up, complete what’s missing, and answer every prompt below in comments. If your lab dataset died on the operating table (it happens, and it’s why we workshop first), find its replacement, run the same pipeline on it, and say in a comment what killed candidate #1.

title: Homework 7 · Workshop Write-Up & Final-Project Dataset Selection
text:
Part 1: The Pipeline Write-Up
Run each step on your proposed dataset. Every prompt marked (comment) gets an explicit written answer in your script.

Import. Working code that reads your dataset into R (read_csv(), read_excel(), or whatever the format requires), including any fixes for columns R guessed wrong — dates especially. I will run your script, so if the data can’t be downloaded from a URL, say where the file comes from in a comment and use a plain relative path (no setwd(), no absolute paths).
Data source (comment). Where the data comes from: who collected it, what it covers (years, geography), and a link or citation. If you had to request, scrape, or hand-download it, say so.
Unit of analysis (comment). One row = one what? (One incident? One person? One agency-year? One neighborhood?) If the answer took you a while to figure out, note what confused you — that confusion is diagnostic.
Key variables and levels of measurement (comment). List the variables you plan to use in the final project. For each, give its level of measurement — nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio, from Session 1 — and note whether R currently stores it sensibly (a nominal variable stored as numbers, like race = 1, 2, 3, is a trap worth flagging now).
Missingness. Count missing values in every column (the across() + pivot_longer() pattern from Lab 7 or any equivalent). (comment) Which of your key variables are affected, why is the data missing (structural, or trouble?), and what is your plan — drop rows, drop a variable, or find supplemental data?
One descriptive finding. A summary table (summarize() or count()) that shows something substantively interesting about a key variable. (comment) State the finding in one precise sentence — numbers included, no more claimed than the table shows.
One visualization. A polished ggplot — labeled axes, title, units. (comment) One sentence on what the plot shows, and one on any surprise or complication it revealed.

title: Homework 7 · Workshop Write-Up & Final-Project Dataset Selection
text:
Part 2: Formal Dataset Selection
This section is your dataset-selection submission for the final project — the declaration the rest of the semester builds on. Parts of it (source, import, preview) already exist in your Part 1 code; what’s new is the commitment. Add a clearly-marked final section to your script that provides:

Dataset name and source — repeated in one place, even if it appears in Part 1.
Your research question, stated in one sentence. A question, not a topic: “does X differ by / relate to Y,” not “sentencing.”
The variables you plan to use to answer it, with each one’s type (numeric, categorical) — a short list, drawn from your Part 1 inventory.
A selection-criteria check (comments) — confirm, honestly, that your dataset:

concerns a criminal-justice topic (e.g., policing, crime rates, courts, corrections, public opinion);
reads into R successfully — via read_csv(), read_excel(), or data() for a built-in set (your Part 1 import code is the proof);
includes numeric variables suitable for correlation and regression analysis — the techniques coming in Sessions 10–11, which your final project will use.

A basic preview — glimpse() and/or summary() of your imported data, with the call left in the script so I see its output when I run it.

Can’t decide between two datasets? That’s allowed at this stage: run Part 1 on your primary candidate, include import code and the Part 2 declaration for both, and come to Session 8 ready to discuss the tradeoff — we’ll settle it at your project checkpoint.

Deliverable and Due Date

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answers to any interpretive questions. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
This homework uses the Alaska traffic-crash data from Lab 5 — 20,000 real-world-style crash incidents. Our research question: do crashes involving an intoxicated driver injure more people than crashes that don’t?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 1: Import and Clean

Import the crash data directly from the web:
library(tidyverse)
crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv")
Check what read_csv() guessed with spec() or glimpse(). One column that should be a date is not. Fix it using mdy() from lubridate (as in Lab 5), and verify your parse worked with sum(is.na(crashes$date)).
Create a year column from your parsed date and count crashes per year. In a comment: one year has almost no crashes — is that a data problem or something else? (Hint: check the latest date in the data with max().)

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 2: Point Estimates

Calculate the mean number of injuries separately for crashes with an intoxicated driver (intox_any == 1) and without (intox_any == 0). You can use the Lab 2 approach:
crashes |> summarize(mean_injuries = mean(injuries), .by = intox_any)
In a comment: write down each mean. Which group has the higher average injury count? Remember what these numbers are — point estimates, not the final word.

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 3: Standard Deviations

Calculate the standard deviation of injuries for each group (add sd() to your summarize()).
In a comment: compare the variability. Which group’s injury counts vary more?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 4: Visualize

Create a boxplot of injuries for the two groups. Because intox_any is stored as 0/1, wrap it in factor():
ggplot(crashes, aes(x = factor(intox_any), y = injuries)) +
  geom_boxplot()
In a comment: interpret the plot. Injury counts are small whole numbers, so the boxes look blocky — can you see a difference between the groups, or do you need inference to settle it?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 5: Sampling Variability

Resample each group (with replacement, at its full size) 100 times and compute the distribution of differences in mean injuries (intoxicated − sober), as we did in class:
set.seed(705)
sober <- crashes$injuries[crashes$intox_any == 0]
intox <- crashes$injuries[crashes$intox_any == 1]

mean_diffs <- replicate(100, {
  mean(sample(intox, length(intox), replace = TRUE)) -
    mean(sample(sober, length(sober), replace = TRUE))
})
Plot a histogram of mean_diffs and compute quantile(mean_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975)).
In a comment: what does the spread of the histogram suggest? Are the resampled differences consistently on one side of zero?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 6: Confidence Interval with t.test()

Run a two-sample t-test comparing injuries across the two groups:
t.test(injuries ~ intox_any, data = crashes)
In a comment: copy down the 95% confidence interval. Does it include 0? What does that tell us about the difference? (Careful with direction: R computes group 0 − group 1 here, so compare the sign against your Part 5 histogram.)

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 7: A Proportion, for Practice

Compute a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all crashes that involve an intoxicated driver:
prop.test(sum(crashes$intox_any), n = nrow(crashes))
In a comment: report the interval in one defensible sentence — one that would survive the “Saying It Out Loud” slide from class.

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Wrap-Up Questions (answer in comments)

How does the confidence interval help us make an inference about the population of Alaska crashes, when we only ever see a sample?
What would happen to the width of the CI if we doubled the sample size? Why?
How does this example compare to John Snow’s inference about the cholera pumps?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
R4DS Exercises (required)
From your R4DS reading for Session 6 — Ch. 19 — Joins and Ch. 18 — Missing values. These use nycflights13 again (installed for Homework 2).
Work these in the same .R script, under a # ---- R4DS ---- header. All four circle one question: which rows didn’t match, and why?

19.2.4 #1 — how do weather and airports relate? Name the key.
19.3.4 #3 — does every departing flight have weather data?
19.3.4 #4 — tail numbers with no match in planes: what do they have in common?
18.3.4 #1 — is that missingness related to carrier? Do this one right after 19.3.4 #4; they are the same investigation from two directions.

This is the skill Session 7’s workshop leans on hardest: joining files that don’t line up cleanly.

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answers to any interpretive questions. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
Parts 1–3 use the built-in mtcars dataset (type mtcars in the console — it’s always available, no loading needed).

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 1: Contingency Tables

Create a contingency table of mtcars showing the number of cars by number of cylinders (cyl) and number of gears (gear). Use either the classic table(mtcars$cyl, mtcars$gear) or the tidyverse route from Lab 3:
library(tidyverse)
mtcars |>
  count(cyl, gear) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = gear, values_from = n)
How many cars have 4 cylinders and 4 gears?
What is the probability that a randomly selected car (out of all 32) has both 4 gears and 6 cylinders? (This is a joint probability — divide the cell count by the grand total, not by a row or column total.)
What is the probability that a randomly selected car has 6 cylinders? (A marginal probability.)

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 2: Conditional Probability

What is the conditional probability that a car has 6 cylinders given that it has 4 gears? Compute it in R (not by eye) — e.g., filter() to the condition and take a proportion, or divide the right counts.
Interpretation (in a comment): your answers to Q3 and Q5 use the same cell of the table but give different numbers. Explain in one or two sentences why — what changed between the two questions?

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 3: Visualizing Distributions

Create a bar plot showing the distribution of cylinders.
Create a bar plot showing the distribution of gears.
Create a grouped bar plot of the number of cars by cyl and gear. You may use ggplot (geom_bar(position = "dodge") — remember to make the grouping variable a factor) or base R’s barplot(..., beside = TRUE) — your choice.

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 4: Real Data

Load the course anchor data:
library(tidyverse)
crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv")
Compute the marginal probability that an incident ended in arrest: P(arrest). (Hint: arrest is logical, and mean() of a logical is a proportion.)
Compute the conditional probability of arrest given each crime category: P(arrest | Violent), P(arrest | Property), P(arrest | Other). (Hint: summarize() with .by = crime_category.)
Compute P(arrest | domestic == TRUE) and compare it to your overall P(arrest) from Q11.
Interpretation (in a comment): based on Q12 and Q13 — which variable (crime_category or domestic) is closer to independent of arrest in these data, and how can you tell? Use the definition from lecture: A and B are independent when P(A | B) = P(A).

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 5: Reversing a Conditional
A roadside field drug test has these properties:

5% of stopped drivers actually carry drugs (the base rate)
The test flags 90% of drivers who carry (sensitivity)
The test also flags 8% of drivers who do not carry (false-positive rate)


For 1,000 stops, build the counting table from lecture — how many carriers get flagged, how many non-carriers get flagged? You can do the arithmetic directly in R (e.g., 1000 * 0.05 * 0.90) or lay it out with tribble(). Report the total number of flagged drivers.
Using your counts from Q15, compute P(carries | flagged) — the probability a flagged driver actually carries.
Interpretation (in a comment): the manufacturer advertises the test as “90% accurate.” In one or two sentences: why is your Q16 answer nowhere near 90%, and which conditional probability does the “90%” actually describe?

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 6: R4DS Exercises (required)
From your R4DS reading for Session 4 — Ch. 5 and Ch. 6. No new packages; table1–table3 ship with the tidyverse.
Work these in the same .R script, under a # ---- R4DS ---- header.

5.2.1 #1 — for table1, table2, and table3: what is one row, and what is one column? (Answer in comments.)
5.2.1 #2 — sketch the steps you’d take to compute a rate. You are not expected to write working code yet; name the moves in comments.
Ch. 5 has only this one exercise block — the pivot_longer()/pivot_wider() sections have no exercises at all.
Ch. 6 has no exercises worth assigning. Instead, do this and say so in a comment: create an RStudio Project for this course (§6.2.3) and move your scripts into it. Every lab from here on assumes you have one.

title: Final Project
text: The final project integrates conceptual understanding with applied statistical skills in R. You will identify a research question, analyze a real criminal justice dataset, and interpret your findings using the tools from this course — building it incrementally across the second half of the semester rather than in a December scramble.

title: Final Project
text:
1. Purpose
Demonstrate your ability to apply statistical reasoning and R coding skills to a real-world criminal justice dataset: identify a research question, analyze data, and interpret findings using the concepts learned throughout the course.

title: Final Project
text:
2. Project components
Your submission must include all of the following:

R script (.R) — fully runnable code that produces your results
Your dataset — submitted so I can reproduce your analysis
Output — tables, figures, and statistical output from R, as applicable, incorporated in your written report
Written report (.docx) — a short report (3–5 pages) explaining your research question, dataset, methods, results, and interpretation

title: Final Project
text:
3. Steps and expectations
Step 1 — Find a dataset. Select a dataset related to criminal justice (policing, courts, corrections, crime, public opinion, etc.) that can be imported into R (CSV, Excel, or an R dataset). It must include enough numeric variables for regression analysis. (Formal selection criteria and the submission form are part of the Session 7 assignment.)
Step 2 — Define your research question. Keep it focused and testable. Examples: “Are violent crime rates associated with police staffing levels?” or “Do education and income predict victimization (or arrests)?”
Step 3 — Apply statistical tools from class. Use descriptive statistics, visualizations, and measures of association. You must include a linear regression or logistic regression for credit. Your final model must be reported in both traditions — the frequentist fit (lm()/glm()) and the Bayesian fit (brm(), default priors are fine — say so) — with at least one sentence comparing what each tells you (e.g., the CI vs. the credible interval, or what the posterior lets you say that the p-value doesn’t). This is the both-traditions course; the capstone shows you can drive both. Supporting analyses (descriptives, correlations) may be run in whichever tradition you prefer.
Step 4 — Write and submit your report. Organize clearly: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. Interpret results in plain language.

title: Final Project
text:
4. Grading criteria
The project is 30% of your course grade: the written report, script, and output are 22%, and the in-class presentation is 8%.

The written report & code (22% of course grade)

Quality of analysis
7%
Right tools for the question; final model in both traditions with sound model choices; assumptions/diagnostics addressed
Correct core analysis; both traditions present but one is perfunctory; minor tool misfits
Wrong tool for the question, a missing tradition, or mechanical errors that change conclusions


Interpretation & honesty
6%
Every claim matches the output; magnitude interpreted in real units; limitations (incl. null or weak results) owned plainly
Mostly accurate; occasional overclaiming or a p-value/posterior misreading; limitations thin
“Significant” treated as “important”; causal language from observational data; results oversold


Organization & writing
4%
Clear Introduction → Methods → Results → Discussion; labeled figures/tables referenced in text; graduate-level prose
Structure present but uneven; figures unlabeled or orphaned
Hard to follow; output pasted without narrative


Completeness & reproducibility
5%
Script runs top to bottom on the submitted data; all four components present; seed set where results are sampled
Runs with minor fixes; a component thin but present
Script errors out, data missing, or a required component absent





The presentation (8% of course grade)
Format: 8 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Presentation order is announced at the Session 12 code clinic. You may present slides or your rendered report on screen — either is fine, but you must show your one key visualization and be ready to walk through any line of your code on request (see the AI policy; not being able to explain your own code will cost you well beyond the presentation points).








Criterion
Weight
What earns it




The question, motivated
2%
A listener knows within a minute what you asked, of what data, and why anyone should care


Sound interpretation, limits included
3%
Findings stated accurately with magnitudes; at least one limitation named without prompting; questions handled honestly (including “I don’t know”)


The key visualization
1.5%
One figure that carries the finding, readable from the back of the room, honestly captioned


Code ownership
1.5%
Any line of your script, explained on request, in your own words



Running long is the classic failure: practice once with a timer. At 8 minutes you’ll be stopped so everyone presents.
