title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different numbers and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 2 (and the midterm’s descriptives section) will feel routine.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
library(modeest)   # for mfv(); install.packages("modeest") once if needed
officers <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/officers.csv")
nbhd     <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/neighborhoods.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Problem 1 · Three kinds of typical
Response times (in minutes) for 10 priority calls one Friday night — nine routine, plus one call that sat in the queue through a shift change:
response <- c(4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 42)
Compute the mean, median, and mode. Which of the three would you not want on the department’s public dashboard, and why?






Tip





Solution

response <- c(4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 42)

mean(response)

[1] 9.8

median(response)

[1] 6

mfv(response)

[1] 6


The one 42-minute call drags the mean to 9.8 minutes even though no routine call took longer than 9 — classic central-tendency behavior: the mean chases outliers, while the median (6) and mode (6) stay with the bulk of the data.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Problem 2 · Same mean, different story
Two detective units both average 30 open cases per detective — but look at the individual caseloads:
unit_a <- c(18, 30, 42)
unit_b <- c(29, 30, 31)
Compute for each unit: the range (with range() and diff()), the deviations from the mean, the sum of squared deviations, and the population variance and SD by hand. Then run var() and sd() — why don’t the built-ins match your hand calculations?






Tip





Solution

unit_a <- c(18, 30, 42)
unit_b <- c(29, 30, 31)

diff(range(unit_a)); diff(range(unit_b))

[1] 24


[1] 2

unit_a - mean(unit_a)

[1] -12   0  12

unit_b - mean(unit_b)

[1] -1  0  1

# Sum of squares
sum((unit_a - mean(unit_a))^2)

[1] 288

sum((unit_b - mean(unit_b))^2)

[1] 2

# Population variance and SD (divide by n)
sum((unit_a - mean(unit_a))^2) / 3; sqrt(sum((unit_a - mean(unit_a))^2) / 3)

[1] 96


[1] 9.797959

sum((unit_b - mean(unit_b))^2) / 3; sqrt(sum((unit_b - mean(unit_b))^2) / 3)

[1] 0.6666667


[1] 0.8164966

# R's built-ins
var(unit_a); sd(unit_a)

[1] 144


[1] 12

var(unit_b); sd(unit_b)

[1] 1


[1] 1


Identical centers, radically different dispersion: unit A’s SD (~9.8 population / 12 sample) says workloads genuinely vary; unit B’s (~1) says everyone carries the same load. The built-ins disagree with your hand math because R divides by n − 1, not n — Session 4 pays off that IOU.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Problem 3 · Audit the briefing note
A draft briefing memo about Problem 1’s data contains two sentences:


“The typical priority call waited about 10 minutes for an officer.”
“Half of priority calls had an officer on scene within 6 minutes.”


One is defensible, one is misleading. Which is which — and rewrite the misleading one in a single honest sentence.






Tip





Solution

response <- c(4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 42)
c(mean = mean(response), median = median(response))

  mean median 
   9.8    6.0 


Sentence (b) is defensible — it is exactly what the median (6) means. Sentence (a) launders the mean (9.8) into the word “typical,” but nine of ten calls beat 10 minutes; only the queued outlier pushes the average there. An honest rewrite: “Half of priority calls had an officer within 6 minutes; one call held during a shift change took 42.” With skewed data, “typical” belongs to the median — and outliers deserve their own sentence, not a hiding place inside the mean.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
section: Problem 4 · Real data: how much do officers sleep?
text:
Problem 4 · Real data: how much do officers sleep?
Using officers, summarize sleep_hours — mean, median, SD, min, max — and make a histogram (binwidth = 0.5). Is the distribution roughly symmetric or skewed? How do you know from the numbers alone?






Tip





Solution

officers |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours), median_sleep = median(sleep_hours),
            sd_sleep = sd(sleep_hours), min = min(sleep_hours), max = max(sleep_hours))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  mean_sleep median_sleep sd_sleep   min   max
       <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1       6.40          6.4     1.40   2.5    10

ggplot(officers, aes(sleep_hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Sleep per night (hours)", y = "Officers")







Mean (6.40) and median (6.4) are essentially identical — the numeric signature of a roughly symmetric distribution, which the histogram confirms. (Compare Problem 1, where mean and median disagreed badly: that gap is the skew detector.)

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
section: Problem 5 · The empirical rule, checked against reality
text:
Problem 5 · The empirical rule, checked against reality
If sleep_hours were perfectly normal, about 68% of officers would fall within ±1 SD of the mean and about 95% within ±2 SD. Compute the actual shares. (Hint: mean(abs(x - m) <= s) — the same mean-of-a-logical move as always.)






Tip





Solution

m <- mean(officers$sleep_hours)
s <- sd(officers$sleep_hours)

mean(abs(officers$sleep_hours - m) <= s)       # within +/- 1 SD

[1] 0.695

mean(abs(officers$sleep_hours - m) <= 2 * s)   # within +/- 2 SD

[1] 0.955


About 69.5% and 95.5% — within a couple points of the empirical rule’s 68/95 benchmarks. That is what “the SD tells you how typical or extreme a value is” means in practice: for bell-shaped data, mean ± 2 SD brackets nearly everyone.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
section: Problem 6 · A Poisson in the wild
text:
Problem 6 · A Poisson in the wild
Using nbhd (500 neighborhoods), make a bar chart of assaults (last year’s count per neighborhood), then compute its mean and variance. Now simulate 500 draws from a Poisson with the same λ — rpois(500, lambda = mean(nbhd$assaults)) — and compare the two count tables. Does the textbook distribution fit the real one?






Tip





Solution

ggplot(nbhd, aes(assaults)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Assaults last year", y = "Neighborhoods")






nbhd |> summarize(mean_assaults = mean(assaults), var_assaults = var(assaults))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_assaults var_assaults
          <dbl>        <dbl>
1          1.07         1.69

set.seed(705)
table(nbhd$assaults)


  0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7 
219 134  87  32  17   4   5   2 

table(rpois(500, lambda = mean(nbhd$assaults)))


  0   1   2   3   4   5 
148 192 102  45  11   2 


The broad shape matches — right-skewed counts of a rare event, exactly the Poisson’s territory. But look closer: the real data have more zeros (219 vs ~148) and a longer tail (counts up to 7 vs 5), and the variance (1.69) exceeds the mean (1.07), where a true Poisson would have them equal. Real CJ counts are usually messier than the textbook distribution — a mismatch called overdispersion that you’ll meet again later in the course.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different numbers and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 4 (and the midterm’s sampling questions) will feel routine. Your random numbers will differ from the solutions’ unless you run set.seed(705) immediately before each simulation — close is what you’re checking for, not digit-for-digit matches.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
nbhd <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/neighborhoods.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 1 · The long run arrives slowly
text:
Problem 1 · The long run arrives slowly
Suppose 12% of intake drug screens at a jail come back positive. Simulate one week (25 screens), one quarter (250), and one decade (25,000) with sample(), and compute the positive proportion for each. How close does each get to 0.12?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 25,    replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.12, 0.88)))

[1] 0.2

mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 250,   replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.12, 0.88)))

[1] 0.156

mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 25000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.12, 0.88)))

[1] 0.12204


This run: ≈ 0.20, ≈ 0.16, ≈ 0.122. A week of screens can sit far from the truth; a decade practically is the truth — the law of large numbers. The practical warning runs the other way: any rate computed from 25 cases deserves deep suspicion.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
text:
Problem 2 · Build a sampling distribution
Treat the 500 neighborhoods in nbhd as a population, and imagine an analyst who can only audit 40 neighborhoods at a time. Using the tibble() + map_dbl() pattern from the Session 4 slides, draw 1,000 samples of 40 and keep each sample’s mean of assaults. Histogram the 1,000 means and mark the true population mean with a geom_vline(). Where is the distribution centered?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
sample_means <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_assaults = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(nbhd$assaults, size = 40))))

mean(nbhd$assaults)                 # the truth

[1] 1.072

mean(sample_means$mean_assaults)    # center of the 1,000 sample means

[1] 1.056875

ggplot(sample_means, aes(mean_assaults)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(nbhd$assaults), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean assaults (n = 40)", y = "Number of samples")







The 1,000 means pile up in a bell centered almost exactly on the true mean (≈ 1.06 vs 1.07 this run) — a sampling distribution in action: individual samples wander, but the collection of sample means is centered on the truth.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 3 · The standard error, both ways
text:
Problem 3 · The standard error, both ways
Session 4’s rule: the formula must survive a simulation check. Compute the SD of your 1,000 sample means from Problem 2, then the formula version sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(40). How close?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
sample_means <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_assaults = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(nbhd$assaults, size = 40))))

sd(sample_means$mean_assaults)     # SE from the simulation

[1] 0.196668

sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(40)       # SE from the formula

[1] 0.2058036


≈ 0.20 simulated vs ≈ 0.21 from the formula — the standard error is just the SD of the sampling distribution, and SD / sqrt(n) predicts it without ever running the simulation. That’s why one sample plus the formula is enough for the inference we start next session.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
text:
Problem 4 · Spot the error
A report on the Problem 2 audit states:

“The standard error of about 0.21 tells us how much individual neighborhoods vary around the citywide average.”

Fix the sentence. Then: if the analyst’s budget grew to n = 160 neighborhoods per audit, what would happen to the SE? Verify with the formula.






Tip





Solution

c(se_40  = sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(40),
  se_160 = sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(160))

    se_40    se_160 
0.2058036 0.1029018 


Wrong quantity: describing how individual neighborhoods vary is the standard deviation’s job (≈ 1.3 here). The standard error describes how much the sample mean would move across repeated audits of 40 — a fix: “If we re-drew the 40-neighborhood audit, the estimated mean would typically shift by about 0.21 assaults.” And quadrupling n to 160 halves the SE (≈ 0.21 → ≈ 0.10) — precision grows with √n, so it gets expensive fast.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 5 · The CLT on a yes/no variable
text:
Problem 5 · The CLT on a yes/no variable
The variable hoa is about as non-normal as data gets — every neighborhood is simply "Yes" or "No". Compute the true population proportion of HOA neighborhoods, then draw 1,000 samples of 60 and keep each sample’s proportion (mean(sample(nbhd$hoa, size = 60) == "Yes")). Histogram the 1,000 proportions. What shape appears, and which theorem predicted it?






Tip





Solution

mean(nbhd$hoa == "Yes")            # true population proportion

[1] 0.354

set.seed(705)
hoa_props <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(prop_hoa = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(nbhd$hoa, size = 60) == "Yes")))

ggplot(hoa_props, aes(prop_hoa)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(nbhd$hoa == "Yes"), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample proportion with an HOA (n = 60)", y = "Number of samples")







A two-category population, yet the sample proportions form an approximately normal bell centered on the truth (0.354) — the central limit theorem. It’s the same magic as the homework’s arrest proportions, and it’s why we can attach a standard error to any rate without the raw data ever looking normal.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 6 · Why n − 1, re-proven on counts
text:
Problem 6 · Why n − 1, re-proven on counts
Session 4 paid the n − 1 IOU with test scores; make it pay again with skewed count data. Draw 2,000 tiny samples of n = 4 from nbhd$assaults and compute each sample’s variance both ways — dividing by n, and with var() (which divides by n − 1). Compare the two averages to the true population variance, mean((x - mean(x))^2). (The slides’ list-column pattern — one map(), then two map_dbl()s — is the move.)






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
var_sims <- tibble(draw = 1:2000) |>
  mutate(
    s           = map(draw, \(d) sample(nbhd$assaults, size = 4)),
    var_div_n   = map_dbl(s, \(x) sum((x - mean(x))^2) / length(x)),
    var_div_nm1 = map_dbl(s, \(x) var(x))
  )

var_sims |>
  summarize(
    true_variance           = mean((nbhd$assaults - mean(nbhd$assaults))^2),
    avg_divide_by_n         = mean(var_div_n),
    avg_divide_by_n_minus_1 = mean(var_div_nm1)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  true_variance avg_divide_by_n avg_divide_by_n_minus_1
          <dbl>           <dbl>                   <dbl>
1          1.69            1.28                    1.71


Dividing by n lands around 1.28 — about 25% below the true variance (≈ 1.69) — while var() averages ≈ 1.7, right on target. Nothing about this trick required bell-shaped data: a sample clusters around its own mean, understating spread, and n − 1 is exactly the correction that makes the estimator unbiased.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different questions and numbers than the homework on purpose — if you can run and read both traditions cold here, Homework 6 (and the midterm’s inference questions) will feel routine.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
library(BayesFactor)   # install.packages("BayesFactor") once, if needed
crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Problem 1 · What a p-value promises
A study compares case-processing times in two courts and reports p = 0.03. Three readings:


“There is a 3% chance the courts truly process cases at the same speed.”
“If the courts truly processed cases at the same speed, a gap this large or larger would show up in about 3% of studies like this one.”
“There is a 97% chance the courts differ.”


Pick the correct one. Then verify the machinery’s actual promise by simulation: run 5,000 t-tests comparing two groups drawn from the same normal distribution (n = 40 each) and compute how often p < .05.






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
null_world_p <- replicate(5000, t.test(rnorm(40), rnorm(40))$p.value)
mean(null_world_p < 0.05)

[1] 0.0552


(b) — and only (b). A p-value is \(P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)\), a statement about data under an assumed null; (a) and (c) both flip it into \(P(H \mid \text{data})\), which frequentism never computes (that flip is Bayes’ job, and it costs a prior). The simulation shows the promise being kept: in a world where the null is true, about 5.5% of our 5,000 tests came up “significant” — right around the advertised 5% false-alarm rate, and no better.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Problem 2 · Translate the evidence
Four studies report Bayes factors: \(BF_{10}\) = 0.24, 2.6, 18, and 240. For each, compute \(BF_{01}\) and classify the evidence on the extended scale (1–3 barely worth mentioning · 3–10 moderate · 10–30 strong · 30–100 very strong · 100+ extreme). Which study’s data actually favor the null — and how strongly?






Tip





Solution

bf10 <- c(0.24, 2.6, 18, 240)
round(1 / bf10, 3)   # BF01: the same evidence, read for the null

[1] 4.167 0.385 0.056 0.004


A Bayes factor is a ratio of predictions, so below 1 means the null predicted the data better: the first study’s \(BF_{10}\) = 0.24 is \(BF_{01}\) ≈ 4.2 — moderate evidence for no effect (something a p-value can never report). The rest, on the scale: 2.6 is barely worth mentioning, 18 is strong, and 240 is extreme evidence for a difference. Same scale in both directions — just flip the fraction.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
section: Problem 3 · Both tests, one new question
text:
Problem 3 · Both tests, one new question
Do crimes on the street happen at different hours than crimes inside a residence? Filter crimes to location_description %in% c("STREET", "RESIDENCE"), compare mean hour by group, then run both tests: t.test() and ttestBF(). Watch each tool’s direction, and say whether the two traditions agree here — in class, on violent-vs-property, they didn’t.






Tip





Solution

sr <- crimes |> filter(location_description %in% c("STREET", "RESIDENCE"))

sr |> summarize(mean_hour = mean(hour), sd_hour = sd(hour), n = n(),
                .by = location_description)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  location_description mean_hour sd_hour     n
  <chr>                    <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1 STREET                    12.6    7.36  7907
2 RESIDENCE                 11.9    6.97  3587

t.test(hour ~ location_description, data = sr)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by location_description
t = -5.471, df = 7283.7, p-value = 4.623e-08
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group RESIDENCE and group STREET is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.0611136 -0.5012974
sample estimates:
mean in group RESIDENCE    mean in group STREET 
               11.85949                12.64070 

street_hours    <- sr$hour[sr$location_description == "STREET"]
residence_hours <- sr$hour[sr$location_description == "RESIDENCE"]

bf <- ttestBF(x = street_hours, y = residence_hours)
extractBF(bf)$bf

[1] 37975.69


Street incidents average hour 12.6 vs 11.9 in residences — about 47 minutes later. Directions differ by tool: t.test() sorts alphabetically (RESIDENCE − STREET, hence the negative t ≈ −5.5 and CI of −1.06 to −0.50 hours), while we handed ttestBF() x = street, y = residence, so its difference runs positive. This time the two traditions agree: p ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁸ and \(BF_{10}\) ≈ 38,000 — extreme evidence for a real difference. Unlike class’s 15-minute violent-vs-property gap, this one is large enough (relative to its precision) that “some difference” out-predicts “no difference” by a mile.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
section: Problem 4 · The number the star hides
text:
Problem 4 · The number the star hides
Both frameworks just endorsed the street-vs-residence difference. Before anyone re-draws a patrol schedule: compute Cohen’s d (pooled-SD version, as in class) and the gap in minutes. What’s the full, honest verdict?






Tip





Solution

sr <- crimes |> filter(location_description %in% c("STREET", "RESIDENCE"))
street_hours    <- sr$hour[sr$location_description == "STREET"]
residence_hours <- sr$hour[sr$location_description == "RESIDENCE"]

sd_pooled <- sqrt((var(street_hours) + var(residence_hours)) / 2)
(mean(street_hours) - mean(residence_hours)) / sd_pooled   # Cohen's d

[1] 0.1090122

(mean(street_hours) - mean(residence_hours)) * 60          # gap in minutes

[1] 46.87233


d ≈ 0.11 — below even the 0.2 “small” benchmark: a 47-minute shift against SDs of about 7 hours. The full verdict has three parts and needs all of them: the difference is almost certainly real (both tests), and it is modest in size (effect size). “Significant” and “decisive” describe our certainty, never the magnitude — report the units a human cares about, every time.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
section: Problem 5 · The sentence you’re licensed to say
text:
Problem 5 · The sentence you’re licensed to say
Session 5 forbade “there’s a 95% probability the truth is in this interval.” Buy the license: draw 10,000 posterior samples from Problem 3’s Bayes-factor model with posterior(), get the 95% credible interval for the difference, and compute the posterior probability the difference is positive. Then write the sentence — in minutes.






Tip





Solution

sr <- crimes |> filter(location_description %in% c("STREET", "RESIDENCE"))
street_hours    <- sr$hour[sr$location_description == "STREET"]
residence_hours <- sr$hour[sr$location_description == "RESIDENCE"]
bf <- ttestBF(x = street_hours, y = residence_hours)

set.seed(705)
post <- suppressMessages(posterior(bf, iterations = 10000))
diff_post <- as.numeric(post[, "beta (x - y)"])

quantile(diff_post, c(0.025, 0.975))

     2.5%     97.5% 
0.4955419 1.0640839 

mean(diff_post > 0)

[1] 1


The licensed sentence: “Given the model and prior, there is a 95% probability that street crimes occur, on average, between about 30 and 64 minutes later in the day than in-residence crimes.” That is exactly what a credible interval means — probability attached to the parameter itself, the reading everyone wants to give a confidence interval. And every one of the 10,000 posterior draws came out positive, so the direction is about as settled as this model can make it.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Problem 6 · The diversion-program trial
A county pilots a pretrial diversion program to reduce failures to appear (FTA). Historically, about 25% of defendants fail to appear — encode that as a Beta(3, 9) prior (mean 0.25, worth about 12 observations). The pilot randomizes 120 defendants: of 60 diversion clients, 12 fail to appear; of 60 controls, 19 do.

Run the frequentist test: prop.test(x = c(12, 19), n = c(60, 60)).
Update the prior for each group with rbeta() (as in the class recidivism example) and compute P(diversion FTA rate < control FTA rate).
Write one sentence for the county board.







Tip





Solution

prop.test(x = c(12, 19), n = c(60, 60))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(12, 19) out of c(60, 60)
X-squared = 1.5658, df = 1, p-value = 0.2108
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.28856877  0.05523544
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.2000000 0.3166667 

set.seed(705)
theta_div     <- rbeta(10000, 3 + 12, 9 + 48)   # posterior, diversion group
theta_control <- rbeta(10000, 3 + 19, 9 + 41)   # posterior, control group

mean(theta_div < theta_control)                 # P(program reduces FTA)

[1] 0.9111

c(mean(theta_div), mean(theta_control))         # posterior means

[1] 0.2079942 0.3054083


The frequentist verdict: p ≈ 0.21 — an 11.7-point gap like this could plausibly arise if the program did nothing, so “not significant,” and the grant report probably ends there. The posterior probability tells the board what it actually asked: given prior experience and the pilot data, there is about a 91% probability the diversion program lowers failure-to-appear (posterior means ≈ 21% vs 31%). One board-ready sentence: “The pilot is too small for a definitive verdict, but the evidence currently runs about 9-to-1 that diversion reduces failures to appear.” Both statements are true of the same data — they answer different questions, and only one of them helps a decision-maker.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different data and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 10 (and Checkpoint 2 on your own project) will feel routine.
Problems that use data need only this setup — cities is the 100 simulated-but-realistic cities you pivoted in Lab 4; today we stay in one year and go cross-sectional. One row = one city, not one person. Keep that in mind: it decides what your sentences are allowed to claim (Problem 6 will test you on it).
library(tidyverse)
library(correlation)

cities <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/cities-wide.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
text:
Problem 1 · Covariance’s units problem
Compute the covariance of vcr_2025 (violent crimes per 100,000 residents) with population_2020, and then with poverty_rate. One of these covariances is roughly 3,800 times the size of the other. Is that association 3,800 times stronger? Settle it: divide each covariance by the two standard deviations involved, then confirm with cor().






Tip





Solution

cov(cities$population_2020, cities$vcr_2025)

[1] 3449575

cov(cities$poverty_rate,    cities$vcr_2025)

[1] 914.0015

# Divide out the units: cov / (sd_x * sd_y)
cov(cities$population_2020, cities$vcr_2025) /
  (sd(cities$population_2020) * sd(cities$vcr_2025))

[1] 0.04429418

cov(cities$poverty_rate, cities$vcr_2025) /
  (sd(cities$poverty_rate) * sd(cities$vcr_2025))

[1] 0.6082377

cor(cities$population_2020, cities$vcr_2025)

[1] 0.04429418

cor(cities$poverty_rate,    cities$vcr_2025)

[1] 0.6082377


The ~3.4-million covariance turns into r = 0.04 — essentially nothing — while the “little” 914 becomes r = 0.61. The first number was huge only because population is measured in hundreds of thousands of people; covariance is glued to its units, so its size is uninterpretable across pairs. Dividing by both SDs cancels the units and puts every pair on the same −1 to +1 ruler.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
text:
Problem 2 · What r can’t see
A training study measures 80 recruits’ pre-qualification anxiety (0–10 scale) and their marksmanship score (100-point course). Simulate it, compute r, and then plot it:

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: keeps this particular draw stable
recruits <- tibble(
  anxiety      = seq(0, 10, length.out = 80),
  marksmanship = 88 - 2.1 * (anxiety - 5)^2 + rnorm(80, 0, 6)
)

A colleague computes cor(), gets roughly −0.04, and writes: “anxiety and marksmanship are unrelated.” What did they miss, and what habit would have caught it?






Tip





Solution

cor(recruits$anxiety, recruits$marksmanship)

[1] -0.04161482

ggplot(recruits, aes(anxiety, marksmanship)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Pre-qualification anxiety (0-10)", y = "Marksmanship score")







r ≈ −0.04, and the plot shows anything but “unrelated”: scores peak around mid-scale anxiety and collapse at both extremes — a strong inverted-U (the classic arousal-performance curve). Because the upslope and downslope cancel, the linear summary lands near zero. r measures straight-line association only; r ≈ 0 means no linear relationship, not no relationship — which is why you plot before you correlate, every time.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 3 · One unit can manufacture a correlation
text:
Problem 3 · One unit can manufacture a correlation
Twenty patrol beats, each with an average 911 response time (minutes) and a resident satisfaction score (0–100). Then the analyst appends beat 21 — the beat covering the airport, a giant low-density parcel: response time 28.4 minutes, satisfaction 31.

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: keeps this particular draw stable
beats <- tibble(
  response_min = rnorm(20, 10, 1.5),
  satisfaction = rnorm(20, 70, 6)
)

beats_all <- beats |>
  add_row(response_min = 28.4, satisfaction = 31)

Compute Pearson’s r and Spearman’s rho for the 20 beats, and again with the airport included. What happens to each — and which coefficient is telling the more honest story about the typical beat?






Tip





Solution

c(pearson_20  = cor(beats$response_min, beats$satisfaction),
  spearman_20 = cor(beats$response_min, beats$satisfaction, method = "spearman"))

 pearson_20 spearman_20 
 0.03864620 -0.01654135 

c(pearson_21  = cor(beats_all$response_min, beats_all$satisfaction),
  spearman_21 = cor(beats_all$response_min, beats_all$satisfaction, method = "spearman"))

 pearson_21 spearman_21 
 -0.8071187  -0.1506494 


Twenty beats show essentially nothing (r ≈ 0.04). Add one unrepresentative unit and Pearson leaps to ≈ −0.81 — a “very strong” negative correlation manufactured entirely by a single point sitting far out in both variables. Spearman moves only from ≈ −0.02 to ≈ −0.15, because to a rank-based measure the airport is just “rank 21,” not “a dozen standard deviations of leverage.” Neither number substitutes for the scatterplot — but when one wild unit is in the data, Spearman describes the typical beats far more honestly, and a Pearson-Spearman gap this large is itself a red flag to go look.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 4 · Inference: the matrix, then the star pair
text:
Problem 4 · Inference: the matrix, then the star pair

Run correlation() on vcr_2025, poverty_rate, unemployment_rate, and police_per_10k. Which pairs survive the Holm adjustment — and why do these p-values need adjusting at all?
The star pair is poverty and violence. Run cor.test() on it and write the one-sentence lecture-style report: r, df, p, CI, direction, strength.







Tip





Solution

cities |>
  select(vcr_2025, poverty_rate, unemployment_rate, police_per_10k) |>
  correlation()

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1        |        Parameter2 |     r |        95% CI | t(98) |         p
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
vcr_2025          |      poverty_rate |  0.61 | [ 0.47, 0.72] |  7.59 | < .001***
vcr_2025          | unemployment_rate |  0.08 | [-0.11, 0.28] |  0.84 | > .999   
vcr_2025          |    police_per_10k | -0.09 | [-0.28, 0.11] | -0.90 | > .999   
poverty_rate      | unemployment_rate |  0.05 | [-0.15, 0.24] |  0.48 | > .999   
poverty_rate      |    police_per_10k |  0.05 | [-0.15, 0.24] |  0.46 | > .999   
unemployment_rate |    police_per_10k |  0.16 | [-0.04, 0.34] |  1.58 | 0.591    

p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979)
Observations: 100

cor.test(cities$poverty_rate, cities$vcr_2025)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  cities$poverty_rate and cities$vcr_2025
t = 7.5858, df = 98, p-value = 1.92e-11
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.4676946 0.7187836
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.6082377 



Exactly one pair survives: poverty with violent crime (r = .61, adjusted p < .001). Every other CI crosses 0, with adjusted p-values from .59 to essentially 1. The adjustment exists because this table runs six tests at once — six chances at a 5% false alarm is Session 8’s pile-of-t-tests problem wearing correlation clothes, and Holm restores the family-wise honesty.
“Across these 100 cities, poverty was moderately associated with the violent-crime rate, r = .61, t(98) = 7.59, p < .001, 95% CI [.47, .72] — cities with higher poverty rates recorded more violent crime per 100,000 residents.” (By the lecture’s bands, .61 is a moderate correlation — and in messy social-science data, a moderate r is a major finding.) A correlation matrix is the map; cor.test() is the full readout you pull for the one relationship your analysis is actually about.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 5 · Bayesian correlation: a strong pair and an honest null
text:
Problem 5 · Bayesian correlation: a strong pair and an honest null
Run the Bayesian version (bayesian = TRUE) twice: once on poverty_rate + vcr_2025, once on unemployment_rate + vcr_2025. For each, read out rho, the 95% credible interval, pd, % in ROPE, and the Bayes factor. For the second pair, also compute 1/BF. What can you say about unemployment that a p-value never could?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: the Bayesian version samples from the posterior
cities |>
  select(vcr_2025, poverty_rate) |>
  correlation(bayesian = TRUE)

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1 |   Parameter2 |  rho |       95% CI |      pd | % in ROPE
---------------------------------------------------------------------
vcr_2025   | poverty_rate | 0.58 | [0.46, 0.70] | 100%*** |        0%

Parameter1 |         Prior |          BF
----------------------------------------
vcr_2025   | Beta (3 +- 3) | 4.25e+08***

Observations: 100

set.seed(705)
bayes_unemp <- cities |>
  select(vcr_2025, unemployment_rate) |>
  correlation(bayesian = TRUE)
bayes_unemp

# Correlation Matrix (pearson-method)

Parameter1 |        Parameter2 |  rho |        95% CI |     pd | % in ROPE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
vcr_2025   | unemployment_rate | 0.08 | [-0.11, 0.25] | 79.83% |    55.05%

Parameter1 |         Prior |     BF
-----------------------------------
vcr_2025   | Beta (3 +- 3) | 0.319°

Observations: 100

1 / bayes_unemp$BF

[1] 3.129932


Poverty: rho ≈ .58 (a touch below the frequentist .61 — the mildly skeptical prior’s pull), 95% CI ≈ [.46, .70], pd = 100%, 0% in ROPE, BF ≈ 4 × 10⁸ — evidence far past “extreme” on Session 6’s scale.
Unemployment: rho ≈ .08, CI ≈ [−.11, .25] straddling 0, pd ≈ 80% (a coin flip barely leaning positive), and over half the posterior sits inside the ROPE — the “practically zero” band. The BF ≈ 0.32 is below 1: taking 1/BF, the data are about 3 times more consistent with no correlation than with one. That’s the sentence a p-value can never earn — the frequentist p ≈ .40 only says “failed to reject”; the Bayes factor gives you positive evidence for the null, stated as such.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
text:
Problem 6 · The sentence audit
Your Problems 4–5 results end up in a briefing. Five draft sentences below — which are defensible, and what exactly is wrong with the rest?


“Cities with higher poverty rates recorded higher violent-crime rates in 2025 (r = .61).”
“Poor residents commit most of the violent crime in these cities.”
“Poverty causes violent crime.”
“City-level poverty statistically accounts for about 37% of the city-to-city variance in violent-crime rates.”
“We found no reliable city-level association between unemployment and violent crime; if anything, the data modestly favor there being none.”








Tip





Solution

cor(cities$poverty_rate, cities$vcr_2025)^2   # the 37% in sentence (d)

[1] 0.3699531


Defensible: (a), (d), and (e). (a) stays at the level of the rows — cities — and claims only association. (d) is r² = .61² ≈ .37, correctly framed as variance accounted for, still at the city level. (e) matches Problem 5’s output, including the BF ≈ 0.32 nuance.
(b) fails — the ecological fallacy. These rows are cities; every resident of a city shares one poverty rate and one crime rate, so the data contain nothing about which residents are involved in violence. (c) fails — a causal claim from a cross-sectional correlation; disinvestment, housing, policing patterns, and more lurk behind both variables. The audit habit: check every sentence for the level the data measure (areas vs. people) and the strength the design supports (association vs. cause).

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. Homework 12 is your own final-project model, so this bank is where you drill the logistic workflow on neutral data first — if you can do these cold, Checkpoint 4 (and the presentation questions afterward) will feel routine.
Problems that use data need only this setup — the 20,000 Alaska crashes from Labs 5, 7, 8, and 12. In lab you modeled whether the driver was intoxicated; here the question flips: does an intoxicated driver make a crash more likely to injure someone? The outcome is a flag we build ourselves:
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)   # only if you re-fit Problem 6's model yourself

crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv") |>
  mutate(injury = as.integer(injuries > 0))   # 1 = someone was injured

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
text:
Problem 1 · Odds ↔︎ probability, three conversions
No data, just the ladder. (a) About 12% of released defendants in a jurisdiction fail to appear: convert that probability to odds, and phrase it as “1 to ___.” (b) A program director says the odds a participant completes supervision are 4: what probability is that? (c) A logistic model reports a baseline log-odds of −1.99: use plogis() to recover the probability — and notice where you’ve landed.






Tip





Solution

0.12 / (1 - 0.12)   # (a) probability -> odds

[1] 0.1363636

4 / (4 + 1)         # (b) odds -> probability

[1] 0.8

plogis(-1.99)       # (c) log-odds -> probability

[1] 0.1202569

qlogis(0.12)        # and back up the ladder: probability -> log-odds

[1] -1.99243



Odds ≈ 0.136 — about 1 to 7.3: for every failure to appear, roughly seven appearances. (b) Odds of 4 (“four to one”) is a probability of 0.80. (c) plogis(-1.99) ≈ 0.12 — you’ve climbed back down to (a), because −1.99 is exactly qlogis(0.12). Probability, odds, and log-odds are three readouts of one quantity; plogis() and qlogis() move you up and down the ladder, and the model does its arithmetic on the log-odds rung.

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
text:
Problem 2 · Fit it: glm(family = binomial)

First check the base rate of injury (you built the flag in Setup — always know the baseline you’re modeling). Then fit injury ~ intox_any + num_vehicles. What do the two coefficients say before any transformation — and what scale are they on?






Tip





Solution

mean(crashes$injury)

[1] 0.478

injury_model <- glm(injury ~ intox_any + num_vehicles,
                    data = crashes, family = binomial)
summary(injury_model)


Call:
glm(formula = injury ~ intox_any + num_vehicles, family = binomial, 
    data = crashes)

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  -0.56478    0.06601  -8.556  < 2e-16 ***
intox_any     0.64840    0.05465  11.865  < 2e-16 ***
num_vehicles  0.23736    0.03570   6.649 2.95e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 27687  on 19999  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 27496  on 19997  degrees of freedom
AIC: 27502

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4


Baseline: about 48% of crashes injure someone — this outcome is nowhere near rare, which will matter in Problem 5. Both coefficients are positive with tiny p-values: intoxication (+0.65) and each additional vehicle (+0.24) raise the log-odds of an injury crash. Sign and significance are readable right off this table; the sizes are not, because nobody thinks in log-odds — which is exactly why the next move is always exp().

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
text:
Problem 3 · Exponentiate: log-odds → odds ratios
Turn the model into odds ratios with confidence intervals (exp(cbind(OR = coef(...), confint(...)))). Interpret each predictor in one sentence with the holding-constant clause — and state what the “no effect” value is for an odds ratio.






Tip





Solution

exp(cbind(OR = coef(injury_model), confint(injury_model)))

                   OR     2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept)  0.568485 0.4994012 0.6468929
intox_any    1.912470 1.7188884 2.1296050
num_vehicles 1.267901 1.1823033 1.3598917




Intoxication: OR ≈ 1.91 [1.72, 2.13] — a crash involving an intoxicated driver has about 91% higher odds of injuring someone than a sober-driver crash, holding the number of vehicles constant.

Vehicles: OR ≈ 1.27 [1.18, 1.36] — each additional vehicle multiplies the odds of injury by about 1.27. (In these data num_vehicles is only ever 1 or 2, so this is really the two-vehicle vs. single-vehicle contrast — check your predictor’s actual values before narrating a “per unit” story.)
For odds ratios the no-effect value is 1, not 0 — both intervals sit clearly above it.

exp() converts every log-odds coefficient into a multiplier on the odds, and 1 is the number that means “nothing happening.”

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
section: Problem 4 · From effects to cases: predicted probabilities
text:
Problem 4 · From effects to cases: predicted probabilities
Odds ratios describe effects; a briefing needs cases. Use predict(type = "response") for two crash profiles — (i) sober driver, single vehicle; (ii) intoxicated driver, two vehicles — then reproduce profile (i) by hand with plogis() and the coefficients. How do the two probabilities compare with the 48% baseline?






Tip





Solution

profiles <- tibble(intox_any = c(0, 1), num_vehicles = c(1, 2))

profiles |>
  mutate(p_injury = predict(injury_model, newdata = profiles, type = "response"))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  intox_any num_vehicles p_injury
      <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>
1         0            1    0.419
2         1            2    0.636

b <- coef(injury_model)
unname(plogis(b[1] + b[2] * 0 + b[3] * 1))   # profile (i), by hand

[1] 0.4188691


A sober single-vehicle crash carries about a 42% predicted probability of injury; an intoxicated two-vehicle crash about 64% — one below the 48% baseline, one well above it. And the by-hand version demystifies the machinery: plug the profile into the log-odds equation, then plogis() climbs down the ladder to a probability. Report odds ratios for effects and predicted probabilities for cases — decision-makers think in probabilities, and predict() is how you hand them one.

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
section: Problem 5 · Audit the memo (the classic mistake)
text:
Problem 5 · Audit the memo (the classic mistake)
A draft memo about your model reads:

“The odds ratio for intoxication is 1.91, so a crash with an intoxicated driver is 91% more likely to injure someone. Since about 48% of crashes cause injury, that works out to roughly 0.48 × 1.91 ≈ 92% of intoxicated-driver crashes causing injury.”

Both bolded claims are wrong — and the second one should already smell wrong (what would an OR of 2.5 imply?). Name each error, then compute what the model actually says happens to a two-vehicle crash’s injury probability when the driver is intoxicated, working through the odds.






Tip





Solution

p_sober <- unname(plogis(b[1] + b[3] * 2))          # sober, two vehicles
p_intox <- unname(plogis(b[1] + b[2] + b[3] * 2))   # intoxicated, two vehicles
c(p_sober = p_sober, p_intox = p_intox)

  p_sober   p_intox 
0.4775014 0.6360684 

odds_sober <- p_sober / (1 - p_sober)
odds_intox <- p_intox / (1 - p_intox)
c(odds_sober = odds_sober, odds_intox = odds_intox, ratio = odds_intox / odds_sober)

odds_sober odds_intox      ratio 
 0.9138807  1.7477694  1.9124700 


Error 1: “91% more likely” reads the odds ratio as a probability ratio. An OR of 1.91 multiplies the odds by 1.91 — nothing else. Error 2: multiplying the baseline probability by the OR (0.48 × 1.91) is arithmetic on the wrong scale; with an OR of 2.5 it would “predict” 120% of crashes causing injury, which is the tell that probabilities don’t multiply this way.
What actually happens: the sober two-vehicle probability of .48 converts to odds of ≈ 0.91; multiply those by 1.91 to get odds ≈ 1.75; convert back and the probability is ≈ .64. The real change is 48% → 64% — about 16 percentage points, a ~33% relative rise, nowhere near 91%. When the baseline probability is small, odds and probability move almost together; at a baseline near 50%, they part company badly — so multiply odds, never probabilities, and use predict() when you want the probability itself.

title: Practice Problems · Session 12
section: Problem 6 · Reading a brms bernoulli output
text:
Problem 6 · Reading a brms bernoulli output
A classmate fits the Bayesian twin of your Problem 2 model and sends you the summary below. Without fitting anything, answer: (a) what do Family: bernoulli and Links: mu = logit tell you about the scale of the Estimate column? (b) Exponentiate the intox_any estimate and both CI bounds — what odds ratio and 95% credible interval do you get, and does it agree with glm()’s? (c) Are there signs of sampling trouble? (d) Write the one Bayesian sentence about intoxication you’re now licensed to say.
 Family: bernoulli
  Links: mu = logit
Formula: injury ~ intox_any + num_vehicles
   Data: crashes (Number of observations: 20000)
  Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 2000

Regression Coefficients:
             Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
Intercept       -0.56      0.07    -0.70    -0.44 1.00     2056     1378
intox_any        0.65      0.06     0.54     0.76 1.00     1795     1378
num_vehicles     0.24      0.04     0.17     0.31 1.00     2081     1415

Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
(Want to reproduce it? The code is below — but budget for the “Compiling Stan program…” pause plus a couple of minutes of sampling on 20,000 rows. The reading practice is the point; the refit is optional.)

injury_bayes <- brm(injury ~ intox_any + num_vehicles, data = crashes,
                    family = bernoulli(),
                    chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)
summary(injury_bayes)







Tip





Solution

exp(c(estimate = 0.65, ci_low = 0.54, ci_high = 0.76))

estimate   ci_low  ci_high 
1.915541 1.716007 2.138276 



bernoulli is brms’s name for a 0/1 outcome and logit is the link — so the Estimate column is in log-odds, exactly like glm()’s coefficient table, and needs exponentiating before anyone speaks.
exp(0.65) ≈ 1.92, with a 95% credible interval of roughly [1.72, 2.14] — landing almost exactly on glm()’s OR of 1.91 [1.72, 2.13], as expected with default priors and 20,000 crashes.
No trouble: Rhat = 1.00 on every row and effective sample sizes in the 1,400–2,100 range mean the two chains agreed and mixed well.
“Given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability that intoxication multiplies a crash’s odds of injuring someone by between roughly 1.7 and 2.1, holding the number of vehicles constant.” Same machinery as every brm() you’ve run — bernoulli is just family = binomial in Bayesian clothing, and the coefficients only become English after exp().

This Week
Topic: Descriptive statistics and statistical vocabulary

Measures of central tendency
Measures of dispersion
Distributions and their shapes

Learning goals: define in your own words — mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation, histogram, normal distribution, Poisson distribution — and use R to describe a small dataset and plot a distribution.

title: Descriptive Statistics

Two Threads, One Course
Starting today, every week builds two things at once — watch for this slide each session:


Statistics thread — lecture + homework

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Three Ways to Say “Typical”



Measure
Meaning




Mean
the average


Median
the halfway point


Mode
the most frequently occurring value



Measures of central tendency summarize a vector of data by locating the typical, the middle, or the most common point.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Mean

rainfall <- c(0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 4)   # rain each day this week

# The hard way:
sum(rainfall) / length(rainfall)

[1] 1.142857




# The easy way:
mean(rainfall)

[1] 1.142857

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Median

rainfall

[1] 0 0 0 2 1 1 4

sort(rainfall)   # middle value of the sorted data?

[1] 0 0 0 1 1 2 4




median(rainfall)

[1] 1

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Mode

rainfall          # which value appears most often?

[1] 0 0 0 2 1 1 4

library(modeest)  # install.packages("modeest") once, library() every session
mfv(rainfall)     # mfv = "most frequent value"

[1] 0

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What Do These Look Like?

stats <- tibble(
  measure = c("Mean", "Median", "Mode"),
  value = c(mean(rainfall), median(rainfall), mfv(rainfall))
)
ggplot(tibble(rainfall), aes(rainfall)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(data = stats, aes(xintercept = value, color = measure),
             linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Rainfall with Mean, Median, and Mode",
       x = "Rainfall (inches)", y = "Frequency", color = NULL)

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: The Same Thing in Real Data
text:
The Same Thing in Real Data
Community-level crime rates in Chicago, 2025:

areas |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate   = mean(crime_rate),
    median_rate = median(crime_rate),
    max_rate    = max(crime_rate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_rate median_rate max_rate
      <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      96.9          82     292.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Who’s Dragging the Mean?

areas |> slice_max(crime_rate, n = 3) |> select(community, crime_rate)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  community          crime_rate
  <chr>                   <dbl>
1 Fuller Park              292.
2 West Garfield Park       220.
3 Englewood                214.


Fuller Park’s rate — nearly 300 crimes per 1,000 residents, inflated by its tiny residential population — pulls the mean above the median: same lesson as the 30-year sentence, in live data. (Rates with small denominators are a recurring CJ trap; we’ll meet it again.)

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: The Same Thing in Real Data
text: The Same Thing in Real Data

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Central Tendency Isn’t the Whole Story
text:
Central Tendency Isn’t the Whole Story
Three people run for city council; only the top two vote-getters win:


Scenario 1

A = 200 votes
B = 300 votes
C = 400 votes


Scenario 2

X = 299 votes
Y = 300 votes
Z = 301 votes


In both cases the average is 300. But scenario 1 has much greater spread in support; scenario 2 is tightly clustered — it’s hard to say who’s truly “preferred.”
→ We need measures of dispersion: range, deviations, variance, standard deviation.

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Seeing the Machinery — Step 1: Raw Votes
text: Seeing the Machinery — Step 1: Raw Votes

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Range

votes1 <- c(200, 300, 400)   # wide spread
votes2 <- c(299, 300, 301)   # tight cluster

mean(votes1); mean(votes2)   # identical means

[1] 300


[1] 300




range(votes1); diff(range(votes1))

[1] 200 400


[1] 200

range(votes2); diff(range(votes2))

[1] 299 301


[1] 2

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Seeing the Machinery — Step 2: Deviations

(Notice the Tight Cluster panel: deviations of −1, 0, +1 are barely visible on the same scale.)

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Deviations from the Mean

votes1 - mean(votes1)

[1] -100    0  100

votes2 - mean(votes2)

[1] -1  0  1



Why can’t we just sum the deviations?

sum(votes1 - mean(votes1))   # they always cancel to zero!

[1] 0

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Seeing the Machinery — Step 3: Squared Deviations
text:
Seeing the Machinery — Step 3: Squared Deviations

Average these and you have the variance; take the square root and you’re back in vote units — the SD.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Sum of Squares
Squaring makes every deviation positive (and emphasizes big misses):

sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2)

[1] 20000

sum((votes2 - mean(votes2))^2)

[1] 2

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Variance

# Variance = mean squared deviation (population formula)
sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2) / length(votes1)

[1] 6666.667

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Standard Deviation, in Words
The standard deviation measures how spread out the data are around the mean.

“On average, how far is each value from the mean?”

We square the deviations (to make them positive and emphasize larger differences), average them (that’s the variance), then take the square root (back to the original units).

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Standard Deviation

# Standard deviation = square root of variance (back to vote units!)
sqrt(sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2) / length(votes1))

[1] 81.64966




var(votes1); sd(votes1)   # R's built-ins use the SAMPLE formula (divide by n-1)

[1] 10000


[1] 100

var(votes2); sd(votes2)   # more on WHY in Session 4

[1] 1


[1] 1

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Why the Standard Deviation?

Same units as the data — variance is in squared units; SD is interpretable
Works with the normal distribution — SD tells us how typical or extreme a value is
The basis for many tools — confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, z-scores, regression all rely on it
Lets you compare variability across datasets with similar scales

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
In CJ Scenarios
Response times for patrol officers:

Low SD → officers respond in consistently similar times
High SD → sometimes fast, sometimes slow — inconsistency that matters for policy, supervision, training

Sentence lengths for the same crime:

High SD might suggest inconsistency — or bias — in sentencing

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Real Data: Consistency Across Communities

# Violent-crime rates: how much do Chicago communities differ?
areas |>
  summarize(
    mean_violent = mean(violent_rate),
    sd_violent   = sd(violent_rate),
    min_violent  = min(violent_rate),
    max_violent  = max(violent_rate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  mean_violent sd_violent min_violent max_violent
         <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1         30.7       22.5           4        111.


The SD is nearly as large as the mean — Chicago communities differ enormously in violence exposure. That inequality is a finding, and it took exactly one line of dispersion statistics to see it.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What Is a Distribution?
A distribution shows how many observations fall at different values — the shape of the data.
It answers:

“Where do most of the values fall?”
“How spread out are they?”
“Are some values rare or common?”

We visualize distributions with a histogram.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Normal Distribution

sims <- tibble(x = rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 100, sd = 10))
ggplot(sims, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey80", color = "white")


Symmetrical, bell-shaped; defined by two numbers — the mean (center) and SD (spread). Try different values!

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: SD and the Normal: the Empirical Rule
text:
SD and the Normal: the Empirical Rule


pct_within <- function(k) 100 * (pnorm(k) - pnorm(-k))
tibble(k = 1:3, pct_within = round(pct_within(1:3), 2))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
      k pct_within
  <int>      <dbl>
1     1       68.3
2     2       95.4
3     3       99.7

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Poisson Distribution

pois_sims <- tibble(x = rpois(n = 1000, lambda = 1))
ggplot(pois_sims, aes(x)) + geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["navy"])


Often skewed, especially when λ is low. Models counts of rare events: 911 calls per hour, crimes per day, cars per minute. One parameter: λ = expected number of events. Try different values!

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Poisson Is Not Hypothetical
Daily robbery counts in our Chicago sample, all of 2025:

daily_robberies <- crimes |>
  filter(primary_type == "ROBBERY") |>
  count(date)

ggplot(daily_robberies, aes(n)) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  labs(x = "Robberies per day", y = "Number of days",
       title = "Real crime counts look Poisson")

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Why We Care About Distributions in CJ
text:
Why We Care About Distributions in CJ

The normal distribution helps us understand common variation (response times, test scores)
The Poisson distribution models event counts, especially rare ones — crimes, incidents — and underlies many forecasting tools
Recognizing the shape of your data is the first step in choosing the right analysis — a theme for the whole semester

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Today’s Lab & Homework

Lab 2: your first ggplots — histograms, boxplots, and bar charts with real corrections data (lab page)
Homework 2: descriptive statistics in R (posted on the Session 2 page)
Read before Session 3: Stanton Ch. 2 · R4DS Ch. 3 (Data transformation) & Ch. 4 (Code style)

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
This Week
Topic: probabilities in the long run and sampling distributions — taught by simulation. We won’t derive anything today; we’ll draw thousands of samples in R and watch the theory appear on screen.
Learning goals: explain in your own words — law of large numbers, sampling distribution, standard error, central limit theorem — and say why R’s var() and sd() divide by n − 1 (Session 2’s IOU gets paid today).

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 2: describing data — center, spread, and the shapes distributions take
Session 3: probability as the long run; conditioning as shrink the world, re-proportion; and Bayes’ theorem — the base rate is never optional
Today: what happens to statistics themselves — means, proportions — when sampling repeats. This is the engine under every inference we make for the rest of the course

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Two Threads, One Course


Statistics thread — lecture + homework
Stanton Ch. 3 → sampling distributions, the standard error, and the CLT

Wrangling thread — lab
R4DS Ch. 5–6 → pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), and tidy data

The two threads meet at the Session 7 workshop — today’s lab skill (reshaping) is what real agency data always needs first.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
A Question to Start

If I told you the chance of being selected for a jury was 10%, and you weren’t selected after 10 tries, would that surprise you? Why or why not?


Two kinds of probability:

Theoretical probability — based on mathematical reasoning (a fair coin is 50/50 by definition)
Empirical probability — observed through repetition (flip it and count)

Today’s whole session is about the gap between these two — and how it shrinks.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Theoretical vs. Empirical Probability
Flip a fair coin 10 times:

flips_10 <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE)
table(flips_10) / 10

flips_10
heads tails 
  0.6   0.4 



Now 10,000 times:

flips_10k <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10000, replace = TRUE)
table(flips_10k) / 10000

flips_10k
 heads  tails 
0.5055 0.4945 


Empirical results fluctuate in small samples but converge toward the theoretical probability — the law of large numbers.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Watching the Long Run Arrive

lln <- tibble(
  flip = 1:10000,
  heads = sample(c(0, 1), size = 10000, replace = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(running_prop = cumsum(heads) / flip)
ggplot(lln, aes(flip, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Proportion of heads in coin flips",
       x = "Number of flips", y = "Proportion heads")


Concept: in the long run, empirical ≈ theoretical. But “long run” might be longer than we think — look how wild the first few hundred flips are.

title: Sampling Distributions
text: Watching the Long Run Arrive

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Simulating Probabilities in CJ (1)
False positive drug tests. Suppose a field test for drugs has a 5% false positive rate. Simulate 100 field tests of non-users:

tests <- sample(c("false positive", "correct"), size = 100,
                replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.95))
table(tests)

tests
       correct false positive 
            91              9 



Discussion: even with a low false positive rate, false positives occur regularly in practice. What do we think about this? Does it matter?

title: Sampling Distributions
section: What Does a Positive Test Mean? (Session 3 Redux)
text:
What Does a Positive Test Mean? (Session 3 Redux)
Our simulation showed false positives are routine. “Does it matter?” has a Session 3 answer — count it out:

Suppose 2% of tested drivers actually carry. In 1,000 tests: 20 carriers, 980 clean
A 5% false-positive rate on the 980 clean drivers → ~49 false alarms
Even if the test catches all 20 carriers: 69 positives in total, of which 20 are real → \(P(\text{carrier} \mid +) = 20/69 \approx 29\%\)
The “5%” describes \(P(+ \mid \text{clean})\). The courtroom cares about \(P(\text{clean} \mid +)\). Never confuse the direction

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Simulating Probabilities in CJ (2)
Stop & frisk outcomes. Suppose 8% of stops yield contraband. What happens over 1,000 stops?

stop_outcomes <- sample(c("found", "nothing"), size = 1000,
                        replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.08, 0.92))
table(stop_outcomes)

stop_outcomes
  found nothing 
     69     931 



Discussion: is that hit rate too low? What if each find were an illegal gun that would have been used in a violent crime? Simulation makes the long-run consequences of a policy concrete.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Random Does Not Mean Balanced
Two runs of 100 dice rolls — same die, same code:

dice <- tibble(
  run  = rep(c("Run 1", "Run 2"), each = 100),
  roll = c(sample(1:6, size = 100, replace = TRUE),
           sample(1:6, size = 100, replace = TRUE))
)
ggplot(dice, aes(x = factor(roll))) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  facet_wrap(~run) +
  labs(title = "Dice roll frequencies — two runs of 100",
       x = "Face", y = "Count")


Does either look fair? Both are. Random does not mean balanced in small samples — remember this every time you see a “streak” in real data.

title: Sampling Distributions
text: Random Does Not Mean Balanced

title: Sampling Distributions
section: A Population We Can Actually See
text:
A Population We Can Actually See
population-data.csv — 10,000 test scores. In real research we never see the whole population; today we get to cheat:

pop |>
  summarize(mean = mean(score), median = median(score),
            sd = sd(score), n = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 4
   mean median    sd     n
  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1  100.   100.  15.0 10000

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
One Sample of 30

samp <- sample(pop$score, size = 30)
mean(samp)

[1] 100.3389

sd(samp)

[1] 13.16761


Close to the truth (mean ≈ 100, SD ≈ 15) — but not exact. That gap is sampling error, and it is not a mistake; it’s a fact of life.

The question that drives the rest of the semester: how wrong can one sample be?

title: Sampling Distributions
section: What If We Sampled From the Tail?
text:
What If We Sampled From the Tail?
Draw 10 scores from the bottom 5% of the population — and look at them in context:

tail_scores <- pop |> filter(score < quantile(score, 0.05))
tail_sample <- sample(tail_scores$score, size = 10)
mean(tail_sample)

[1] 70.02723

title: Sampling Distributions
section: …And What If We Didn’t Know It?
text:
…And What If We Didn’t Know It?
Now pretend that sample is all we ever get to see:

If this were your dataset, you’d report a “typical” score near 70 — and you’d be badly wrong. How often does that actually happen with a random sample? Let’s find out.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Do It a Thousand Times
The key move of this whole session — instead of drawing one sample, draw 1,000 samples of 30 and keep each sample’s mean:

sample_means <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_score = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(pop$score, size = 30))))

sample_means

# A tibble: 1,000 × 2
   draw mean_score
  <int>      <dbl>
1     1       99.7
2     2       97.4
3     3       97.5
4     4       99.6
5     5      105. 
6     6      104. 
# ℹ 994 more rows




map_dbl(draw, \(d) …) reads as “for each draw, do this and return one number” — Session 3’s replicate(), tibble-flavored. See the simulation verbs reference.

title: Sampling Distributions
section: The Sampling Distribution of the Mean
text:
The Sampling Distribution of the Mean

ggplot(sample_means, aes(mean_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(pop$score), color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample means (n = 30 each)",
       x = "Sample mean", y = "Number of samples")


This histogram of means is a sampling distribution. It’s centered on the true population mean — and it’s much narrower than the population itself.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Two Distributions, Side by Side

Same center. Radically different spread. Individual scores wander all over; averages of 30 stay close to home.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
The Standard Error
The SD of the sampling distribution has its own name: the standard error. And it has a formula — which our simulation can check:

sd(sample_means$mean_score)   # SE from the simulation

[1] 2.648695

sd(pop$score) / sqrt(30)      # SE from the formula: SD / sqrt(n)

[1] 2.733584




The standard error answers: “if I re-ran my study, how much would my estimate typically move?”

That single number is the foundation of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests — the rest of this course.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Sample Size Buys Precision

many_ns <- expand_grid(n = c(5, 30, 100), draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_score = map_dbl(n, \(k) mean(sample(pop$score, size = k))))
ggplot(many_ns, aes(mean_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = crju_colors["navy"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(pop$score), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean", y = "Count")



many_ns |>
  summarize(simulated_se = sd(mean_score), formula_se = sd(pop$score) / sqrt(first(n)),
            .by = n)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
      n simulated_se formula_se
  <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
1     5         6.84       6.70
2    30         2.77       2.73
3   100         1.49       1.50


The SE shrinks like 1/√n: to halve your uncertainty you need four times the data.

title: Sampling Distributions
text: Sample Size Buys Precision

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
The Least Normal Variable Imaginable
Back to our 30,000 real Chicago incidents. Whether an incident ended in arrest is as far from a bell curve as data gets — every value is TRUE or FALSE:

crimes |> count(arrest) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  arrest     n  prop
  <lgl>  <int> <dbl>
1 FALSE  25176 0.839
2 TRUE    4824 0.161



Treat these 30,000 incidents as the population. True arrest proportion: 0.161.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Sample 100 Incidents. Repeat 1,000 Times.
Imagine an analyst who can only pull 100 case files at a time:

arrest_props <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(prop_arrest = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(crimes$arrest, size = 100))))


ggplot(arrest_props, aes(prop_arrest)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample arrest proportions (n = 100 incidents each)",
       x = "Proportion of sampled incidents with an arrest", y = "Samples")

title: Sampling Distributions
section: A Bell Curve Out of TRUE/FALSE Data
text:
A Bell Curve Out of TRUE/FALSE Data
That’s the central limit theorem:

Whatever shape the population has — even a two-bar TRUE/FALSE stack — the sampling distribution of a mean (or proportion) becomes approximately normal as n grows, centered on the true value.


It’s why polls of ~1,000 people work for a country of 330 million
It’s why we can attach a standard error to an arrest rate, a clearance rate, a recidivism rate — without ever seeing the full population
It’s why the normal distribution keeps showing up even though raw CJ data almost never look normal

title: Sampling Distributions
section: The CLT Also Obeys the √n Rule
text:
The CLT Also Obeys the √n Rule

At n = 25 a sample could easily tell you the arrest rate is 8% or 28%. At n = 400 you’re rarely off by more than a couple of points.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Session 2’s IOU
In Session 2 we noticed var() and sd() divide by n − 1, not n, and I promised you’d see why. Simulation pays the debt. Draw 5,000 tiny samples (n = 5) and compute the variance both ways:

var_pop <- mean((pop$score - mean(pop$score))^2)   # true population variance

variance_sims <- tibble(draw = 1:5000) |>
  mutate(
    s            = map(draw, \(d) sample(pop$score, size = 5)),
    var_div_n    = map_dbl(s, \(x) sum((x - mean(x))^2) / length(x)),
    var_div_nm1  = map_dbl(s, \(x) var(x))          # R's built-in: n - 1
  )



map() builds a list column — each row’s s holds an entire 5-value sample; map_dbl() then computes one number per sample. Don’t worry about the list-column mechanics — watch the two averages on the next slide.

title: Sampling Distributions
section: Divide by n, and You’re Biased
text:
Divide by n, and You’re Biased

variance_sims |>
  summarize(
    true_variance   = var_pop,
    avg_divide_by_n = mean(var_div_n),
    avg_divide_by_n_minus_1 = mean(var_div_nm1)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  true_variance avg_divide_by_n avg_divide_by_n_minus_1
          <dbl>           <dbl>                   <dbl>
1          224.            179.                    224.

title: Sampling Distributions
section: Divide by n, and You’re Biased (cont.)
text:
Divide by n, and You’re Biased (cont.)

Dividing by n systematically underestimates the population variance — across 5,000 samples, not occasionally
Why? A sample clusters around its own mean, which is always closer to the sample’s values than the true mean is — so measured spread comes up short
Dividing by n − 1 inflates each estimate just enough to land, on average, on the truth. That’s all “unbiased estimator” means

title: Sampling Distributions
section: What If the Population Is Unknown?
text:
What If the Population Is Unknown?
In real life you never get the left-hand panel. One draw from a mystery population:

unknown_population <- rnorm(1000, mean = 100, sd = 50)   # don't peek!
mystery_sample <- sample(unknown_population, size = 30)
mean(mystery_sample)

[1] 95.44168



Based on 30 points, you might assume normality — or skew, or outliers — and be wrong. Sampling-distribution logic is what lets us say how wrong we’re likely to be.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Why This Matters in CJ

Almost every number in CJ research is a sample statistic: a survey of officers, a sample of case files, one year of one city’s incidents
Every one of those statistics has a sampling distribution — it would come out differently if the study were re-run
The standard error turns “it would come out differently” into a number
Starting next session: use the SE to build confidence intervals — a range of values the truth is likely to be in

title: Sampling Distributions
section: In-Class Exercise: Probabilities in the Long Run
text:
In-Class Exercise: Probabilities in the Long Run
Work in pairs; record your code and results in a script.

Long run: simulate 10,000 rolls of a fair die and get the proportion of each face (sample(), count()). Then just 10 rolls. Then repeat the 10-roll version five times. How much do small samples vary?
Known population: create rnorm(10000, mean = 100, sd = 15), plot it, and mark the 1st/5th/95th percentiles with quantile(). Draw a sample of 30 — where does its mean fall?

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
In-Class Exercise (cont.)

Unknown population: run unknown_pop <- rnorm(1000, 100, 50) without plotting it. Sample 30 values, plot the sample, and write down what you’d conclude about the population. Then peek. Were you right?
