text:
This Week
Topic: hypothesis testing — twice. One question, both great traditions.

The Null Hypothesis Significance Test: its logic, and its fine print
p-values: what they are — and what they are not
Bayes’ theorem — back from Session 3, now pointed at hypotheses instead of diagnoses
Bayes factors and posteriors with the BayesFactor package

Learning goals: run t.test() and ttestBF() on the same question; state correctly what each output licenses you to claim.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Two Threads, One Course


Statistics thread — lecture + homework
Stanton Ch. 5 → hypothesis testing, both ways: t.test() and ttestBF()

Wrangling thread — lab
R4DS Ch. 19 (+ Ch. 18 skim) → left_join() on our two Chicago files

Last new wrangling skill before next week’s workshop — after today, you own the whole pipeline.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 3: Bayes’ theorem — beliefs update by evidence; ignore the base rate and “90% accurate” becomes a 15% answer
Session 4: sampling distributions — sample statistics fluctuate in predictable ways
Session 5: confidence intervals — an honest range; our violent-vs-property gap came out detectable but tiny (≈4–27 min)
Today: the formal machinery for “is there a difference?” — then a second tradition answering the question you meant to ask


If this course has a thesis, today is it: the two traditions are complements, not rivals — and you will leave able to use both.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Remember Our Question?
Session 5 asked whether violent crimes happen later in the day than property crimes:

vp |> summarize(mean_hour = mean(hour), sd_hour = sd(hour),
                n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  crime_category mean_hour sd_hour     n
  <chr>              <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1 Violent             12.8    6.87  9148
2 Property            12.5    6.63 10371



Violent incidents average about 15 minutes later. Session 5 gave us an interval for that gap. Today we get the test — a yes/no verdict machine.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Let’s Pretend We Sampled Repeatedly
Bootstrap each group’s mean 10,000 times — Session 4’s logic, applied to both groups at once:

boot <- tibble(
  Violent  = replicate(10000, mean(sample(violent_hours,  replace = TRUE))),
  Property = replicate(10000, mean(sample(property_hours, replace = TRUE)))
)

boot |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "group", values_to = "boot_mean") |>
  ggplot(aes(boot_mean, fill = group)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(crju_colors[c("blue", "garnet")])) +
  labs(title = "10,000 bootstrap means per group",
       x = "Mean hour of day", y = "Count", fill = NULL)

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text: Let’s Pretend We Sampled Repeatedly

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Difference and Its 95% CI
Subtract, pair by pair, and the difference gets its own distribution:

boot_diff <- boot$Violent - boot$Property

quantile(boot_diff, c(0.025, 0.975))

      2.5%      97.5% 
0.06299314 0.44033505 



The middle 95% of plausible differences runs from about 0.06 to 0.44 hours — the interval sits entirely above zero.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Difference, Seen

Zero is not among the plausible values. The data lean toward a real (if small) gap.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: What If the Interval Crossed Zero?
text:
What If the Interval Crossed Zero?
Erase the real gap on purpose — shift every violent incident earlier by the observed difference — and re-run the exact same machinery:

When zero sits comfortably inside, the data are consistent with no difference. Formalize this intuition and you have invented the NHST.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Null Hypothesis Significance Test

State the null, \(H_0\): no difference (\(\mu_V - \mu_P = 0\)). The boring world.
State the alternative, \(H_1\): some difference. Note how little we commit to.
Compute a test statistic: \(t = \text{observed difference} \,/\, SE\) — the gap, in SE units.
Ask: how often would \(|t|\) this large appear by luck in the boring world? The p-value.
Verdict: \(p < \alpha\) (usually .05) → “reject \(H_0\).” Otherwise → “fail to reject.”
Note: the machine only weighs evidence against the null — \(H_1\) never gets scored.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: Watch the p-Value Do Its Job
text:
Watch the p-Value Do Its Job


As the true difference grows, the overlap shrinks and p falls. Black = null · green = one alternative · orange = overlap · blue dashes = the α = .05 cutoffs.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: What a p-Value Is — and Is Not
text:
What a p-Value Is — and Is Not
It is: the probability of data this extreme or more, if the null is true and the model is right.

It is not:

the probability the null hypothesis is true — that’s \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data})\), which frequentism never computes
the probability the result “is due to chance” — same confusion, folksier outfit
1 − the probability the alternative is true
a measure of how big or important the effect is — with enough data, microscopic effects earn microscopic p-values (hold that thought)

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
t.test() on the Real Question

t.test(hour ~ crime_category, data = vp)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by crime_category
t = -2.6061, df = 19021, p-value = 0.009164
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Property and group Violent is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.44272107 -0.06263688
sample estimates:
mean in group Property  mean in group Violent 
              12.54334               12.79602

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Reading the Verdict

R orders groups alphabetically, so this tests Property − Violent (hence the negative signs — same finding as our bootstrap, mirrored)
\(t = -2.61\), and \(p = 0.009\)


\(p < .05\) — “statistically significant.” Reject the null. Publish the press release?


Hold that thought until Act III. First, some fine print about what this machine quietly assumed.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Assumption 1 · The Null Stands Alone

We computed how surprising the data are under the null — and never once said what the alternative world looks like.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
…But the Alternative Could Be Anywhere

“Reject the null” tells you where you aren’t. It never tells you where you are.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Assumption 2 · The Shape Itself

The p-value came from this specific curve — which assumes (roughly) normal-enough data, independent observations, well-behaved variances.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: …And Many Shapes Fit the Same Data
text:
…And Many Shapes Fit the Same Data

How often do researchers test those assumptions before trusting the p-value? Less often than you’d hope.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Bayes’ Theorem — Recap from Session 3
\[
P(H \mid \text{data}) = P(\text{data} \mid H) \times P(H) \,/\, P(\text{data})
\qquad \small{\text{posterior} = \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior} / \text{evidence}}
\]

Session 3’s move: conditioning is shrink the world, re-proportion — Bayes’ theorem reverses the direction. Ianfluenza: prior 1% + “90% accurate” → posterior ≈ 15%
New today: look where the p-value lives — entirely in the likelihood, \(P(\text{data} \mid H_0)\). It never becomes \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data})\)
Bayesian testing finishes the flip — \(P(H \mid \text{data})\), the question your chief, judge, or city council actually asked — at the price of a stated prior

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: The Two Traditions, Side by Side
text:
The Two Traditions, Side by Side









Frequentist
Bayesian




Asks
How surprising are these data if \(H_0\) is true?
How probable is each hypothesis, given the data?


Probability attaches to
Data, over imagined repeated samples
Hypotheses and parameters directly


Prior knowledge
None used
Explicit, stated up front


Output
p-value, confidence interval
Posterior distribution, Bayes factor, credible interval


“95%” means
The procedure captures the truth in 95% of replications
95% probability the parameter lies in this interval

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Bayesian t-Test: ttestBF()
Same question, second tradition. We supply the groups ourselves, so the direction is ours: x − y = Violent − Property.

# install.packages("BayesFactor")   # once, if you don't have it
bf <- ttestBF(x = violent_hours, y = property_hours)
bf

Bayes factor analysis
--------------
[1] Alt., r=0.707 : 0.4887026 ±0.05%

Against denominator:
  Null, mu1-mu2 = 0 
---
Bayes factor type: BFindepSample, JZS

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Reading a Bayes Factor

extractBF(bf)$bf        # BF10: evidence for a difference vs. no difference

[1] 0.4887026

1 / extractBF(bf)$bf    # BF01: the same evidence, read the other way

[1] 2.046234



A Bayes factor is a ratio of predictions: how well did “some difference” predict these data vs. “no difference”?
\(BF_{10} = 0.49\) — below 1. The data are about 2 times more consistent with the null
Rules of thumb: 1–3 barely worth mentioning · 3–10 moderate · 10–30 strong · 30–100 very strong · 100+ extreme (mirror image below 1)

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Hold On — the p-Value Said “Significant”









Frequentist
Bayesian




Result
\(p = 0.009\) → reject \(H_0\)
\(BF_{10} = 0.49\) → mild evidence for \(H_0\)




With ~19,500 cases, the test can detect microscopic gaps — and 15 minutes is microscopic
The BF asks a harder question: did “a difference of plausible size” predict the data better than “zero”? This close to zero, the null predicted slightly better
Neither is wrong. They answer different questions — and only one is impressed by sheer sample size

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Posterior for the Difference
The Bayes factor compares models. The posterior describes the difference itself — drawn by a sampler (the machinery, called MCMC, is in tonight’s optional appendix):

post <- suppressMessages(posterior(bf, iterations = 10000))
diff_post <- as.numeric(post[, "beta (x - y)"])

quantile(diff_post, c(0.025, 0.975))

      2.5%      97.5% 
0.06518506 0.44053059 

mean(diff_post > 0)

[1] 0.9953

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Posterior, Seen


Now say the sentence Session 5 forbade — legally: “There is a 95% probability the true difference lies between about 4 and 26 minutes.” Under the Bayesian license (given the model and prior), that is exactly what this interval means.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Detectable, Probable — and Tiny
One more number every report owes its reader — a standardized effect size (Cohen’s d):

sd_pooled <- sqrt((var(violent_hours) + var(property_hours)) / 2)
(mean(violent_hours) - mean(property_hours)) / sd_pooled

[1] 0.03742312



Benchmarks: 0.2 “small” · 0.5 “medium” · 0.8 “large.” We measured ~0.04
A ~15-minute shift against SDs of nearly 7 hours. Would any commander re-draw a patrol schedule over this?
The full picture: the difference is probably real (posterior), utterly trivial (d), and “significant” (p) only because n is enormous. Report all three; never let the star do the talking

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Setup

Context: typical recidivism runs about 60% — that’s our prior belief
Design: randomized trial of a reentry program — 100 treated, 100 control
Outcomes: control 50/100 reoffend · treatment 40/100 reoffend
Question: did the program reduce recidivism?


Ten percentage points, exactly the kind of effect a city would fund. Both traditions, go.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Frequentist Answer

prop.test(x = c(40, 50), n = c(100, 100))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(40, 50) out of c(100, 100)
X-squared = 1.6364, df = 1, p-value = 0.2008
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.24719748  0.04719748
sample estimates:
prop 1 prop 2 
   0.4    0.5

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Frequentist Answer, Read Aloud

prop.test(x = c(40, 50), n = c(100, 100))$p.value

[1] 0.2008251



\(p = 0.20\) — not statistically significant
Honest reading: a 10-point gap like this could plausibly occur even if the program did nothing
The grant report writes itself — “no significant effect” — and the program probably dies there

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Bayesian Answer
Prior: Beta(6, 4) — mean 0.6, worth about 10 observations. Update each group, then ask the question we care about directly:

set.seed(705)
theta_treat   <- rbeta(10000, 6 + 40, 4 + 60)   # posterior, treatment
theta_control <- rbeta(10000, 6 + 50, 4 + 50)   # posterior, control

mean(theta_treat < theta_control)   # P(program reduces recidivism)

[1] 0.9122



Given the prior and the data, there is about a 91% probability the program reduces recidivism.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text: The Posteriors, Seen

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Same Data, Different Questions









Frequentist
Bayesian




Verdict
\(p = 0.20\): cannot reject “no effect”
\(P(\text{treatment} < \text{control}) \approx 0.91\)


Plain English
“This gap could plausibly be luck”
“9-to-1 odds the program works”




Both statements are true of the same data. Neither is a trick
A policymaker deciding whether to fund the program next year: which sentence actually helps?
Your homework asks you to sit with exactly this discomfort

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The p-Value and Sample Size
Fix a trivial true effect (Δ = 0.1) and just keep collecting data:

The effect never grows — only n does — and p still dives below .05. Given enough data, everything is “significant.”

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Bayes and Sample Size
Same trivial effect, Bayesian glasses — watch the posterior for the difference as n grows:

More data doesn’t flip a verdict — it sharpens the estimate, which visibly converges on “about 0.1, i.e., almost nothing.” The tininess stays in view. (This is Act III’s collision, run in slow motion.)

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
What We Learned Today

NHST: standardized and everywhere — but it only asks how surprising are the data under the null?, never scores the alternative, and rewards sheer n
p-values are not the probability any hypothesis is true, and are silent about size
Bayes answers \(P(H \mid \text{data})\) at the price of a stated prior; MCMC made it computable (appendix, if you want the machinery)
The same data can yield \(p < .05\) and a BF favoring the null — or \(p = 0.20\) and 91% posterior confidence
Whatever tradition you use: report the effect size, in units a human cares about

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Ugly Denominator
Not on any exam — this is the machinery behind the two-second ttestBF() call, for the curious.
\[
P(H \mid \text{data}) = \frac{P(\text{data} \mid H)\,P(H)}{\color{#73000A}{P(\text{data})}}
\]
That innocent-looking denominator is the probability of the data under every possible hypothesis, weighted by its prior:
\[
\color{#73000A}{P(\text{data}) = \int P(\text{data} \mid \theta)\, P(\theta)\, d\theta}
\]

For realistic models this integral is intractable — for most of the 20th century, Bayes was philosophically beautiful and practically unusable.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Enter MCMC
How Markov chain Monte Carlo “measures the curve” without solving the integral:

We don’t know the whole posterior curve — but we do know its formula up to a constant (likelihood × prior)
A sampler evaluates that formula at its current spot and at a proposed spot
Compare the two values: if the new spot is higher → accept; if lower → accept with that probability
The impossible constant appears in both numerator and denominator — it cancels in the ratio. We never need to know it

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
MCMC, Watched Live
A Metropolis sampler exploring a distribution (left) while its samples pile up into that very shape (right):

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: We End Up With the Probability Distribution
text:
We End Up With the Probability Distribution

The pile of accepted samples is the posterior — to any precision you like, just run longer
Think back to Session 4: we approximated sampling distributions by drawing samples and stacking them. MCMC plays exactly the same trick on the posterior
This is why modern Bayes is possible at all — and it is what BayesFactor quietly does for you in about two seconds

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
This Week
Topic: comparing three or more group means — and your first Bayesian model workflow

Why “just run a bunch of t-tests” backfires
The core idea: two kinds of variance and their ratio, F
aov() + Tukey’s HSD — enough to read the output you’ll meet in the literature
brms + emmeans — the workflow you’ll reuse in every remaining session
Real data: does Chicago’s clock differ by crime category?

Learning goals: explain what F compares; read a one-way ANOVA in both traditions; run the posterior workflow you’ll use for the rest of the course.
Also this week: Homework 8 includes Project Checkpoint 1 — your first graded step on your final-project dataset.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 6: two groups — is this mean different from that one? t-tests, in both the frequentist and Bayesian traditions
Session 7: the applied workshop — you took a messy file through the whole pipeline and picked your final-project dataset
Today: the question that comes up constantly in real research — what if there are three groups? Or six?

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Experiments: IVs and DVs
Independent variable (IV): what we change or compare — the groups.
Dependent variable (DV): what we measure — the outcome that (maybe) depends on the IV.







Independent variable
Dependent variable




Type of training program
Test score


Type of fertilizer
Plant height


Region of the country
Annual precipitation


Patrol strategy assigned to a beat
Response time (minutes)

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Why ANOVA?

A t-test compares 2 means
ANOVA compares 3+ means
Use it when the IV is categorical (the groups) and the DV is numeric (the outcome)
The name is strange: ANalysis Of VAriance — we’re asking about means, but the test works by comparing variances. That’s the whole trick, and it’s coming up.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: Why Not Just Run a Pile of t-Tests?
text:
Why Not Just Run a Pile of t-Tests?
Three groups means 3 pairwise tests. Six groups means 15. Each test carries its own 5% false-alarm risk, and the risks pile up:

tibble(groups = c(2, 3, 4, 6, 10)) |>
  mutate(
    pairwise_tests   = choose(groups, 2),
    p_false_alarm    = round(1 - 0.95^pairwise_tests, 2)
  )

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  groups pairwise_tests p_false_alarm
   <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl>
1      2              1          0.05
2      3              3          0.14
3      4              6          0.26
4      6             15          0.54
5     10             45          0.9

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
ANOVA’s Answer: One Omnibus Question
By six groups you have a coin-flip’s chance of at least one bogus “significant” difference.

ANOVA asks one omnibus question — are all the group means plausibly equal? — at a single 5% risk. (When we go pairwise afterward, we’ll adjust for this. Hold that thought.)

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Where ANOVA Actually Lives

ANOVA is standard in experiments — assign units to conditions, compare outcomes. That is what it was built for.
But open a criminology journal and you’ll rarely see it as a final model. Observational CJ research runs on regression.
So why learn it? You will read it. Older literature, program evaluations, and lab studies are full of ANOVA tables — and output you can’t read is output you have to take on faith.
And it is regression in disguise. The between/within logic you build today is the machinery behind R², the F-test, and every categorical predictor from Session 11 on. We’ll prove it before class ends.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Imagine Three Classrooms

classrooms <- tibble(
  score     = c(75, 80, 78, 74, 77,    # Class 1
                88, 90, 92, 85, 87,    # Class 2
                70, 65, 68, 72, 66),   # Class 3
  classroom = factor(rep(c("Class 1", "Class 2", "Class 3"), each = 5))
)

class_stats <- classrooms |>
  summarize(class_mean = mean(score), class_var = var(score), .by = classroom)
class_stats

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  classroom class_mean class_var
  <fct>          <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Class 1         76.8       5.7
2 Class 2         88.4       7.3
3 Class 3         68.2       8.2


Two different kinds of “spread” are hiding in this table.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Two Kinds of Variance
Within-group variance: how much scores bounce around inside each classroom.
Between-group variance: how much the classroom averages differ from each other.

mean(class_stats$class_var)   # WITHIN: average spread inside a class

[1] 7.066667

var(class_stats$class_mean)   # BETWEEN: spread of the class means

[1] 102.76



Between (102.8) dwarfs within (7.1) — the class averages are far more spread out than chance bouncing inside classes would suggest. Signal-to-noise ratio ≈ 14.5. These classes look genuinely different.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text: The Picture

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Stanton’s Rain Example (From the Book)
Now flip the situation: three groups where nothing differs — by construction. precip holds annual precipitation for 70 U.S. cities. Draw three random groups of 20 from the same 70 cities:

data("precip")
set.seed(705)   # so we all draw the same "random" groups
group1 <- sample(precip, 20)
group2 <- sample(precip, 20)
group3 <- sample(precip, 20)

c(mean(group1), mean(group2), mean(group3))

[1] 34.100 31.835 31.255



The means differ a little — but any differences here are pure sampling luck. The null hypothesis is true by construction.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Rain: Within vs. Between

mean(c(var(group1), var(group2), var(group3)))    # WITHIN

[1] 132.6697

var(c(mean(group1), mean(group2), mean(group3)))  # BETWEEN

[1] 2.260108



Within ≈ 133, between ≈ 2.3. The classrooms gave us 7.1 vs. 102.8 — completely flipped. Why?

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Why So Lopsided?

City-to-city rainfall varies a lot (Phoenix vs. Mobile) → big within-group variance. But each group’s mean averages 20 cities, and Session 4 taught us means fluctuate far less than raw values (\(SE = \sigma/\sqrt{n}\)).
With no real group differences, between-group variance is nothing but the tiny sampling noise of three means.
The diagnostic: between ≫ within → something real separates the groups. Between ≪ within → noise. All we need is a ruler for “how much bigger is big enough” —

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
The F-Statistic
\[F \;=\; \frac{\text{between-group variance}}{\text{within-group variance}} \;=\; \frac{\text{signal}}{\text{noise}}\]

When the null is true, F bounces around low values by luck of the draw
If our F lands far in the tail of the F distribution → our data are unlikely under the null — same logic as every test we’ve run
The F distribution describes the F values a null world produces. Its shape depends on two df: groups − 1 and N − groups

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: What F Looks Like When the Null Is True
text:
What F Looks Like When the Null Is True

set.seed(705)
f_null <- tibble(
  design = rep(c("F(2, 57) — our rain design",
                 "F(8, 101) — more groups, bigger N"), each = 10000) |> fct_inorder(),
  f      = c(rf(10000, df1 = 2, df2 = 57), rf(10000, df1 = 8, df2 = 101))
)
cutoffs <- f_null |> summarize(cut = quantile(f, 0.95), .by = design)

ggplot(f_null, aes(f)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = cutoffs, aes(xintercept = cut),
             color = crju_colors["garnet"], linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~design, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "10,000 F values from a null world, for two designs",
       subtitle = "Garnet line = 95th percentile — F values beyond it are rare when nothing differs",
       x = "F value", y = "Count")

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: What F Looks Like When the Null Is True
text: What F Looks Like When the Null Is True

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: First, We Need a Data Frame
text:
First, We Need a Data Frame
aov() wants the data in the long format we’ve used all semester — one row per observation, one column saying which group it belongs to:

rain <- tibble(
  rainfall = c(group1, group2, group3),
  group    = factor(rep(c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3"), each = 20))
)
rain

# A tibble: 60 × 2
  rainfall group  
     <dbl> <fct>  
1     49.2 Group 1
2     35.1 Group 1
3     31.7 Group 1
4     30.8 Group 1
5     34.4 Group 1
6     17.4 Group 1
# ℹ 54 more rows

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
aov() Does the Whole Thing

rain_model <- aov(rainfall ~ group, data = rain)
summary(rain_model)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
group        2     90    45.2   0.341  0.713
Residuals   57   7562   132.7               



F = 0.34, p = 0.71. That F sits squarely in the fat part of F(2, 57) — nowhere near the 95% cutoff (≈ 3.2). No evidence the groups differ. Correct answer — they’re the same population by construction.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: The Table Is Our Two Variances, Dressed Up
text:
The Table Is Our Two Variances, Dressed Up

Mean Sq Residuals = 132.7 — exactly the within-group variance we computed by hand ✓
Mean Sq group = 45.2 — our between-group variance (2.26), scaled by the group size. F = 45.2 / 132.7 = 0.34.


Why the scaling? A 2-inch gap between means built on 20 cities each is stronger evidence than the same gap built on 2, so aov() bakes sample size into the signal. That’s the only reason your hand-computed ratio and R’s F won’t match — same logic, different units. You do not need to reproduce this by hand; you need to read the table.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Let’s Make a Difference Artificially
Shift Group 3 down 15 inches — now there is a real difference, and we know exactly where it lives:

rain_shifted <- rain |>
  mutate(rainfall = if_else(group == "Group 3", rainfall - 15, rainfall))

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Redo the ANOVA

shifted_model <- aov(rainfall ~ group, data = rain_shifted)
summary(shifted_model)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value     Pr(>F)    
group        2   3775  1887.7   14.23 0.00000972 ***
Residuals   57   7562   132.7                       
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



The within-group noise didn’t move (132.7 — shifting a whole group doesn’t change the spread inside it). The between-group signal exploded. F = 14.2, p ≈ 0.00001 — deep in the tail.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: A Significant F Only Says “Something Differs”
text:
A Significant F Only Says “Something Differs”
Which pairs? Tukey’s HSD: all pairwise comparisons, with the family-wise 5% false-alarm rate restored — the fix for the t-test pile-up problem from the top of class:

TukeyHSD(shifted_model)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = rainfall ~ group, data = rain_shifted)

$group
                   diff      lwr       upr     p adj
Group 2-Group 1  -2.265 -11.0301  6.500103 0.8087836
Group 3-Group 1 -17.845 -26.6101 -9.079897 0.0000246
Group 3-Group 2 -15.580 -24.3451 -6.814897 0.0002129

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Reading the Tukey Output

Group 3 differs from both others — intervals exclude 0, adjusted p-values tiny. Exactly where we put the difference.
Group 1 vs. Group 2: interval spans 0, p = 0.81 — no evidence, as designed
The omnibus F said “something’s there”; Tukey pointed at what, without inflating the false-alarm rate

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Two New Packages

brms — Bayesian Regression Models using Stan: writes the model, compiles it, samples the posterior
emmeans — estimated marginal means: takes any fitted model and returns group means and group differences

install.packages(c("emmeans", "brms"))






brms compiles models with your computer’s C++ toolchain. Install before the lab, and expect the first model of each session to pause ~a minute at “Compiling Stan program…” — that’s normal, not a crash.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Same Formula, Bayesian Machinery

bayes_rain <- brm(rainfall ~ group, data = rain,
                  chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


Identical formula syntax to aov() — this pattern carries through the rest of the course
Priors: we didn’t state any, so brms used its defaults — more on what that means on the next slide
chains = 2, iter = 2000: two independent MCMC runs, 2,000 draws each → a full posterior distribution for every group mean
refresh = 0 just silences the sampling progress log

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
The Prior We Just Used

brms’s defaults: essentially flat on the group coefficients, weakly informative on the intercept and spread
Flat priors = “the data do the talking.” Fine at this n — but say so: “we used brms default priors” belongs in any writeup that reports a posterior
One logic, several badges: ttestBF() (S6), brm() (today), correlation (S10) — different interfaces, same move: prior + likelihood → posterior
Session 10 shows what happens when you deliberately change the prior — and when it matters

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Posterior Group Means

rain_post <- emmeans(bayes_rain, ~ group)
rain_post

 group   emmean lower.HPD upper.HPD
 Group 1   34.2      28.8      38.9
 Group 2   32.0      27.1      37.1
 Group 3   31.4      26.5      36.5

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 



One row per group: the posterior median and a 95% HPD interval — the range holding the most credible values for that group’s mean, given the data.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Posterior Means, Seen

plot(rain_post) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(rain$rainfall),
             linetype = 2, color = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  labs(x = "Posterior mean rainfall (inches)", y = NULL)


All three intervals swallow the grand mean (dashed line). No group separates from the pack.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
section: What We Really Care About Are Differences
text:
What We Really Care About Are Differences

pairs(rain_post)

 contrast          estimate lower.HPD upper.HPD
 Group 1 - Group 2    2.233     -5.05      9.20
 Group 1 - Group 3    2.733     -4.34      9.93
 Group 2 - Group 3    0.506     -7.00      7.57

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 



Every 95% HPD interval for a pairwise difference crosses 0
Bayesian reading: zero — “no difference” — remains a credible value for every contrast. No credible difference between any pair.
Same verdict as F = 0.34, p = 0.71. Two traditions, one conclusion.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Differences, Seen

plot(pairs(rain_post)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = crju_colors["garnet"])


Zero sits comfortably inside every interval. When a difference is real, its interval abandons 0 — watch what real data do next.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
This Workflow Is the Point
The four lines you just ran are the ones you keep:
model <- brm(outcome ~ predictor, data = df)   # fit
post  <- emmeans(model, ~ predictor)           # posterior summaries
plot(post); pairs(post)                        # see it; compare

Session 10 — the same brm() call, a numeric predictor
Sessions 11–12 — the same call again, several predictors, then a binary outcome
Your final project — the Bayesian half of your both-traditions model
The ANOVA was the excuse to learn this. The workflow is the thing you keep. Also true of the interval rule: crosses 0 → not credible; excludes 0 → credible, forever after.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
The Question
In Session 5 we found violent crimes average slightly later in the day than property crimes — two groups. But our Chicago data sort every incident into three categories. ANOVA takes all three in one shot:

crimes |> summarize(mean_hour = mean(hour), sd_hour = sd(hour),
                    n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  crime_category mean_hour sd_hour     n
  <chr>              <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1 Violent             12.8    6.87  9148
2 Other               12.1    6.95 10481
3 Property            12.5    6.63 10371



Violent runs latest (12.8), Other earliest (12.1). Gaps of fractions of an hour, with SDs near 7. Real structure, or noise? And remember: n = 30,000 — big samples detect tiny things.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text: Look First

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Frequentist: aov()

chicago_model <- aov(hour ~ crime_category, data = crimes)
summary(chicago_model)

                  Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value          Pr(>F)    
crime_category     2    2351  1175.3    25.3 0.0000000000105 ***
Residuals      29997 1393374    46.5                            
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



F(2, 29997) = 25.3, p ≈ 10⁻¹¹. Something differs, emphatically. But that’s all the omnibus F will ever tell us — which pairs, and by how much?

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Which Pairs? Tukey

TukeyHSD(chicago_model)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = hour ~ crime_category, data = crimes)

$crime_category
                      diff        lwr       upr     p adj
Property-Other   0.4285629 0.20732516 0.6498006 0.0000168
Violent-Other    0.6812419 0.45269164 0.9097921 0.0000000
Violent-Property 0.2526790 0.02356458 0.4817934 0.0263613



All three intervals exclude 0 — every category differs from every other. Now look at the sizes: 0.25 to 0.68 hours. That’s 15 to 41 minutes.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Bayesian: Same Workflow, Real Data

bayes_chicago <- brm(hour ~ crime_category, data = crimes,
                     chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)

The exact pattern from the rain example — brm(), then emmeans(), then pairs(). Nothing new to learn; only the data changed.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Bayesian Differences

chicago_post <- emmeans(bayes_chicago, ~ crime_category)
pairs(chicago_post)

 contrast           estimate lower.HPD upper.HPD
 Other - Property     -0.427    -0.610    -0.248
 Other - Violent      -0.681    -0.858    -0.487
 Property - Violent   -0.256    -0.454    -0.065

Point estimate displayed: median 
HPD interval probability: 0.95 



Every HPD interval excludes 0 — all three differences are credible. (Watch the signs: emmeans orders groups alphabetically, so these are Other − Property, Other − Violent, Property − Violent — the mirror image of Tukey’s table. Same gaps.)

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Detectable ≠ Dramatic (Reprise)

Both traditions agree: mean incident hour genuinely differs across all three categories
But the biggest gap is 41 minutes and the smallest is 15 minutes — on a 24-hour clock, with SDs near 7 hours
30,000 incidents give us the power to detect differences this small. Detecting them is not the same as their mattering.
Your job as the analyst: report direction and size, every time. “Significant” without magnitude is malpractice — Session 6’s lesson, now with three groups.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
It Was Regression All Along
Promised at the top of class. Same data, same question, one function swapped:

anova(lm(hour ~ crime_category, data = crimes))

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: hour
                  Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value           Pr(>F)    
crime_category     2    2351 1175.31  25.302 0.00000000001048 ***
Residuals      29997 1393374   46.45                             
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



The identical F and p-value. aov() is a thin wrapper around lm() — ANOVA is a regression with one categorical predictor. In Session 11 you’ll fit that same model and read its coefficients as differences between groups, which is what Tukey was showing you all along.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
How to Report It

Frequentist: “Mean incident hour differed across crime categories, F(2, 29997) = 25.3, p < .001. Tukey’s HSD: violent crimes averaged 0.25 hours (≈ 15 minutes) later than property crimes, 95% CI [0.02, 0.48], with similarly small gaps for the other pairs.”


Bayesian: “The posterior difference in mean hour (Violent − Property) was 0.26 hours, 95% HPD [0.06, 0.45], excluding zero — a credible but small difference.”

Both sentences state the difference, the uncertainty, and the magnitude.

title: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments
text:
Today’s Lab & Homework

Lab 8: the full ANOVA workflow, both traditions — three classrooms, then Alaska crash data (lab page)
Homework 8: ANOVA on Stanton’s chickwts data — plus Project Checkpoint 1: descriptive statistics and one plot on your final-project dataset (Session 8 page)

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
This Week

Least squares, the line of best fit, and R²
Two predictors: the best-fitting plane — you’ll spin it with your mouse
“Holding the others constant” — reading coefficients honestly
Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
The Bayesian version with brms; reporting both traditions

Learning goals: fit, interpret, and diagnose lm() with several predictors — and say what a coefficient does and doesn’t mean.
Project: Homework 11 contains Checkpoint 3 — your first regression on your data.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 10: correlation — r measured how tightly two variables move together; r² was the variance they share; the Bayesian version gave us a posterior instead of a single number
Two humility rules came with it: correlation is not causation, and area-level patterns are not people-level claims (the ecological fallacy)
Today: correlation says that two variables travel together. Regression answers the sharper question: how much — and with several predictors, how much does each matter after accounting for the others?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The New Question
Correlation is a one-lane road between two variables.
Multiple regression adds more lanes — but all the traffic still arrives at one place: the outcome, \(Y\). Each predictor lane contributes part of how we got there.

The question multiple regression answers:

“How much does Y change when \(X_1\) changes by one unit, holding \(X_2\) constant?”



That phrase — holding constant — is the entire value added today. We’ll earn it slowly.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Model, With One Predictor
\[Y = a + bX + e\]



Piece
Name
Meaning




\(Y\)
outcome
the thing we’re predicting (DV)


\(a\)
intercept
predicted \(Y\) when \(X = 0\)


\(b\)
slope
change in predicted \(Y\) per one-unit change in \(X\)


\(e\)
error
what the line leaves unexplained



The model is a claim: knowing X, here’s my best guess at Y — plus some miss.
The residual is each observation’s miss: actual \(Y\) minus predicted \(Y\).

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Ten Students, Hours and Scores


# seed 1 kept from the 2025 deck — the three
# candidate lines coming up were tuned to this draw
set.seed(1)
students <- tibble(
  hours = 1:10,
  score = 40 + 5 * hours + rnorm(10, 0, 5)
)

ggplot(students, aes(hours, score)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  labs(x = "Hours studied", y = "Exam score")









Some line through this cloud is the “best” one. Best by what ruler?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Three Candidate Lines

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: The Ruler: Sum of Squared Residuals
text:
The Ruler: Sum of Squared Residuals
For any candidate line, measure every vertical miss, square it (so misses above and below don’t cancel), and add them up:

SSR <- function(a, b) {
  predicted <- a + b * students$hours
  sum((students$score - predicted)^2)
}

SSR(20, 5)      # too low

[1] 4405.871

SSR(50, 3)      # too flat

[1] 584.9933

SSR(37, 5.2)    # roughly right

[1] 196.9529



Smaller total = better line. Least squares = find the line with the smallest total of all.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
lm() Finds the Winner
No trial and error — lm() solves for the one line that minimizes SSR:

fit_hours <- lm(score ~ hours, data = students)
coef(fit_hours)

(Intercept)       hours 
   39.15588     5.27366 

SSR(coef(fit_hours)[1], coef(fit_hours)[2])

[1] 130.9173



Our best hand-picked guess left 197 in squared misses; lm() gets it down to 131 — and no other line does better.
Read the slope: each additional hour of studying predicts about 5.3 more points, in this sample.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Watching the Search Land

The line tilts until the SSR stops shrinking — then it’s the least-squares line.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: What the Line Leaves Behind

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: R²: How Much Did We Explain?
text:
R²: How Much Did We Explain?

summary(fit_hours)$r.squared

[1] 0.9460216

cor(students$hours, students$score)^2

[1] 0.9460216



R² = the proportion of the outcome’s variance the model accounts for. Here, hours studied explain ~95% of the spread in scores (it’s simulated data — real life will humble us shortly).
Notice the second line: with one predictor, R² is just Session 10’s correlation, squared. Same quantity, new outfit.
With multiple predictors, R² keeps the same meaning — variance explained by the whole team — but no single correlation owns it anymore.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Model, Full Form
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_k X_k + e\]

\(\beta_0\) — intercept: predicted \(Y\) when every \(X\) is zero (often a nonsense scenario; it anchors the model, it doesn’t need to be meaningful)
\(\beta_1 \ldots \beta_k\) — slopes: the effect of each \(X\) holding the others constant
\(e\) — error: what’s still unexplained


Each \(\beta\) is conceptually a partial relationship — how \(X_1\) relates to \(Y\) after removing the overlap with the other predictors. That’s what makes multiple regression more than a stack of correlations.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
From Line to Plane

One predictor: the model is a line through a 2-D cloud
Two predictors: the model is a plane floating in a 3-D cloud — one slope along each predictor’s axis
The ruler never changes: least squares — minimize the total squared vertical distance from every point to the surface
Three or more predictors: a hyperplane in a space we can’t draw. The math shrugs; only our eyes give out.


Two predictors is the last stop where we can actually see the model. So let’s look at it properly.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Best-Fitting Plane, Live






Grab it and spin it.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Guided Tour
Points above the plane are positive residuals; below, negative. For the walkthrough again later — same plane, narrated:

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Remember the Lurker?
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated. Every summer. Reliably.

set.seed(705)
lurk <- tibble(
  temperature    = runif(100, 60, 100),
  icecream_sales = 20 + 5 * temperature + rnorm(100, 0, 30),
  drownings      = -10 + 0.8 * temperature + rnorm(100, 0, 10)
)

ggplot(lurk, aes(icecream_sales, drownings)) +
  geom_point(color = crju_colors["navy"], size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  labs(title = paste0("r = ", round(cor(lurk$icecream_sales, lurk$drownings), 2),
                      " — ban ice cream?"),
       x = "Ice cream sales", y = "Drownings")

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Remember the Lurker?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Model 1: Ice Cream “Predicts” Drownings

lurk_m1 <- lm(drownings ~ icecream_sales, data = lurk)
summary(lurk_m1)$coefficients |> round(4)

               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)     -0.3876     7.5245 -0.0515    0.959
icecream_sales   0.1315     0.0175  7.5165    0.000



The coefficient is positive and the p-value has ten zeros in it
It’s statistically significant. The model says it’s real.
Do we believe it? No — but notice that nothing in this output warns us. The model can only see the variables we gave it.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Model 2: Give the Model the Lurker
text:
Model 2: Give the Model the Lurker

lurk_m2 <- lm(drownings ~ icecream_sales + temperature, data = lurk)
summary(lurk_m2)$coefficients |> round(4)

               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    -10.0979     6.5333 -1.5456   0.1255
icecream_sales  -0.0339     0.0299 -1.1352   0.2591
temperature      0.9884     0.1553  6.3634   0.0000



Holding temperature constant, ice cream’s coefficient collapses to ~0 (and goes nonsignificant). Temperature was driving both variables the whole time.
This is holding constant doing real work: comparing days with the same temperature, ice cream tells you nothing about drownings.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Side by Side












model
icecream coef
icecream p
temperature coef
R²




drownings ~ icecream
0.132
0.000000000027
—
0.37


drownings ~ icecream + temperature
-0.034
0.26
0.99
0.55






A “significant” bivariate relationship evaporated once the right third variable entered
Beware the evil lurking third variable. It does not announce itself.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Seeing “Holding Constant”
An added-variable plot shows the ice cream–drownings relationship after temperature’s contribution is removed from both:

Flat. That flat line is the multiple-regression coefficient for ice cream.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Moral

Multiple regression can hold constant only the variables you measured and included
Every observational model has potential lurkers you didn’t measure — so coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects
“Holding constant” is a statistical operation, not a controlled experiment
This is why theory matters: which variables belong in the model is a substantive question, not a statistical one


Keep this loaded. We’re about to fit real Chicago models, and the temptation to talk causally will be enormous.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Look First. Always.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
One Predictor First

chi_m1 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)
summary(chi_m1)



Each additional percentage point of unemployment is associated with 3.3 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, and unemployment alone accounts for 71% of the between-area variance. Strong — but is unemployment getting credit for other disadvantage it travels with?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
One Predictor First


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-32.137  -6.340  -2.670   5.843  43.339 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value            Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -2.7444     2.8629  -0.959               0.341    
unemployment_rate   3.3007     0.2463  13.400 <0.0000000000000002 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.27 on 75 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7054,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7014 
F-statistic: 179.5 on 1 and 75 DF,  p-value: < 0.00000000000000022

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing
text:
Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing

chi_m2 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)
summary(chi_m2)



Both predictors earn significant coefficients, and R² climbs from 0.71 to 0.82.
Watch unemployment’s slope: 3.3 → 2.1. Some of what looked like “unemployment” in the simple model was shared with vacancy. That shrinkage is “holding constant” — the lurker lesson, on real data.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing
text:
Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-27.6759  -5.8167  -0.9943   4.5144  26.7266 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value         Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -9.2679     2.4616  -3.765         0.000332 ***
unemployment_rate   2.1156     0.2620   8.075 0.00000000000935 ***
pct_vacant          1.9352     0.2859   6.769 0.00000000264664 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.708 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.818, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8131 
F-statistic: 166.3 on 2 and 74 DF,  p-value: < 0.00000000000000022

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Reading the Coefficients Out Loud

Intercept (-9.3): predicted rate when both predictors are 0 — no Chicago area looks like that; it anchors the plane, nothing more
unemployment_rate (2.12): +1 point of unemployment ↔︎ ~2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, vacancy held fixed
pct_vacant (1.94): +1 point of vacancy ↔︎ ~1.9 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, unemployment held fixed

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
What These Coefficients Are Not

Not causal effects. Adjusted associations between areas — and every lurker we didn’t measure is still at large
Not people-level claims. An unemployed person is not “2.1 crimes more dangerous.” Area-level in, area-level out — Session 10’s ecological fallacy rides along with every coefficient today
Not the full story. The model holds constant only what’s in the model

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Watch the Units
Coefficient size is meaningless until you check the predictor’s units. Median income, in dollars:

coef(lm(violent_rate ~ median_income, data = areas))

  (Intercept) median_income 
68.5585257487 -0.0005221118 

areas |>
  mutate(income_10k = median_income / 10000) |>
  lm(violent_rate ~ income_10k, data = _) |>
  coef()

(Intercept)  income_10k 
  68.558526   -5.221118 



Same model, same fit. But −0.0005 “looks like” nothing; the honest reading is about 5 fewer violent crimes per 1,000 residents per $10,000 of median income. Rescale before you interpret.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Does a Third Predictor Earn Its Keep?
text:
Does a Third Predictor Earn Its Keep?
Add the share of adults without a high-school diploma:

chi_m3 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant + pct_no_hs_diploma,
             data = areas)
summary(chi_m3)$coefficients |> round(3)

                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)         -8.853      2.862  -3.093    0.003
unemployment_rate    2.140      0.276   7.741    0.000
pct_vacant           1.923      0.291   6.613    0.000
pct_no_hs_diploma   -0.039      0.135  -0.290    0.773



Coefficient ≈ 0, p ≈ 0.77 — with unemployment and vacancy already in, it adds nothing detectable; adjusted R² (R² with a per-predictor penalty) actually falls: 0.813 → 0.811
More predictors ≠ more truth. Every variable argues its way in — theory first, fit second

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Residual Plot
Regression assumes the misses are patternless. So look at the misses:

chi_diag <- tibble(fitted = fitted(chi_m2), residual = resid(chi_m2))

ggplot(chi_diag, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = crju_colors["navy"], size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. fitted values — the all-purpose diagnostic",
       x = "Fitted violent-crime rate", y = "Residual")

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: The Residual Plot

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Reading Our Residual Plot Honestly

What we want: a patternless horizontal band around zero
What we have: centered on zero with no obvious curve (good — the straight-plane assumption isn’t visibly wrong), but the spread widens at higher fitted values — the model misses by more in high-violence areas
That fanning (heteroscedasticity) is common with rate outcomes. It doesn’t bias the coefficients, but it makes the SEs less trustworthy at the extremes — worth a sentence when you report
A curve in this plot would be worse news: it would say the model’s shape is wrong, not just its noise

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Multicollinearity: When Predictors Tell the Same Story
text:
Multicollinearity: When Predictors Tell the Same Story
If two predictors move in near-lockstep, the model can’t tell whose coefficient the shared variance belongs to — estimates get wobbly and standard errors balloon.

VIF (variance inflation factor, from the car package) measures how redundant each predictor is with all the others.
Common rules of thumb: VIF > 5 — pay attention; VIF > 10 — you have a problem.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
VIF on Our Model

vif(chi_m2)

unemployment_rate        pct_vacant 
         1.807177          1.807177 



~1.8: unemployment and vacancy are correlated (r ≈ 0.67), but each still carries plenty of its own information
If VIF were high: drop one predictor, combine them into an index, or accept wide intervals — you cannot p-value your way out

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Two Traditions, One Formula








Approach
What it estimates
The 95% statement




Frequentist
Point estimates and confidence intervals
“If we repeated this study many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true β.”


Bayesian
A full posterior distribution for each β
“Given the data and priors, there’s a 95% probability β lies in this range.”




Same formula, same data — but the Bayesian statement is the one everyone wants to make (remember Session 5’s forbidden sentence? Here it’s allowed).

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Fitting It: brm()
Identical formula, Bayesian machinery — the same brms workflow you’ve run since ANOVA week:

chi_bayes <- brm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
                 data = areas,
                 chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


fixef(chi_bayes) |> round(2)

                  Estimate Est.Error   Q2.5 Q97.5
Intercept            -9.25      2.42 -13.93 -4.68
unemployment_rate     2.12      0.27   1.58  2.64
pct_vacant            1.92      0.29   1.36  2.48



Posterior means land almost exactly on the least-squares estimates — with brms’s default priors (flat on the slopes, weakly informative on the intercept and spread) and decent n, they should. (Full summary(), with its convergence checks, in today’s lab.)



The Session 10 rule travels: defaults are fine, but say which prior you used. One sentence in your methods — “brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705” — covers it.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Posteriors, Seen

mcmc_areas(chi_bayes, pars = c("b_unemployment_rate", "b_pct_vacant"),
           prob = 0.95) +
  labs(title = "Posterior distributions: predictors of violent-crime rate",
       subtitle = "Shaded = central 95% credible interval — both sit clear of zero")

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Saying It in Each Tradition
Frequentist:

“Holding vacancy constant, each percentage point of unemployment was associated with 2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents (b = 2.12, 95% CI [1.6, 2.6], p < .001).”

Bayesian:

“Given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the unemployment coefficient lies between 1.6 and 2.6 — zero is not a credible value.”

Both are area-level, adjusted associations — neither sentence licenses “unemployment causes violence.”

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Your Turn (5 minutes, with a neighbor)
text:
Your Turn (5 minutes, with a neighbor)
The fitted model:
\[\widehat{\text{violent rate}} = -9.3 + 2.12\,(\text{unemployment}) + 1.94\,(\text{vacancy})\]

Predict the rate for an area with 10% unemployment, 10% vacancy — then 23% and 25% (roughly Englewood). Which prediction does the residual plot say to trust more?
Write one defensible sentence interpreting the vacancy coefficient. Swap and audit: does it say holding unemployment constant? Any smuggled causal verbs (“drives,” “increases”)? Fix what you catch.

text:
Course Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Identify the role of statistics in criminology and criminal justice research.
Distinguish between different types of data and levels of measurement.
Import, clean, transform, and visualize real data in R using modern (tidyverse) tools.
Apply descriptive statistics to summarize and interpret data.
Explain the concepts of probability and distributions as they relate to criminological data.
Conduct and interpret basic statistical tests — from both frequentist and Bayesian perspectives — including t-tests, ANOVA, correlation, and regression.
Critically evaluate statistical claims in criminal justice policy and research.
Effectively communicate statistical findings in both written and visual formats.

Consider the following (simulated data, courtesy of an approach by Steven Miller): a simple linear regression of a student’s final grade on percentage of classes attended suggests an increase of one percent in attendance leads to an estimated increase of 0.704 in the final grade. One missed class is roughly a five-percent decrease in semester attendance — an estimated decrease of 3.52 in the overall grade. The effect is precise (t = 20.37) and the likelihood of no actual relationship is almost zero (R² = 0.342).

title: Session 2 · Descriptive Statistics & EDA
text:
📽️ Slides: Descriptive Statistics · 🧪 Lab 2: First Plots with ggplot2 · 📝 Homework 2 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 1 handed you the raw material — variables and their levels of measurement — and swirl got your fingers moving in R. This week you start actually describing data: where a distribution centers, how much it spreads, and what shapes distributions take (including the normal and the Poisson, which turn out to be everywhere in criminal justice). It’s also the week the course’s two threads officially launch: statistics in lecture and homework, data wrangling in lab, beginning with your first real ggplots. Every later topic — probability, inference, regression — rests on being able to describe a distribution honestly, so this vocabulary never leaves.

title: Session 2 · Descriptive Statistics & EDA
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

define in your own words: mean, median, mode, variance, and standard deviation — and say when the mean misleads
compute and interpret measures of center and spread in R
recognize a distribution’s shape from a histogram — normal, skewed, or Poisson-like counts — and say why shape matters for what comes next
build a histogram, bar chart, and boxplot with ggplot2

title: Session 4 · Sampling Distributions
text:
📽️ Slides: Sampling Distributions · 🧪 Lab 4: Tidy Data — Pivoting Longer and Wider · 📝 Homework 4 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 3 gave you the rules single random events follow; this week zooms out to what happens when sampling repeats. Draw a thousand samples and the sample means themselves form a distribution — with a predictable shape, a predictable center, and a width you can compute (the standard error). Nothing gets derived: it’s all live simulation, watching the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem appear on screen, including with 30,000 real Chicago incidents. This is the engine under every inference in the rest of the course — Session 5 cashes it in for confidence intervals.

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
📽️ Slides: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian · 🧪 Lab 6: Joining Data · 📝 Homework 6 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
This is the signature week of the course: the same research question answered by both of statistics’ great traditions, side by side — the reason we use the Stanton book at all. Session 5’s confidence intervals grow into the Null Hypothesis Significance Test (fine print included), and then Session 3’s Bayes’ theorem returns — pointed at hypotheses instead of diagnoses, answering the question you probably meant to ask. Every method from here to the end of the course runs in both traditions, so this week’s vocabulary is permanent.

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

run t.test() and ttestBF() on the same question, and state correctly what each output licenses you to claim
explain in plain language what a p-value is — and name the things it is not
read a Bayes factor and a posterior distribution, and report a credible interval honestly
join related tables with left_join(), inner_join(), and anti_join(), checking keys and missing values first

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Before class

Read: Stanton Ch. 5 (Bayesian & Frequentist Hypothesis Testing)
Read: Mourtgos, S. M. (2023). “Bayesian Inference in Criminological Research.” Police Forum, 32(1), 7–16 — PDF posted on Canvas. Yes, I assigned my own article; consider it a preview of where your instructor’s sympathies lie, and feel free to argue with it in class
Read: R4DS Ch. 19 — Joins; skim Ch. 18 — Missing values — plus the exercises assigned in Session 5
Install the Bayesian engine before class so we can use it together: install.packages("BayesFactor")

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
In class
This week’s two threads: hypothesis testing in both traditions (lecture + homework) · joins (lab).

From Session 5’s confidence intervals to the Null Hypothesis Significance Test: bootstrap logic, the null, the verdict machine — and an animation of what the p-value is actually doing
What a p-value is, and the long list of things it is not
The fine print: NHST never scores the alternative hypothesis, and rarely checks the distribution it assumes
Bayes’ theorem, recapped from Session 3 — and the new insight: the p-value lives entirely in the likelihood, and never becomes P(H₀ | data); the two traditions side by side
Optional self-study appendix (end of the deck): why Bayes was long impractical (the intractable denominator) and how MCMC solved it, watched live
Both traditions on our real Chicago question — t.test() says significant, ttestBF() mildly favors the null, the posterior says the difference is almost surely real and almost surely trivial. Sorting out that collision (effect sizes!) is the heart of the week
The recidivism trial: p = 0.20 vs. a 91% posterior probability the program works — same data, different questions
Sample size pathologies, animated: p-values dive below .05 for trivial effects as n grows; posteriors just sharpen around the truth
Lab 6: joining the two Chicago files — left_join(), inner_join(), anti_join(), key checks, and the missing-values discipline (lab page)

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces today’s live demos step by step.

title: Session 8 · Comparing Three or More Groups
text:
📽️ Slides: Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments · 🧪 Lab 8: ANOVA — Three Classrooms, Then Real Crashes · 📝 Homework 8 + Project Checkpoint 1 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 6 compared two group means; this week asks the question real research runs into constantly — what if there are three groups, or six? A pile of t-tests backfires (the false alarms compound), so ANOVA asks one omnibus question instead, built from two kinds of variance you already understand from Session 4’s sampling distributions.
Two honest notes about what this session is really for. You will rarely see ANOVA reported as a final model in criminal justice research — that world runs on regression — so we treat aov() and Tukey at the level you actually need them: reading the output you’ll meet in older literature and program evaluations, and understanding that ANOVA is a regression with one categorical predictor (we prove it in class with a single line of code). What you’ll keep from today is the other half: the brms + emmeans workflow, which you will run again in Sessions 10, 11, 12, and your final project. It’s also the week your project turns graded — Checkpoint 1 rides along with Homework 8 — and Session 9 is the midterm.

title: Session 8 · Comparing Three or More Groups
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

explain what the F-ratio compares: between-group signal against within-group noise
read a one-way ANOVA table and a Tukey output without needing to reproduce either by hand
run the brm() + emmeans() + pairs() workflow, and state the interval rule (crosses 0 → not credible)
explain why ANOVA is a regression with one categorical predictor, and what that buys you in Session 11
report direction and magnitude every time, including when a pair shows no credible difference

title: Session 8 · Comparing Three or More Groups
text:
Before class

Read: Stanton Ch. 6 (Comparing Groups and Analyzing Experiments)
Install two new packages before class: install.packages(c("emmeans", "brms")). brms compiles models on your machine, so the install can take a while and the first model of a session pauses at “Compiling Stan program…” — both are normal. If the install errors, email me the message before class.
Bring your laptop and make sure your final-project dataset (selected in Session 7) opens on it — Homework 8 contains your first project checkpoint
No new R4DS reading — the wrangling thread is complete

title: Session 8 · Comparing Three or More Groups
text:
In class

Why comparing 3+ group means with a pile of t-tests backfires (false-alarm rates compound), and how ANOVA asks one omnibus question instead
The core idea: within-group variance (noise) vs. between-group variance (signal), built by hand on three small classrooms
Stanton’s rain example: three random groups from the same 70 cities, where the null is true by construction — and why between-group variance collapses when nothing differs (Session 4’s sampling distributions, cashed in again)
Where ANOVA actually lives: standard in experiments, rare as a final model in CJ journals — so we learn it as a reading skill and a conceptual bridge, not as a technique to publish
The F-ratio and the F distribution; aov() and how its table is just our two variances with the group size baked into the signal
A significant F only says something differs — Tukey’s HSD finds which pairs, with the family-wise false-alarm rate held at 5%
The Bayesian version: brm() with the same formula, then emmeans() for posterior group means and pairs() for differences — the interval-crossing-zero reading. This is the workflow you keep: it returns in Sessions 10, 11, 12, and your final project
“It was regression all along”: anova(lm(hour ~ crime_category)) returns the identical F and p-value as aov() — the bridge to Session 11
Real-data thread: does mean incident hour differ across Chicago’s Violent / Property / Other categories? Both traditions say yes for every pair — by 15 to 41 minutes. Detectable ≠ dramatic, now with three groups.
Lab 8: the full workflow yourself — the classrooms, then injuries by crash cause in the Alaska data (including one pair with no credible difference, so you practice saying that out loud)

title: Session 10 · Measures of Association: Correlation
text:
📽️ Slides: Associations Between Variables — Correlation · 🧪 Lab 10: Correlation — Chicago Areas, Then a Null Worth Reporting · 📝 Homework 10 + Project Checkpoint 2 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Before the midterm, every test had the same shape: a categorical grouping variable and a numeric outcome. The second half of the course drops the groups — this week both variables are numeric, and the question becomes whether two measures move together. Covariance grows into Pearson’s r, inference runs in both traditions, and the real-data thread climbs to Chicago’s 77 community areas — which forces the semester’s standing warning, the ecological fallacy, out into the open. Correlation is the doorway to regression in Sessions 11–12, where your final project lives; Checkpoint 2 computes the first associations in your own data.

title: Session 10 · Measures of Association: Correlation
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

interpret r’s sign and size — and explain why you always plot before you trust it (Anscombe’s quartet is the cautionary tale)
test a correlation in both traditions: cor.test(), then the correlation package’s Bayesian output (posterior, credible interval, Bayes factor)
explain the ecological fallacy in one sentence, and catch a claim that commits it
report a null association honestly, letting the Bayes factor say “there’s nothing here”

text:
Before class

Bring your laptop and your final-project dataset — Homework 10 contains Project Checkpoint 2, which computes the first associations in your data

title: Session 10 · Measures of Association: Correlation
text:
In class

A new kind of question: both variables numeric, no groups — do two measures move together? (The doorway to regression in Sessions 11–12.)
Association vs. causation: ice cream and violent crime, and the lurking third variable
Covariance — the right idea, glued to its units — and Pearson’s r, the rescaled version that always lands between −1 and +1
What r cannot see: Anscombe’s quartet (four datasets, identical r, wildly different shapes), curved relationships, and one outlier manufacturing a correlation out of noise — plus Spearman’s rho, the rank-based backup
Real-data thread moves to the anchor dataset’s second level (codebook): Chicago’s 77 community areas. Unemployment tracks violent-crime rates at r = 0.84; median age gives a genuine zero; income shows why Pearson and Spearman can disagree
The ecological fallacy, named and practiced: area-level associations license no claims about individuals — the codebook has been promising this conversation all semester
Inference on r, both traditions: cor.test() (t on n − 2 df, CI) and the correlation package — correlation matrices with Holm-adjusted p-values, then bayesian = TRUE for posterior medians, credible intervals, pd, and Bayes factors, including what the "medium" vs. "wide" prior actually changes
Lab 10: the full workflow yourself — Chicago areas, then the Lab 3 neighborhoods (real associations) and the Lab 6 officers, where the honest answer is a null and the Bayes factor lets you say so

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces today’s live demos step by step.

title: Session 12 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
📽️ Slides: Logistic Regression · 🧪 Lab 12: Logistic Regression — Chicago Neighborhoods, Then Alaska Nights · 📝 Homework 12 + Project Checkpoint 4 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Every model so far predicted a number; this week the outcome is yes or no — arrest or not, reoffend or desist — which is the form most criminal-justice questions actually take. A straight line can’t live on a 0/1 outcome, so probability climbs the ladder to odds and log-odds, and lm() becomes glm(family = binomial). It’s also the week the course pays off its opening promise: the Session 1 bank-robbery model you couldn’t read gets re-fit and finally read, line by line. This is the last session of new statistical content — the toolbox is complete, and Checkpoint 4 (the final one) fits your actual project model.

title: Session 12 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

explain why lm() fails on a 0/1 outcome, and how the probability → odds → log-odds ladder fixes it
fit a logistic regression in both traditions: glm(family = binomial) and brm(family = bernoulli())
translate coefficients into odds ratios and predicted probabilities — and keep the two straight
say logistic results in plain language a police chief could act on, without confusing odds with probability

title: Session 12 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes

title: Session 12 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
In class

Why criminal justice runs on binary outcomes (arrest, failure to appear, re-arrest, intoxicated or not) — and why lm() predicts impossible probabilities when you feed it one
Closing the loop on Session 1: the bank-robbery case study that opened the course was a logistic regression — we re-fit the exact model and finally read its table (coefficients are log-odds; exp() them into odds ratios; West Zone’s odds ratio is why the cars went west)
The ladder: probability → odds → log-odds, and why a straight line can only live on the last rung
glm(family = binomial) — one argument away from lm() — and the two interpretation moves: odds ratios for effects, predicted probabilities for cases
The 3D logistic surface: Session 11’s flat plane, bent into an S-shaped probability sheet — built live from predict() on a 40 × 40 grid, plus the recorded guided tour
The Bayesian version: brm(family = bernoulli()) with the Session 8 settings, posterior odds ratios, and the credible-interval sentence you’re allowed to say
Real-data thread: which Chicago community areas are high-violence? Unemployment (OR ≈ 1.45 per point) and vacant housing (OR ≈ 1.33 per point) both raise the odds; predicted probabilities run from ~3% (Forest Glen) to over 99% (West Garfield Park). Associations, not causes — and we say so.
Lab 12: the whole workflow yourself — Chicago walkthrough, then intoxicated-crash odds in the Alaska data with lubridate-built night/weekend flags, plus odds-ratio translation drills
Code clinic (final half hour): open floor for your project — live debugging, interpretation workshopping, and the presentation order draw. Bring a runnable draft and your two hardest problems — Checkpoint 4 is due the following Sunday, so the clinic is where you get unstuck before you finish it.
